catalogFullDescription:
The level of education required for success in the accounting profession has increased significantly. Graduate education not only facilitates entry into the profession but also enhances career progress and job mobility. The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, National Association of State Boards of Accountancy, Utah Association of CPAs, and many other professional organizations strongly endorse graduate accounting education. The School of Accounting at the David Eccles School of Business offers the Master of Accounting (MAcc) degree to develop highly qualified professionals for leadership positions in the accounting profession and to encourage education for judgement beyond a technical accounting degree.

Our MAcc program provides students with in-depth accounting knowledge, a reputation for sound judgment and the relevant, transferable skills they need to succeed in today's multidisciplinary world. The MAcc prepares students for careers in public and/or corporate accounting, tax auditing and advising, non-profit, government accounting, and financial reporting.

Our flexible hybrid schedule allows you to complete the program in as little as one year or over multiple semesters while working full-time. At every pace, the MAcc builds upon a solid foundation of accounting principles learned during a bachelor of accounting program.

Throughout the program, the School of Business places a strong emphasis on analytical thinking, communication skills and professionalism. Our nationally-ranked faculty-including two former academic fellows at the SEC-combines pioneering research and dynamic instruction to engage students in helping to shape the future of accounting. By learning the language of business, our students graduate with a versatile skill set that translates into high quality job placement with opportunity for advancement. In fact, over the past decade an average of 95-98% of our MAcc students have secured employment within three months of graduation.

catalogFullDescription:
Periodontics is designed for students who are considering periodontics as a full-time career or as an adjunct to clinical practice. The pathway will provide a structured curriculum around periodontics principles and may provide students with opportunities to serve as peer teachers. The Pathways to Periodontology course is designed for not only those applying to periodontal residencies, but any dental student who desires greater knowledge in periodontal procedures and dental implant surgery.

Students will have the opportunity to:

  1. Develop a deeper understanding of periodontal etiology and pathogenesis

  2. Understand the 2017 Classification of Periodontal and Per-implant Diseases and Conditions

  3. Gain a greater understanding of the relationship of periodontal inflammation and systemic conditions

  4. Provide basic periodontal surgeries that may include gingival graft, periodontal flap surgery and regenerative periodontal surgery

  5. Provide site preparation surgery for the future placement of dental implants

  6. Provide the placement of 1-3 dental implants

catalogFullDescription:
The Certificate in Advanced General Dentistry in Endodontics program is designed to allow dental students interested in endodontics the opportunity to explore the field of endodontics at a deeper level than allowed in the dental school curriculum. This program will cover more advanced topics such as pain, retreatment, endodontic surgery, regenerative endodontics, vital pulp therapy, procedural misadventures, and practice management.

The course structure will be mostly in-person seminars and discussions. Students will prepare case portfolios and present cases to each other and discussing what went well, what could be improved, and what they learned from the case. Students will have the opportunity to practice more advanced procedures in the simulation lab such as accessing through crowned teeth, removing gutta percha from previously treated teeth, and locating calcified canals. Students will be exposed to working under the dental operating microscope and be expected to use it in the clinic. Students in this course will have to complete either an independent research project or a critically appraised topic report. These projects will be presented at the annual student research symposium and if elected at a local, state, or national meeting.

Students will also learn to critically evaluate literature. They will learn about materials and methods along with statistical analysis to prepare them as future lifelong learners.

learningOutcomes.name: Practice more advanced endodontic procedures, as determined by the AAE case difficulty form, in the simulation clinic. They will also apply this knowledge in the clinic with cases approved by the endodontic section head.
learningOutcomes.assessment: DENT 7651, DENT 7562, DENT 7563, DENT 7564, DENT 7565
learningOutcomes.justification:
a. Using the AAE Case Difficulty Form students will select cases that fall within the moderate to high difficulty level of extracted teeth and will perform root canal treatment in a typodont in the simulation clinic.

b. Once a student has had experience in the simulation clinic on these moderate to high difficulty cases in the simulation lab, the endodontic section head will select specific cases to be completed in the patient clinic.

c. Grading rubrics are the same in the simulation clinic as in the patient clinic.

learningOutcomes.name: Critically assess their own endodontic treatment and present this information to others in the program.
learningOutcomes.assessment: DENT 7651, DENT 7562, DENT 7563, DENT 7564, DENT 7565
learningOutcomes.justification:
a. Using the rubric from the patient clinic, the student will self-assess their work in the simulation clinic as well as cases in the patient clinic.

b. Students will create a portfolio of cases to present to their peers

learningOutcomes.name: Critically evaluate current and classic literature
learningOutcomes.assessment: DENT 7651, DENT 7562, DENT 7563, DENT 7564, DENT 7565
learningOutcomes.justification:
a. Students will read literature chosen by the course director and will discuss each article in a small group.

b. Students must critique the article’s material and methods and statistical analysis to determine if the conclusion and discussion are appropriate for the study presented.

c. Students are assessed using a presentation rubric.

learningOutcomes.name: Design and conduct an independent research project to be presented at the annual student research symposium
learningOutcomes.assessment: DENT 7651, DENT 7562, DENT 7563, DENT 7564, DENT 7565, DENT 7880
learningOutcomes.justification:
a. Students are responsible for developing their own research project that can be completed within 1-2 semesters, including a literature review, proposal, IRB approval, materials and methods, statistical analysis, data collection, and discussion.

b. Students will create a poster presenting their research results and present this poster at the UUSOD Research Day and possibly the Utah Dental Association annual meeting.

learningOutcomes.name: Debate current issues in endodontics and defend their position with peer-reviewed literature. Learning Outcomes Assessment
learningOutcomes.assessment: DENT 7651, DENT 7562, DENT 7563, DENT 7564, DENT 7565
learningOutcomes.justification:
a. In a small group discussion, students will be given a topic and asked to pick a position to debate. They must use literature to defend their position.

b. A debate rubric will be used to assess these sessions.

catalogDisplayName: Advanced General Dentistry in Oral Research
catalogFullDescription: Research in Oral Health and Foundational Sciences is designed for students who are considering dental research as a full-time career or as an adjunct to clinical practice. The Oral Research Pathway is designed to provide the student with the essential steps in the development of a research project. The student will be guided through selection of a research mentor, draft of research proposal, IRB submission and approval process, active research, and completion of the research project with presentation and/or publication. This course will serve to implement research activities at the University of Utah School of Dentistry with the main goal of providing research experience to dental students by establishing both a multi-faculty network and a coordinated set of procedures and expectations, as detailed below. The course consists of approximately one year of work in a research lab as well as attendance to lectures (research ethics, critical thinking, and abstract/poster guidelines). After the research project is completed, the student will be required to present their work at the University of Utah Student Research Day, at national scientific conference or in another appropriate venue, by approval of the faculty advisor and course director.

catalogDisplayName: Advanced General Dentistry in Oral and Maxillofacial Radiology
catalogFullDescription: Integrated Oral Radiology is designed for students who are considering oral radiology as a full-time career or as an adjunct to general practice. Pathways of Integrated Oral Radiology will allow the student interested in advancing their knowledge of oral radiology, especially 3D digital imaging, as well as its integration with existing and emerging digital technologies. Opportunities will be provided to study and engage in activities that will lead to a better working knowledge of how to utilize imaging technology to enhance all areas of dental practice. The opportunity to gain experience in acquiring, interpreting, and applying CBCT imaging will be at the heart of this pathway. Exposure to medical imaging modalities will also be part of this pathway. To develop experience integrating CBCT imaging with intraoral scanning, milling and 3D printing to make surgical guides, occlusal guards, milled abutments, etc. is a goal of this pathway. D3 and D4 participants in this pathway will have an opportunity to help in the spring semester basic radiology lab as teaching assistants. Possible opportunities to be involved with imaging related clinical research exist for those interested.

catalogDisplayName: Advanced General Dentistry in Public Health Dentistry
catalogFullDescription: Public Health Dentistry is designed for students who are considering dental education as a full-time career or as an adjunct to clinical practice. The Pathways in Public Health Dentistry Course is intended to introduce the student to the transitional concept Clinical Prevention and Population Health as it relates to the community as a whole rather than individual patient care. Understanding community oral health needs and operations is key to this dental specialty. This course will provide understanding of Clinical Prevention and Population Health, Oral Health Epidemiology, and Dental Public Health Policy and Advocacy. Additionally, students will receive increased awareness and understanding of Statistical Methods for Oral Health Research, Oral Health Program Planning and Evaluation, and Applied Research Methods in Qualitative, Quantitative, and Mixed Research Methods. At completion of the pathway course, students will have developed and implemented an Applied Policy in Oral Health and created a presentation with a portfolio of Community Dentistry Project Work.

catalogDisplayName: Advanced General Dentistry in Temporomandibular Dysfunction and Sleep Dentistry
catalogFullDescription: Temporomandibular Dysfunction and Sleep Dentistry is designed for students who desire to increase understanding of key concepts and competencies in patient care for temporomandibular disorders (TMD) and dental sleep medicine (DSM) in all areas of etiology, history, examination, diagnosis, and treatment. Student will receive an in-depth review of the healthy masticatory system with emphasis on the functional stability of masticatory muscles and temporomandibular joints examining the dysfunctional states of the masticatory system and the associated etiologies including Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) and concepts of Dental Sleep Medicine (DSM). Students will learn how to collect patient history, exam, diagnosis, and treatment methods via clinical observation, assisting and providing clinical experience in TMD and DSM. Students will take an active part in clinic attending and supervision of other students who are providing patient care for TMD and DSM patients. Their role will be to teach and guide clinical functions rendered by other students.

customFields.ztYeO:
This proposal describes the creation of an on-campus Graduate Certificate in Aerospace Engineering (AEGC), which will be offered and administered by the Department of Mechanical Engineering (ME).  Currently, there is a proposal to start a Master’s of Science in Aerospace Engineering (MSAE) that will hopefully be approved for Fall 2025. The AEGC represents about half of the MSAE, and thus the AEGC is considered a sackable certificate.

 The idea of a stackable certificate toward a graduate degree is a popular concept.  About halfway through an MSAE degree, students will be able to earn the AEGC .  These stackable certificates may help with recruitment toward the MSAE as students can commit less time and still achieve a credential from the U.  Many students that finish a stackable certificate decide to continue on for the MS degree.  Successfully completing a AEGC does not guarantee admission into the MSAE degree. Students still need to apply for the MSAE degree and be admitted by both the department and the Graduate School.

An additional benefit of stackable certificates is that students not pursuing an MSAE can still earn a AEGC with their degree.  This could be a likely path for students pursuing a Master of Science in Systems Engineering or Master of Engineering Management.  Students from either program could complete the AEGC without taking any additional courses. 

 The MSAE proposal expects 20-30 students to pursue it every year.  Every MSAE student will qualify for a AEGC .  The department expects to award about 5 additional certificates to students pursuing other graduate degrees or for students just earning the AEGC .  Thus, the department expects over 20 certificates to be awarded each year.

 Finally, ME will not hire any faculty or advisors to offer this certificate.  There is not a need to include an advertising budget as all marketing materials will list both the MSAE and the AEGC .  There is some additional advising burden to support a certificate; however, this effort is minimal and should constitute less than a week of work by the graduate advising staff in ME.  With almost zero cost, ME can offer the AEGC to students at the university. Thus, ME decided to propose the AEGC to benefit the U’s students.
customFields.yVI7x:
The plan is for the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs to advise all students. The main Aerospace Engineering pages will also provide detailed advising information for the AEGC .  Through these two sources, students should have quality advising.

One of the department's three full-time graduate advisors is assigned part-time to help with both the AEGC and AEMS students.  If the program continues to grow, more individuals will be hired to assist with the workload.  Since the AEGC costs almost nothing, the program should have sufficient funds to provide quality advising to all students regardless of how much growth this program experiences.

customFields.qeWTW:
The USHE proposal to start an AEMS degree estimates that the program will have over 20 students enrolled in this program.  Since almost every student earning the AEMS will also be awarded an AEGC, the demand for this certificate will be substantial.  Below we describe some general categories of students that will be earning this certificate.

 The most popular emphasis in the MEENBS degree is the Aerospace emphasis.  It is believed that many of these students will stay for the AES degree.  Some will enroll directly, others will try to pursue the degree through a concurrent MEENBS/AEMS pathway. (A proposal for this pathway will hopefully be approved for August 2025.)  Thus, the department expects about 5 students will finish the MEENBS and continue immediately on to the AEMS, which will allow them to earn the AEGC .

 The MSAE has a thesis option.  It is reasonable to expect that each aerospace faculty member will have a graduate student pursuing the MSAE degree.  This is another five to ten students that would be earning a AEGC . 

 For 20 years, ME has run a remote program with Northrop Grumman.  When new degrees have become available, Northrop Grumman’s enrollment typically grows by about 5 students.  Thus, 5 additionally students are expected to earn a AEGC degree through this remote program.

Many people graduate and work for a few years and then realize that their careers would progress faster with graduate education.  The program anticipates that each year 5-10 people will return to school to pursue either just a AEGC or an AEMS.

Finally, the Systems Engineering in Utah has extremely close ties to the aerospace industry.  The MSSE program began admitting students in Fall 24.  There are already almost 20 students enrolled in this program.  The department believes that some students will pursue the MSSE with a AEGC, which can be done with no additional courses by carefully selecting MSSE elective courses.  This should result in an additional 5 students earning the certificate each year.

 In summary, the program expects 20-30 students will earn a AEGC each year.
customFields.wFFLu:
The belief is that the U and USHE will approve the Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering.  The concept of a stackable graduate certificate has been encouraged by these groups.  Stackable certificates typically make a lot of sense at the graduate level.  The cost to offer them is negligible, and the U’s students benefit by earning an additional credential. 

 The impact upon other USHE institutions is minimal.  USU offers a Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering, but it does not offer a graduate certificate.  Thus, this will be the first AEGC in the state.
customFields.71aB1:
There is no recurrent cost to implement this program.  The Director of the Aerospace Engineering  Programs is also in charge of the AEGC .  Advising and awarding the AEGC will be part of the department’s Graduate Advisor’s and the Director’s duties. 

The department provides one month of summary salary for the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs for the additional work running, advising and assessing both the AEMS and the AEGC. Of the three full-time graduate advisors in the department, one is assigned part-time to help support both the AEMS and AEGC. The additional funding for this work is part of the AEMS proposal, and the AEGC does not need any additional funds as it is part of the assigned duties for both individuals. As the program grows, additional funds could hire an additional graduate advisor or move the current graduate advisor to full-time support for the AEMS and AEGC.

 Since the Department of Mechanical Engineering already is offering all of the core courses for the MSAE, no new courses need to be created or offered for students to earn the AEGC .  Thus, there is a negligible cost to implement and administer the AEGC .

 Finally, the AEGC benefits the department as it may help with recruiting students into the MSAE.  Students pursuing the AEMS or other degrees will be able to demonstrate on their transcript knowledge of Aerospace Engineering prior to graduation.  Thus, the AEGC is essentially a zero cost that benefits all stakeholders.

customFields.afMfd:
Students will gain many student learning outcomes by pursuing the AEGC. The student learning outcomes will be partially based upon the student's chosen coursework. Of these many student learning outcomes, the AEGC will assess its effectiveness based upon the number of yearly graduates, job placement, starting salaries, and the following assessed student learning outcomes.  When and where these outcomes will be assessed is contained in the next section.

1.   Identify and apply thermodynamic and fluids principles and theories for aerospace engineering.

2. Identify and apply materials and structures for aerospace applications.

3. Identify and apply dynamics for aerospace applications.

4. Identify and apply systems principles for aerospace applications.

5. Recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in aerospace engineering.

6. An ability to acquire and apply new knowledge using appropriate learning strategies.

These outcomes will be assessed through courses used to satisfy the requirements of the AEGC.

Program Assessment

For anything that is assessed through coursework, having 90% of students that earn the equivalent of a B or better on the assessed homework, case study, project, test or entire class will be sufficient to show acceptable student learning outcomes for the program. The instructor is required to determine a suitable assessment for the student learning outcome assigned to the class. Additionally, through a report the faculty will report the results of the assessment to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs.

The department’s required AEGC Graduation Form also has questions related to student learning outcomes. This form is filled out during the student’s AEGC awarding semester. Having 95% of students meet the equivalent of a “B” or better on the questions from this form indicates acceptable student learning outcomes for the program.

Annually, the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs will convene at least 3 faculty teaching core topics.  These individuals will evaluate all of the assessment data, including summaries of the past 6 years of data.  The individuals will provide recommendations, whether or not existing problems have been resolved, and the general trend of the student learning in the program.

At the conclusion of this assessment meeting, the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs is responsible to write an annual report summarizing the discussions and recommendations from the meeting.  It is vitally important that any issues are tracked from year to year.  Any items that are below the program assessment levels need to tracked for several years in the reports.  This will allow the program to track its performance through years and to determine the impact of program changes.

The Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs is also responsible to convey any suggestions or recommendations from the annual assessment meeting to the relevant faculty.  If suggestions relate to the curriculum, the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs will be responsible to develop proposals to change/modify the curriculum or courses.  Such proposals will need to follow the typical university procedures, which include departmental, college and Faculty Senate approvals.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply thermodynamic and fluids principles and theories for aerospace engineering.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed in the thermodynamics and fluid core requirement. Students must take either ME EN 6710 Aerodynamics or ME EN 6830 Aerospace Propulsion. The Aerodynmics class covers the theories, principles and mathematical models of aerodynamics. Covered topics include: flow around bodies, inviscid flow, airfoil theory, lift, drag, boundary layers, and many other topics. The Aerospace Propulsion class covers the theories, principles and models of propulsion. Covered topics include: compressible flow, combustion, turbojets, rocket propulsion systems, liquid engines and many other topics.  These topics are fundamental aerospace thermodynamics or fluid principles and theories.  Both of these classes are dedicated entirely to this learning outcome.  As a result, a student earning a B or better shows an understanding and application of thermodynamic and fluids principles and theories for aerospace engineering.  Since every graduating students must take this course and earn a B or better in one of these two courses, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.  The instructors are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.
learningOutcomes.justification: Either ME EN 6710 Aerodynamics or ME EN 6830 Aerospace Propulsion

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply materials and structures for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core Solid Mechanics courses.  Students must take either ME EN 6510 Applied Finite Element Analysis or ME EN 7530 Fracture and Fatigue.  Both classes focus on materials and their strength and performance.  This is a vital skill for aerospace engineers as the material chosen must satisfy strict requirements and has a massive impact upon safety and performance.   A student earning a B or better in one of these two courses shows a fundamental mastery of materials and structures.  Since every graduating students must take one of these courses and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome. The instructors are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.
learningOutcomes.justification: Either ME EN 6510 Applied Finite Element Analysis or ME EN 7530 Fracture and Fatigue

learningOutcomes.name: 3.   Identify and apply dynamics for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core Dynamics courses.  Students must take one course of ME EN 6410 Intermediate Dynamics, ME EN 6960 Orbital Mechanics, or ME EN 6960 Flight Dynamics.  All classes focus on dynamics and provide fundamental theory, models, physical interpretations, and applications of dynamic systems.  This knowledge is vital to understand how to build and operate aerospace products that can function in atmospheric flights or space missions involving complex environments, various mission requirements, and other highly dynamic conditions.      Both of these classes are dedicated entirely to this learning outcome.  A student earning a B or better in any of these classes shows a fundamental mastery of dynamics.  Since every graduating students must take one of these courses and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome. The instructors are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.
learningOutcomes.justification: Either ME EN 6410 Intermediate Dynamics, ME EN 6960 Orbital Mechanics, or ME EN 6960 Flight Dynamics.

learningOutcomes.name: 4.   Identify and apply systems principles for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core systems area where the students must take SIME 6800 Aerospace Systems and Ethics course.  This course provides a detailed introduction to systems engineering with a focus on aerospace.  The vast majority of failures in aerospace are a result of some unforeseen complication involving the interaction of computers, mechanical systems and humans. This class will help students identify these issues throughout their careers and help them avoid some horrendous mistakes. The entire SIME 6800 class is not dedicated to systems principles.  As such, the instructor will need to assign homeworks, projects, or exams that allow students to demonstrate their ability to master this learning outcome.  The instructor will prepare a report describing how this learning outcome was assessed and the percent of students earning the equivalent of a “B” on the assessed works.  This report will go to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.
learningOutcomes.justification: SIME 6800

learningOutcomes.name: 5.	Recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in aerospace engineering.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core systems area where the students must take SIME 6800 Aerospace Systems and Ethics course.  This course provides an introduction to ethics in aerospace, along with an introduction to the complexities of the systems in aerospace. The faculty in the Department of Mechanical Engineering believe that teaching ethics in Aerospace Engineering requires a substantial amount of technical and engineering knowledge.  Being able to explain to students how the incorrect analysis occurred, why the testing in a manufacturing plant failed to detect an error, why the systems failed to seamlessly integrate are vital for future students to create reliable and safe aerospace products.  Thus, the faculty believe that a very technical course (similar to SIME 6800) is the best way to instruct MSAE students regarding the ethics in Aerospace Engineering. The entire SIME 6800 class is not dedicated to ethics.  As such, the instructor will need to assign homeworks, projects, or exams that allow students to demonstrate their ability to master this learning outcome.  The instructor will prepare a report describing how this learning outcome was assessed and the percent of students earning the equivalent of a “B” on the assessed works.  This report will go to the Director of Aerospace Engineering Programs along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.
learningOutcomes.justification: SIME 6800

learningOutcomes.name: 6.   An ability to acquire new knowledge using appropriate learning strategies.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This student learning outcome will be assessed through the 15 hours of aerospace engineering courses required by the AEGC.  Graduate engineering courses are intellectually challenging.  The fact that a student can take and pass five graduate courses with a sufficient grade demonstrates that the student can acquire new knowledge.  Furthermore, a student earning a passing grade demonstrates that the student must be using learning strategies that are appropriate and effective for that particular student. A student earning a B or better in all of their GCAE courses demonstrates success in this learning outcome.  Since every graduating student must take five such courses and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome. 	The instructors in all of these elective aerospace engineering classes are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome.

customFields.9VKoN:
Students pursuing a Masters of Science in Aerospace Engineering (AEMS ) degree typically have a bachelor's degree in a STEM field from an accredited US institution or a comparable institution recognized by the Ministry of Higher Education in one's home country. Applicants with degrees from other areas or nonaccredited institutions will be considered, but students may be assigned additional course work.

 Graduate degree applications will be considered holistically based upon the students' ability to have sufficient expertise to complete the AEMS .  Admitted students typically have an undergraduate GPA of 3.2 or higher, and the university requires a 3.0. Additionally, students should have taken at least one class in statics, dynamics, thermodynamics, fluid mechanics, strength of materials, and controls.  However, students with lower GPAs or lacking the requisite preliminary course knowledge, but have evidence of the student's ability to succeed are encouraged to apply.  The personal statement from such students should explain their individual circumstances and describe why the student believes that they will succeed and earn an AEMS degree. 

GRE scores are not required for admission.  However, a GRE may improve a student's ability to be evaluated for graduate research funding.

 Students that earned their bachelor's degree in a foreign country may also need to satisfy the university's English proficiency requirements.

 In addition to these requirements, all students must complete the university's graduate application process. This application process may include:

  •    Transcripts

  •    Letter(s) of recommendation

  •    Personal statement

  •    Professional resume
customFields.XwfIO:
To graduate, students must complete 30 credit hours (15 Core, 6 Aerospace Electives, 9 engineering or science electives that could be thesis hours) of approved graduate coursework as indicated on their Program of Study which must satisfy the curriculum requirements of the program. The student must have at least a 3.0 GPA and a minimum of a B- in each course. The student must earn a grade of B or better in each core course. 

Besides the coursework and grade requirements, the Graduate School states “a final exam that covers breadth and integration of material in the field is required.”  Students pursuing the AEMS will be required to pursue a capstone project and pass a capstone exam to earn the AEMS degree.

Capstone Project and Capstone Exam

The vast majority of successful aerospace engineers are able to draw knowledge and solutions from multiple areas. The purpose of the capstone project is for the students to demonstrate mastery of aerospace knowledge and integrate topics into a cohesive solution. Every student must have a capstone project and pass a capstone exam to graduate.

For students pursuing a thesis, their research is the project, and the thesis defense is the capstone exam.

At the beginning of the "graduating" semester, a coursework only student emails the Director of the AEMS .   This email contains the real-world problem the student plans to study for their capstone project.  The student proposes at least three classes from their Program of Study that will be applied to create a real-world solution.  The director will respond and offer advice or suggestions, if necessary. 

During the semester, the student will research and develop a solution to the problem that incorporates and integrates knowledge from these three courses.  Although a student can always reach out for assistance, it is anticipated that the student will demonstrate their mastery of the material and create their solution with minimal assistance.

The capstone exam is a 20-25 minute presentation where the student presents their solution.  This presentation must also discuss any ethical implications of their proposed solution.  Additionally, the presentation should discuss the student's consideration of public health, safety, welfare, and economic factors. 

Typically the Director of the AEMS acts as the examiner and represents the Supervisory Committee.  A week before the Capstone Exam, the student should email the AEMS Director their slides. This provides the ability for final feedback in case adjustments should be made. 

The Capstone Exam examiner votes to pass or fail the student and also fills out a student learning assessment form.  If the examiner votes to pass, then the supervisory committee agrees and the student passes the capstone exam.  If the examiner votes to fail, then a second capstone exam is scheduled with the remaining members of the Supervisory Committee.  If both members of the Supervisory Committee vote to pass, then the student passes the capstone exam with a vote of 2-1.  Otherwise the student has failed the capstone exam. 

The deadlines and rules for the capstone exam are identical to the defense of a master's thesis and are established by the Graduate School. Some of the rules include the maximum number of attempts, the minimum amount of time between retakes and the semester graduation deadlines.
customFields.Z6vKf: ABET is the accrediting body for engineering degrees.  However, ABET will only accredit one degree with a particular name at any university. There are 62 institutions with an accredited Aerospace Engineering degree [7].  It needs to be emphasized that ABET currently accredits 0 MS in Aerospace Engineering degrees.  To further emphasize this, Utah State University's BS Mechanical Engineering is ABET accredited, but their MS Aerospace Engineering is not.    Every program has chosen to only accredit BS degrees.  As a result of this national and international avoidance of ABET accreditation for AEMS degrees, the ME department decided to not pursue ABET accreditation for the AEMS.  If the department ever decides to pursue a BSAE, then ABET accreditation will be a primary requirement for such a program, if it were ever to exist.  However, such a plan does not currently exist.   The AEMS will be accredited through the Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities (NWCCU).  The assessment plan will still follow many of the ABET assessment methodologies as part of its accreditation with NWCCU.  The assessment will evaluate student learning outcomes and have feedback to the program so that the program can have continuous improvement. customFields.ztYeO:
This proposal is to create a Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering (AEMS) at the University of Utah. The AEMS will be offered as a coursework only degree or with a MS thesis option. Additionally, a concurrent BS in Mechanical Engineering/MS in Aerospace Engineering pathway is currently being proposed for students pursuing both degrees at the U.

 

The AEMS will be directed through the Department of Mechanical Engineering (ME).  There is substantial synergy between Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering. Many Mechanical Engineering departments teach aerospace courses and offer aerospace degrees. In fact, the students pursuing the U's BS in ME can currently earn an emphasis in Aerospace. Currently, there are over 120 students pursuing this emphasis. There is clearly substantial student demand for a specialization and additional knowledge in aerospace.

 

To help satisfy the students' interest and using the Engineering Initiative Funds offered by the Utah's Legislature, the department hired three tenure-track faculty in Aerospace in the past 2 years. Besides these recent hires, the department already had several faculty productively doing research in Aerospace Engineering. Additionally, the department has 5 faculty in Systems Engineering, which is a closely related field. Thus, the department now has a critical mass of faculty to be able to offer an AEMS degree without asking for or reallocating any sizable amount of budget.  As a result, the benefit to cost ratio of establishing this degree is incredibly high, because the cost is so low and the benefit is so high.

 

Recently, the U's Vice President of Research Office provided substantial seed money to start an Aerospace Research Hub.  Dr. Jacob Hochhalter in the Department of Mechanical Engineering is the director and leading this multidisciplinary research effort.  Establishing an AEMS with a thesis will provide graduate researchers capable of advancing research in this exciting field.  Thus, creating the AEMS is in direct alignment with a current high priority research effort at the U.

 

The amount of industry in Utah based in Aerospace is astounding. According to the Governor's Office of Economic Opportunity [1], 944 aerospace and defense companies such as Boeing, Lockheed Martin, L3Harris and Northrop Grumman along with Hill Air Force base employ over 30,000 people in Utah. To put this in perspective, almost 2% of employed Utahans are in the aerospace/defense sector, which is far greater than the 1.4% average nationally [2].  Additionally, the Department of Defense spent 2.1 billion in Utah in 2019 and 8.6 billion in 2023, which shows the rapid growth in the aerospace fields [3]. Utah's Department of Workforce Services estimates a current statewide employment of 1,141 and projected employment growing to 1,567 [4]. In June, Indeed [5] had 114 openings when searching for aerospace engineers. A direct search of Northrop Grumman's job openings in December 2024 resulted in 73 openings and this is just a single company [6].  All this evidence points to a massive need for more AEMS graduates. 

 

Training more experts in aerospace will be beneficial to the state's economy. Students earning the Master of Science in Aerospace Engineering degree will have advanced knowledge in aerospace. The graduates can then lead innovative concepts in aerospace and continue Utah's strong growth in the defense and aerospace industry.

customFields.cJsXu: The AEMS requirements are fairly straightforward.  None of the core classes have a prerequisite chain, and so scheduling is fairly straightforward.  Students may start any semester.  As a result, a flow chart is unnecessary and only the requirements for the degree are given here.
customFields.afMfd:
Students will gain many student learning outcomes by pursuing the AEMS degree. The student learning outcomes will be partially based upon the student's chosen coursework. Of these many student learning outcomes, the AEMS degree will assess its effectiveness based upon the number of yearly graduates, job placement, starting salaries, and the following assessed student learning outcomes.  Many of these outcomes are taken from ABET's suggested learning outcomes for Aerospace degrees. When and where these outcomes will be assessed is contained in the next section.

1.   Identify and apply aerodynamic principles and theories.

2.   Identify and apply propulsion principles and theories.

3.   Identify and apply materials and structures for aerospace applications.

4.   Identify and apply dynamics for aerospace applications.

5.   Identify and apply systems principles for aerospace applications.

6.   An ability to communicate effectively.

7.   Recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in aerospace engineering.

8.   An ability to acquire and apply new knowledge using appropriate learning strategies.

AEMS Program Assessment

The AEMS program assessment is based upon the assessed student learning outcomes. For anything that is assessed through coursework, having 90% of students earn a B or better course grade will be sufficient to show acceptable student learning outcomes for the program.  For items assessed during the capstone exam, the evaluator will provide a score between 1 and 5 for the student learning outcomes.  A score of a 5 signifies exceptional demonstration of the student learning outcome, 3 being adequately representing the learning outcome and 1 having minimal knowledge and application of the learning outcome.  The program is meeting its student learning outcome if 95% of student students earn a 3 or better on anything that is assessed during the capstone exam. 

Annually, the director of the AEMS Director will convene at least 3 faculty teaching core topics.  These individuals will evaluate all of the assessment data, including summaries of the past 6 years of data.  The individuals will provide recommendations, whether or not existing problems have been resolved, and the general trend of the student learning in the program.

At the conclusion of this assessment meeting, the AEMS Director is responsible to write an annual report summarizing the discussions and recommendations from the meeting.  It is vitally important that any issues are tracked from year to year.  Any items that are below the program assessment levels need to tracked for several years in the reports.  This will allow the program to track its performance through years and to determine the impact of program changes.

The AEMS Director is also responsible to convey any suggestions or recommendations from the annual assessment meeting to the relevant faculty.  If suggestions relate to the curriculum, the AEMS Director will be responsible to develop proposals to change/modify the curriculum or courses.  Such proposals will need to follow the typical university procedures, which include departmental, college and Faculty Senate approvals.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply aerodynamic principles and theories.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core ME EN 6710 Aerodynamics.  This class covers the theories, principles and mathematical models of aerodynamics. Covered topics include: flow around bodies, inviscid flow, airfoil theory, lift, drag, boundary layers, and many other topics.     
This class is required by all AEMS students.  A student earning a B or better shows a fundamental mastery of aerodynamic principle and theories.  Since every graduating student must take this course and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.
The instructor is responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the AEMS Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply propulsion principles and theories.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core ME EN 6830 Aerospace Propulsion.  This class covers the theories, principles and models of propulsion.  Covered topics include: compressible flow, combustion, turbojets, rocket propulsion systems, liquid engines and many other topics.   
This class is required by all AEMS students.  A student earning a B or better shows a fundamental mastery of aerospace propulsion.  Since every graduating students must take this course and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.
The instructor is responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the AEMS Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply materials and structures for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core Solid Mechanics courses.  Students must take either ME EN 6510 Applied Finite Element Analysis or ME EN 7530 Fracture and Fatigue.  Both classes focus on materials and their strength and performance.  This is a vital skill for aerospace engineers as the material chosen must satisfy strict requirements and has a massive impact upon safety and performance.  
A student earning a B or better in one of these two courses shows a fundamental mastery of materials and structures.  Since every graduating students must take one of these courses and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.
The instructors are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the MSAE Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply dynamics for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core Dynamics courses.  Students must take one course of ME EN 6410 Intermediate Dynamics, ME EN 6960 Orbital Mechanics, or ME EN 6960 Flight Dynamics.  All classes focus on dynamics and provide fundamental theory, models, physical interpretations, and applications of dynamic systems.  This knowledge is vital to understand how to build and operate aerospace products that can function in atmospheric flights or space missions involving complex environments, various mission requirements, and other highly dynamic conditions.     
A student earning a B or better in any of these classes shows a fundamental mastery of dynamics.  Since every graduating students must take one of these courses and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.
The instructors are responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the MSAE Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: Identify and apply systems principles for aerospace applications.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core systems area where the students must take SIME 6800 Aerospace Systems and Ethics course.  This course provides a detailed introduction to systems engineering with a focus on aerospace.  The vast majority of failures in aerospace are a result of some unforeseen complication involving the interaction of computers, mechanical systems and humans. This class will help students identify these issue throughout their careers and help them avoid some horrendous mistakes.
Every AEMS student is required to take SIME 6800.  A student cannot earn a B in this course without a fundamental understanding of systems in aerospace applications.  Since every graduating students must earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.
The instructor is responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the AEMS Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: An ability to communicate effectively
learningOutcomes.justification:
Written communication will be assessed in the core Systems area.  This requirement can only be satisfied by SIME 6800 Aerospace Systems and Ethics.  Students are required to write extensive reports for their projects.  The writing component is essential to systems engineering and a students inability to communicate effectively in a written format would result in a grade of B- or below.    
Oral communication will be evaluated during the capstone exam.  The student must give a thesis defense or a 20-25 minute presentation for their capstone defense.  Thus, the examiner will be able to assess the student's oral communication skills.
Coupling both of these assessments together shows that the student can effectively communicate both in written and oral. Since every MSAE student is required to pass the capstone exam and earn a B or better in SIME 6800, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.

learningOutcomes.name: Recognize ethical and professional responsibilities in aerospace engineering.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This student learning outcome will be assessed in the core systems area where the students must take SIME 6800 Aerospace Systems and Ethics course.  This course provides an introduction to ethics in aerospace, along with an introduction to the complexities of the systems in aerospace.

A question was raised about who should teach ethics for the AEMS students.  Ethics in aerospace engineering are surprisingly different than typical ethics found in almost every other discipline.  The vast majority of products in aerospace have the following properties:
     Expensive to produce and maintain.
     Complex with millions of parts and interactions between various systems. 
     Travel at a fast speeds.
     Weigh a substantial amount.
     Require substantial energy/fuel.
As a result, when an aerospace device does not function properly, there is a massive financial loss and frequently the death or endangerment of numerous people.  In fact, if a commercial jet crashes well over 100 people typically die.  Errors, whether in analysis, testing, manufacturing or judgment, are extremely unforgiving in aerospace.

Engineers and individuals working in aerospace want their product to function correctly and understand some of the massive impact when the product does not function properly. The aerospace ethical issues most frequently occur due to a lack of knowledge, specialization, technology or integration between systems.  In other words, aerospace ethics is primarily not about right, wrong or morals, but rather the competence to design, manufacture and operate these incredibly complex products.  As a result, the ethics is assessed in the Aerospace Systems and Ethics course.  Through this course, students will be able to view both the complexities from an engineering standpoint of aerospace systems and also the ethical and safety implications.  

The faculty do not wish to minimize the impact of ethical decisions related to aerospace.   The space shuttle Challenger exploded due to a desire to have a launch at an abnormally cold temperature. The managers desired the shuttle to be in orbit for the State of the Union Address, but should have listened to the engineers. A more recent ethical question exists regarding unmanned drones firing upon “enemies” without human intervention.  This is an important ethical issue, but is primarily the responsibilities of individuals that are in “upper management/military/politics” and not typically the decisions made by recent AEMS graduates.  For this curriculum, a more important ethical outcome is that if a decision is made, the aerospace product should work appropriately.  That is, if the drone fired, the weapon should travel to the intended target and not hit the school or private residence next door. 

The faculty in the Department of Mechanical Engineering believe that teaching ethics in Aerospace Engineering requires a substantial amount of technical and engineering knowledge.  Being able to explain to students how the incorrect analysis occurred, why the testing in a manufacturing plant failed to detect an error, why the systems failed to seamlessly integrate are vital for future students to create reliable and safe aerospace products.  Thus, the faculty believe that a very technical course (similar to SIME 6800) is the best way to instruct AEMS students regarding the ethics in Aerospace Engineering.

Every AEMS student is required to take SIME 6800.  A student earning a B in this course shows a recognition of the students professional and ethical responsibilities in aerospace applications.  Since every graduating students must take this course and earn a B or better, every graduating student will have achieved this learning outcome.

The instructor is responsible to assign sufficiently complex work so that the students can demonstrate their knowledge of this student learning outcome and to supply this knowledge to the AEMS Director along with any suggestions for improved student learning improvement.

learningOutcomes.name: An ability to acquire and apply new knowledge using appropriate learning strategies.
learningOutcomes.justification:
This learning outcome will be assessed in the capstone exam. The students pursuing the thesis have created new knowledge for the field. If the student passes their thesis defense, then the student has clearly excelled at this learning outcome.

Students pursuing the coursework AEMS must pass the capstone exam.  To pass this exam, students identify a problem and show how they use knowledge from three of their courses to solve the complex problem.  The fact that the student integrates knowledge from three different courses demonstrates how they applied new knowledge.  Furthermore, if the student passes this exam, then they have demonstrated appropriate learning strategies.

Since every AEMS student is required to pass the capstone exam, every graduating 
student will have achieved this learning outcome.

catalogFullDescription: The Artificial Intelligence minor prepares students with basic skills and competence in artificial intelligence (AI). The discipline studies the automation of tasks that usually require human-like intelligence, such as learning, perception, reasoning, and decision-making. It fuses skills of computer programming and machine learning. It leverages representative data and experiences to provide sensible and automated interactions -- through language, via physical devices such as robots, within games such as chess, and generating feasible outcomes for design. The minor complements an undergraduate degree in a field that works with data, language, design, or computers, and enhances their studies with the tools to apply AI towards those goals. Students in the minor will also learn about ethical considerations in applying AI in a responsible way. These AI skills are useful in a wide variety of occupations within the sciences, engineering, medicine, policy, the creative sector and more.

customFields.ztYeO:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) the discipline is about how to make sense and interact with the world around us. In particular, it is about how to automate this process and train computers to successfully interact in a way that often mirrors the patterns and capabilities of humans. Advances in these technologies enable the translation and generation of languages (e.g., ChatGPT), the design and execution of strategies (for games like AlphaGo), the interpretation of images (e.g., DALL-E) and the creation of novel physical and biological materials (e.g., the 2024 Nobel Prize winning work on protein design). Building on these incredible breakthroughs, AI is driving many fields including Engineering, Science, Medicine, Art, and Policy.    

The drivers of these technologies are the synthesis of computer science -- to program the automation -- and in particular machine learning -- to identify patterns in observations to predict the next likely outcomes. For instance, the large language models that power tools like OpenAI's ChatGPT are built by complex computer programs which digest all of the world's language, represent it through neural networks, generate strings of text that respond to prompts in that language, ultimately synthesizing knowledge to provide informative answers. The field of artificial intelligence invokes these machine learning tools in an interactive way by identifying a goal, then step-by-step generating responses that are likely to meet these demands while adhering to the patterns of the world. These techniques are finding applications and driving innovation in many fields.   

At the same time, the core techniques behind these methods have become better understood, simpler to explain, and the tools for programming with these techniques have become more streamlined. As such, students are eager to learn them, and incorporate them into their education and technical skill set. Students who can firmly grasp the core approaches and apply them in their domains will be in high demand to build economic growth in the state. As such, it is a critical time to launch a minor in AI. 

 The Kahlert School of Computing is the natural home for AI education given that AI emerged in the 1950s and 1960s as a core area of computer science. In fact, the US News and World Report ranks computer science programs based on just four research areas, one of which is AI. We propose to build on the substantial foundations of AI education in the Kahlert School of Computing to broaden its reach across campus, offering a minor in Artificial Intelligence for undergraduates. The Kahlert School already has a substantial education and training programs in AI. The Price College's Upskilling in AI (U-AI) program, led by Kahlert School faculty, has trained about 70 faculty in AI concepts from main campus and School of Medicine, with the goal of improving research competitiveness and AI-related education across campus. The USHE-funded Deep Learning certificate program has conferred 24 certificates, with 14 additional students anticipated to complete certificates this year. A recent AI track for MS and PhD students has 40 students, with 14 faculty teaching courses in the track. A rich set of AI electives for both undergraduate and graduate students are taught in diverse areas such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotics, computer vision and image analysis, ethics associated with AI, and security of machine learning models; over 25 distinct such courses have been offered in the last year.   

With the recent prominence of AI and its impact across many technical areas, we anticipate that other AI-related curricula will be proposed that are specialized for different technical domains. For example, we are aware of a proposal for a Business AI Minor from the Eccles School of Business. Our proposed minor is distinguished from other domain-specific programs as it trains students in foundational AI knowledge as well as practical machine learning skills independent of the technical domain.

Students pursuing the minor in Artificial Intelligence will be advised by the Kahlert School of Computing undergraduate advising staff, which consists of six full-time advisors. The current ratio of undergraduate computing majors and minors to advisors according to the Spring 2025 census is 333:1. We will closely monitor this ratio, and increase the advisors if the ratio increases beyond 350:1.    The requirements for admission to the AI minor are the same as our existing majors (computer science, data science, software development) and minor (computer science). Therefore, the Kahlert School's advisors are already adept at providing consistent guidance for all students before or during admission to the minor.   As we do with other specialized programs, such as certificates, one advisor will be tasked with guiding students after admission to the minor, as well as how to help students select between the CS3190 and CS 3350 options. Furthermore, the advisors will be in close contact with the Kahlert School's AI faculty who can help answer any questions beyond the advisor's expertise.   

Advisors will add information about the minor in AI to other activities for prospective and early students such as major expos and Price College's Engineering Day.

General Overview: Adding additional courses and Allied Departments (ENV and CRIM) to our Major and Major emphases to give students more choices to facilitate graduation. Removing some classes from relevant emphases that are no longer being offered by the Department (ANTH 5714, 5716, and 3481).

Some of the courses being added are brand-new (ANTH 3490; or newly "unretired," ANTH 4150), and ANTH 3486 has been recently revitalized and assigned to a new professor.

Aside from the class additions or subtractions, which make up the large majority of our changes, here are some more specific justifications:

2) Changed the wording in the Allied section of the Arch. Science emphasis to reflect the requirement of GEOG 3100 plus 8 additional credits (had read GEOG 3100 plus 7 additional credits). This was necessary as GEOG 3100 had been a 5 credit course, but was changed to a 4 credit course last cycle. The adjustment therefore keeps the overall number of Arch. Science Allied credits at 12 total.

2) Addition of a "methods" course to the Cultural Emphasis, the majority of which are Geographic Information Science/Systems (GIS) classes. The profession of cultural anthropology is changing rapidly and our lead cultural faculty requested this addition. Although it will result in the Cultural emphasis being slightly longer (3-4 credits), our cultural faculty feel that the addition is justified in order to facilitate greater success in the profession as many cultural anthropology jobs now integrate GIS technology.

Approved by Anthropology Curriculum Committee on November 14, 2024.

catalogFullDescription: The field of applied ethics consists in the analysis of ethical issues as they arise in the management and resolution of real-world problems. Applied (or as it is sometimes called, practical) ethics promotes an ongoing conversation between specific cases and pressing issues, on the one hand, and theory and meta-theory on the other. Bioethics, business ethics, and environmental ethics are but a few of the areas of applied ethics that have flourished in recent years, and all three areas are well represented by the faculty at the University of Utah. In the applied ethics minor, students will learn skills of ethical reasoning and analysis in the context of their preferred area of study. Course work may include: ethics, political philosophy, political thought, or democratic theory; course applying ethical analysis to health care, business and the professions, engineering and the environment, global or social justice, law and politics, or communication and the media; and courses in these particular fields illustrating ethical issues. No prerequisites are required. The minor will be of particular interest to students planning careers in one of the subject matter areas who wish to be able to bring ethical perspectives and skills to their field.

catalogFullDescription:
The professional program leading to the Master of Architecture (M.Arch) degree prepares students for careers as licensed architects and is a foundation for success in many other fields.

The Master of Architecture program is predicated upon a strong pre-professional degree in architecture. The curriculum features a series of studio courses integrated with co-curricular courses, leading to a degree in which students gain experience in design research, critical thinking, and leadership, as well as design process, architectural history and theory, communication skills, and building and environmental technologies. Electives may be drawn from the offerings in architecture and urban planning as well as a broad list of graduate level courses offered by the University. Electives may be used toward the completion of a graduate certificate. Graduate certificates are offered in historic preservation, urban design, urban planning, and real estate development.

A highlight of the M.Arch program is the immersive experience at the start of the final year. Students select from design-build, community engagement, urban design, and other offerings. The program culminates in a self-directed final studio project, in which the student completes focused research on an area of their choice and integrates information from an elective course taken outside of the College of Architecture + Planning.

Students may enter the Master of Architecture program from several different backgrounds:

2-Year Program: Students who hold a B.S. in Architectural Studies from the University of Utah may be admitted to the 2-year program leading to the professional Master of Architecture degree. Applicants should submit a portfolio directly to the School of Architecture, plus an online University of Utah application, along with a personal statement, GRE scores, and other required documentation (as noted on the School of Architecture website), by January 10th.

Students who completed a pre-professional degree in architecture at another university may be admitted to the 2-year program leading to the professional Master of Architecture degree. If necessary, based on portfolio and transcript reviews and possible diagnostic examination, some prerequisite work may be required. Applicants should submit a portfolio directly to the School of Architecture, plus an online University of Utah application, along with two letters of recommendation, a personal statement, GRE scores, and other required documentation (as noted on the School of Architecture website), by January 10th.

3+ Program: Students who hold a baccalaureate degree in a field other than architecture may be admitted to the three-year plus one summer course of study, referred to as the 3+ Program, to obtain the professional Master of Architecture degree. Prior to admission, students need to have completed one course in calculus and one trigonometry based college-level general physics course. Students should possess at least an introductory-level ability in drawing with emphasis in freehand sketching. Applicants should submit a portfolio directly to the School of Architecture, plus an online University of Utah application, along with two letters of recommendation, a personal statement, GRE scores, and other required documentation (as noted on the School of Architecture website), by January 10th. Upon admission, the student registers for a group of intensive courses during the summer. The following fall and spring semesters, the student registers for courses that are similar to those listed for the final year of the B.S. degree in Architectural Studies. With the successful completion of those courses, the student then completes the requirements of the 2-year Master of Architecture program.

Students who complete a full architecture program not accredited by NAAB (usually a foreign architecture degree) may be admitted to the 2-year program leading to the professional Master of Architecture degree. If necessary, based on portfolio and transcript reviews and possible diagnostic examination, some prerequisite work may be required. A minimum of four semesters in residence are required for the M.Arch. degree. Applicants should submit a portfolio directly to the School of Architecture, plus an online University of Utah application, along with two letters of recommendation, a personal statement of purpose, GRE scores, and other required documentation (as noted on the School of Architecture website), by January 10th.

Further application information and portfolio guidelines can be found on the School of Architecture website (soa.cap.utah.edu).

They will able to analyze diverse communities and cultural phenomena and interpret the same in architectural terms.

The Bachelor of Arts in Architectural Studies (BAAS) is an undergraduate, liberal arts degree that provides a well-rounded academic foundation for immediate careers in architectural design and allied disciplines.  It prepares the student for advanced academic standing in 3+ Master of Architecture professional programs.

The BAAS curriculum challenges students to explore design, socio- cultural influences, spatial reasoning, sustainability, resilience, material properties, political and economic structures, landscape ecologies, construction practices, building technologies, among other related themes.  It situates architecture as a complex, multi-faceted discipline within the broader university, professional, and civic contexts.

The program encourages students to use their elective credit hours to concentrate in a particular aspect of architectural studies and/or minor in an area outside of the SoA to further support this interdisciplinary approach to education.

The process of developing and proposing this new major was a collaborative one. First, the college convened a committee composed of representatives from all academic units, The Design Foundations Task Force, to address College graduation rates. Our current 4-year graduation rate is 32%. The Design Foundations program is a common core for first-time freshman and transfer students in the Architectural Studies, Urban Ecology, and Multi-Disciplinary undergraduate degrees.

Each year Approximately 120 students enter the program expressing an interest in architectural studies. However, we can only admit 50 students into our BSAS program in their sophomore year. This program is a resource intensive studio sequence that requires low student teacher ratios and extensive use of studio spaces in the college. In addition, this program has prerequisites in calculus and physics which can be difficult for some students to complete within their first year of study. This has led to delays in student eligibility for admission into the BSAS while they complete these courses. This results in many qualified students leaving the university after multiple attempts to get into the BSAS program.  The proposal is designed to allow more students interested in Architectural Studies to complete and graduate four years. 

The design foundations discussion proposed several solutions but the BAAS degree was deemed the best way to provide students who express an interest in architecture but who cannot get into the BSAS program a path to completion, opportunities for employment in the field and a path to graduate studies and licensure.  The College leadership team discussed this proposal as did the college at, our College retreat, and at School of Architecture faculty meetings. The School of Architecture has a responsibility to provide a path to completion to the many talented students we cannot accept into the BSAS program

This program will provide students who are interested in Architectural Studies an alternative pathway that allows for greater levels of persistence and completion with a functional four-year degree plan. It also prepares students for graduate study in a professional three-year degree such as our NAAB Accredited 3+ master’s degree, which has consistently fallen below our enrollment goals. The new BAAS program would therefore strengthen 4-year graduation rates for undergraduates, while also providing a larger pool of applicants to our 3+ program. 

The Bachelor of Arts in Architectural Studies (BAAS) would be the only BAAS program offered in the USHE system and, the state of Utah. There are several colleges in the US that provide multiple paths to graduation including University of Washington, Kent State University, University of Minnesota, and Massachusetts Institute of Technology. In each case the distinction between the two degrees is similar, with one degree understood as a pre-professional degree emphasizing the professional and technical aspects of architectural practice particularly and the other offering a broader arts and humanities focus.

Finally, The BAAS will include courses that emphasizes the full range of work in the field of architecture. This includes issues like design justice and community engaged design, both aspects of the field that expand our students understanding of the who architecture is designed for and what role architectural production has in developing community resilience. Students’ capacity to serve broad community interest will be strengthened by the interdisciplinary emphasis of the BAAS degree including the general education language requirement. The capacity to communicate with community members where they are is a critical aspect of community focused architectural practice and an important feature of this degree. The language requirement is one example of the benefit of this degree and the distinction between the BSAS and the BAAS.

The names reflect a standard in the field and allow our students to pursue a masters in the field. However we will study naming conventions, poll students, and develop a clear presentation of the distinction between the two degrees to be used in student orientation, information secessions, and advising to ensure that the difference between the two degrees is clear. There is an increasing labor market demand for architects across the United States. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics on Occupation Outlook for Architects (September 2022), employment of entry level positions in architectural firms with bachelor’s degree is projected to grow by 3% from 2021 to 2031. It is estimated that there are 9,100 job openings for architects annually, with 125,500 jobs held in 2021. Among these openings, there is higher demand for architects with expertise and a set of skills in the areas of sustainable design, building information modeling, building systems, research methods, etc. than other areas. Our proposed BAAS program will allow students to develop skills and expertise in a range of areas including sustainable design and information modeling. As the architectural profession is changing to embrace a variety of research methods and specializations, it is imperative that the structure of architectural education change as well. 

In addition, a review of the data provided by Utah DWS Occupation Data and the Occupation Outlook Handbook shows a clear demand for qualified workers in the field of Architecture and other allied fields in the state of Utah. The occupation outlook provided by Utah DSW states: “This occupation is expected to experience much faster than average employment growth” Data shows that Statewide there is a demand for entry level workers in the field with a bachelor’s degree providing an annual median income of $76,120. The DSW data also shows a 4.07% increase in demand statewide with a five-star rating (https://jobs.utah.gov/jsp/utalmis/#/occupation/17-1011.00/report).

According to the Occupational Outlook Handbook Jobs in Architecture in 2023, jobs in the field provide a median pay of $93,310 annually with an 8% Job Outlook for the years 2023 – 2033 which is faster than average. See table below. The State Agency emphasizes that architects with up-to-date technical abilities and skills, especially with strong knowledge and understanding of CAD (Computer-Aided Design) and BIM (Building Information Modeling),, as well as experience in sustainable design will have an advantage over others who do not possess those skills and expertise. According to the World Population Review (2022), the State of Utah is the fourth fastest growing state in the United States, with annual growth of 1.45%. Utah will continue to expand in every sector including the construction industry.

In addition to these traditional jobs, there are many new opportunities in the field of architecture. The field of architecture is undergoing a significant transformation, driven by advancements in technology, a growing focus on sustainability, and the increasing importance of design in various industries. For example, a burgeoning area of practice is in “design management,” which involves leading an architectural firm’s approach and process. Specifically, design management touches on the implementation and upkeep of AI-driven technologies that improve a firm’s Internal operational and production efficiency, monitoring and analysis of built work, design and simulation of different options, decision-making and optimization. The broad focus on this degree will provide students with the opportunity to focus in these transforming areas of the architectural design and production processes. 

Additional career opportunities include project designer, project manager/coordinator, landscape architecture, engineering, art, construction, urban planning, urban design, historic preservation, or for graduate studies in the professional Master of Architecture program, in business fields or in law. Employment opportunities also exist at the community level, particularly in those communities that traditionally have not been served by professional architectural practice. The overall aim of the undergraduate program is to establish a strong foundation for many careers and to provide for mobility and flexibility to suit changing individual opportunities.
