This degree supports several aspects of University values, most notably Student Success, Sustainability, and Community.

According to the University’s mission and set of values: “The U is committed to providing the financial assistance, personalized support, and engaged learning experiences that increase access to the university and facilitate persistence through degree completion.”

This degree is designed to support student success by providing students multiple paths to degree completion. Currently The School of Architecture (SoA) has only one path to completion, the Bachelor of Science in Architectural Studies for these students, and this path is limited is several ways. The College of Architecture + Planning (CAP) admits over 100 students who are interested in perusing a degree in Architecture into the Design Foundations program. But the BSAS is a studio intensive course with a fixed student to faculty ratio. We can only admit 60 students into this program (50 into the sophomore BSAS cohort and then 10 additional transfer students from SLCC and other community colleges) . In addition, this program has advanced math and physics courses as prerequisites. This often makes it difficult for students interested in a degree in Architecture to persist in their degree progress. Finally, the current degree is a lock step degree which does not allow for an interdisciplinary lens on architectural studies and practice, or scheduling flexibility for students who need to work and participate in athletics, or other extracurriculars. This new degree would address all these issues or obstacles to completion allowing student to create a path to graduation that does not require math and physics beyond the general education requirements, that provides opportunities for a concentration or minor in allied areas of study outside of the SoA, and that has a more flexible pedagogy that allows for larger student to faculty ratios.

Another University value that this program supports is sustainability: “The U contributes to a more sustainable world through research, teaching, and demonstrating best practices in protecting and enhancing the natural and built environment on the campus and environs, making it a great place to live, learn, work, play, create, recreate, and visit.” This degree would not only have core courses in sustainability, bit this will also be an area of focus that gives students deeper knowledge in the relationship between design and construction practices and sustainability. Sustainability is also one of the primary aspects of the CAP mission focused on resilience. This new degree makes the connection between sustainability theory and action.

Finally, the University mission states: “The U maintains a strong sense of community among students, faculty, and staff, and cultivates meaningful university, neighborhood, city, region, state, and global partnerships.” Our program will offer courses on community engaged collaboration as well as a clear ethical focus on the communities in which we live and build. The main questions that we will utilize to assess our curriculum are:

  • How is the integrated curriculum model working? Are there any challenges or opportunities for improvements?

  • Are we meeting the identified learning objectives for our undergraduate and graduate programs in all courses?

  • How are students performing in our courses, where performance indicators include grade distribution, quality of design work, technical aptitude?

  • How do students’ performance indicators relate to demographic data (i.e. are we meeting our overarching commitment to instituting justice, equity, diversity and inclusion in our teaching)?

  • How are students satisfied with the course contents and teaching methods for every class?

We will use qualitative and quantitative methods to collect data and to answer these questions. Qualitative methods will include interviews and focus groups with students, as well as collecting and analyzing course evaluations for all courses. Quantitative methods will include collection of students’ performance indicators, demographic data, and analysis of data. We recognize the need to conduct both individual and team assessments of the curriculum on a regular basis. We also recognize the need to comparatively examine outcomes of studio-based learning over time.

We have designed multiple types of self-assessment to help us monitor the ongoing challenges and successes of the curriculum in meaningful and timely ways. Our Curriculum Committee Provides leadership and oversite for curricular assessment. Our current curricular self-assessment tools include:

  1. Independent evaluation – Faculty Teaching Reports (FTR)

  2. Small group assessments – SWOT analysis and Course Objective review

  3. Special assessments – Rotating review of work in disciplinary areas

1.     Independent evaluation – Faculty Teaching Reports (FTR)
Every faculty member is responsible for collecting and analyzing data for their courses, and submitting the following information to the Curriculum Committee, Administrative Officer/Graduate Advisor and the Chair:

  • Course syllabi for every class/every semester (at the beginning of the semester)

  • Course evaluations for every class/every semester (at the end of every semester)

  • Faculty Teaching Reports (FTRs) summarizing teaching methods, learning objectives, students’ performance indicators (grades, grade distribution, quality of work/reflection, technical aptitude) as stand-alone metrics, as well as in relation to anonymous demographic data for every class/every semester.

The FTRs will be submitted at the end of each semester by faculty. FTR forms include the following information: teaching methods, learning objectives, student performance indicators, and analysis of performance indicators in relation to Demographic data (to the degree possible), suggestions for changes to improve the course based on the data.

The Curriculum Committee will conduct a comprehensive review of FTRs at the end of each semester and will provide summary reports to the Chair, faculty and staff (two reports per year). The findings of the Curriculum Committee’s analysis will be discussed at the beginning of each semester, where the assessment for previous semester will be used to determine necessary changes and improvements to the curriculum that must occur during that academic year. This will ensure continuous data collection, analysis, and implementation for curricular assessment and development. 

2.     Small group assessments – SWOT analysis and Course Objective review
On a rotating basis we perform small group SWOT analysis of our curriculum, including individual courses and integrated courses. This method will be used to access all design courses offered in the undergraduate curriculum including the capstone integrated experience. These assessments are scheduled by the Director of Undergraduate Studies. They will pare faculty teaching the course being evaluated along with other faculty whose expertise is appropriate for the course being evaluated. The syllabus, assignments and student work are evaluated first by SWOT analysis and then with the following questions:

  • What outcomes do we hope to see for this course?

  • Describe how we intend to produce those outcomes, including pedagogy, required materials, and assignments.  

  • How closely have we gotten to achieving the outcomes? Wherein the assignments and student work as we seeing evidence of these outcomes?

  • Can we imagine changes to the curriculum, pedagogy, assignments, that would be more effective in meeting these outcomes

  • After we make these changes who do we check for progress?

3.     Disciplinary assessments – SWOT analysis and Course Objective review in disciplinary areas
On a rotating basis we perform small group analysis of each disciplinary area in our curriculum, including architectural design, communications, history, theory, + criticism (HTC), professional practice, and building technology. This method will be used to access all courses offered in the undergraduate curriculum. These assessments are scheduled by the Director of Undergraduate Studies. They will include all faculty teaching in a particular area coming together to look at the entire sequence in context. For example, the entire sequence of undergraduate HTC will be evaluated in relation to the program goals in that area. This allows an assessment of the objectives, assignments, outcomes, and student accomplishments across each area of study within each degree program. The syllabus, assignments and student work are evaluated first by SWOT analysis and then with the following questions (note questions are unique to each disciplinary area.)

  • What Content and methods of design history, theory and criticism do we most fully cover?

  • How diverse is our design history in representation of cultures, gender, stakeholder role?

  • What bodies of theory are most central to our attention? Do we attend to theory as a method as well as in content?

  • Where do we teach this array of knowledge and methods in the curriculum?

  • How do we support a rich understanding of history and theory beyond the curriculum?

  • Which elements of “social, cultural, economic, and political forces do we attend to? Which do we need to reinforce or introduce into our curriculum?

  • What evidence of student understanding can we show? Are there pedagogies or projects that might introduce to help us evaluate student understanding.  

Although only the Master’s Degree in Architecture is an accredited, we have modeled this assessment plan on the accreditation process. The primary reference for the plan  is Herb Childress’ book, “Program Assessment in Design Education: Methods and Strategies for continual Improvement on Your Own Terms” Published by the Association of Collegiate Schools of Architecture in 2021 to assist programs in building assessment plans in preparation for accreditation.

Rotating Schedule for Assessment: Our assessment cycle is 8 years to correspond with our accreditation cycle.

Year 1

  • Fall 25            
    Program goes live;

    • First Classes are offered in Communications, History, and Design areas as well as the cohort seminar

    • Individual FTR reports on new courses and curriculum committee review

  •  Spring 26       
    Continuing Course development:

    • develop courses for year 2: theory, technology, research methods

    • Individual FTR reports on new courses offered and Curriculum committee review

 Year 2

  • Fall 26         
    Second year of program courses offered

    • Individual FTR reports on all courses and Curriculum committee review

  • Spring 27    
    Develop capstone experiences and approve through curriculum committee 

    • Individual FTR reports on all courses and Curriculum committee review

Year 3

  • Fall 27         

    • First Disciplinary assessments

    • Individual FTR reports on all courses and Curriculum committee review

  • Spring 28    
    First assessment report for BAAS, to include curriculum committee summary reports as well as results of Disciplinary assessments.

    • Make changes and adjustments to curriculum based on assessments.

Year 4

  • Continue collecting FTR reports and providing curriculum committee review and summary

  • Perform first small group assessment of capstone experience

  • Individual FTR reports on all courses and Curriculum committee review

  • Make adjustments to capstone experience and approve experiences for next cohort.

Year 5

  • Second Disciplinary assessments + FTR

  • Second Assessment Report with adjustments as needed

 Year 6            

  • Second small group assessment + FTR                                   

Year 7            

  • Program and Curriculum Assessment Synthesis, external review, and strategic goal setting    

  • Adjustments to program and assessment cycle as needed

learningOutcomes.name: Students are expected to have a well-developed liberal arts education as well as a fundamental understanding of the values of architectural design as a method for engaging the material and cultural aspects of place. In addition, students will have the ability to develop complex ideas and communicate in verbal, written and graphic forms.

Students will understand the historic evolution of architectural design against the context of culture and society at large, including pressing issues such as social equity, global citizenship, ecological resilience, and agency. They will be able to position themselves with regard to both the processes of design and civic society, politics, and ethics. They will have a respect for diversity and the relationship between human behavior and the physical environment. They will understand the fundamental role of the architect in society and their ethical responsibility to sustain and preserve the environment within which they construct.

Students will have developed skills of research, including: how to build an argument, construct a question, propose a research agenda, and conduct formal analysis to explore complex problems of various scales and complexities, as well as composition, theoretical perception, critical thinking and the qualitative assessment of design and its processes. This will be demonstrated through the integration of research and design, writing and craft, analysis and production. The design skills will demonstrate an understanding of distinct scales of operation including urban context evaluation, site design, building program development and concept design, building systems, constructability, and detail and material development.

Students will learn to value the activist potential of architecture and its allied fields, to think and act at various scales, and to be cognizant of their positionality in relationship to others. They will be able to analyze diverse communities and cultural phenomena and interpret the same in architectural terms. Finally students will be able to identify their own cultural patterns and put them into comparison with cultural patterns different from their own.

catalogFullDescription:
The Master of Science in Architectural Studies (MSAS) program is a post-professional graduate degree, designed for students seeking education in a specialty area of architectural research. The program can be completed by students in approximately two years of study and prepares students for research or professional practice in a specialty area of architecture. This degree is not accredited to gain licensure for practice as an architect. Any student wishing to enter the program must apply for acceptance in the fall semester prior to their first year of study.

The MSAS program is a 36-credit hour program of study. The program is characterized by choice and flexibility. The student assembles a program tailored to their individual interests. The program includes an introductory seminar on research methods, electives, and a research project, which culminate in the final Master's thesis.

The thesis research work will comprise of an independent research project in which the student demonstrates proficiency in academic requirement areas. The student proceeds under the direction of a three-member faculty committee, consisting of a primary advisor, and at least two committee members. The committee chair must be a tenure-line or career-line faculty member of College of Architecture + Planning.

The Art Teaching BFA Kindergarten – Twelfth Grade Licensure Program Description:

The purpose of the BFA Art Teaching Kindergarten – Twelfth (K-12) Grade Licensure Program is to prepare elementary, junior high, middle school, and high school visual art educators. Competent K-12 visual art teaching requires both in-depth knowledge of subject matter (art) and skill in applying educational concepts and principles that are developmentally appropriate. The College of Education’s Urban Institute for Teacher Education (UITE) oversees teacher licensure at the University of Utah. UITE is located in SAEC 2264.

Note: Licensing is dictated by specific deadlines. Students pursuing an educator license should contact the UITE as soon as possible to learn about deadlines, background check requirements, and student teaching.

For students in the Art Teaching BFA degree program who are interested in not pursuing a K-12 teaching license, please schedule an appointment to see a CFA Advisor to discuss alternative class options available within the program of study.

catalogFullDescription:
The Art History MA prepares students for professional careers or further advanced study. We welcome applicants with an outstanding scholastic record from an accredited college or university and expect that you will have a BA degree in Art History or a cognate discipline suitable to the study of art history and visual studies. The two-year competitive program culminating in a scholarly project or thesis offers students an opportunity to develop a specific research focus among the visual cultures of East Asia, ancient Imperial Rome, Middle Ages and Byzantium; Early Modern Europe (Renaissance and Baroque); or Modern and Contemporary Europe, Latin America, and the United States (18th to 21st centuries). The curriculum is oriented towards an interdisciplinary global perspective.

Financial Assistance: The Art History MA admissions committee automatically reviews all applications for assistance and offers financial aid to incoming students on a competitive basis. Students advanced to candidacy are also eligible for merit-based funding in the form of teaching assistantships, fellowships, and research and conference travel grants during the second year of residency. Funding for summer language study is also available. Please see specific details on the https://www.art.utah.edu/art-history-program/ma-in-art-history/ Program in Art History and Visual Studies website.

Other funding and subsidized packages such as http://gradschool.utah.edu/tbp/insurance-information/ health insurance are offered through the http://gradschool.utah.edu/tbp/graduate-fellowship-opportunities/ Graduate School.

customFields.9VKoN:
The deadline for submission of all materials to the University is February 1, and students are admitted only to the Fall Semester.

Application to the Art History MA is handled through the Graduate School, which sets minimum admissions criteria for all applicants. Students complete forms through the Graduate Admissions office's “Apply Yourself“ web portal. International students must comply with all application procedures and deadlines, including meeting English-language proficiencies as outlined by the University of Utah's International Admissions Office. Students matriculated into the MA Program for whom English is a second language may be required to take ESL classes in addition to departmental coursework. The GRE is not required for application to the MA Program in Art History.

In addition to basic documentation required by the Graduate School, the Program in Art History and Visual Studies requires the following supplementary materials from each applicant:

  • Statement of purpose to explain your preparation, interests, and goals in the graduate study of art history. You should also identify one or two faculty members in the Program in Art History and Visual Studies who you believe would be best suited to mentor you in your area of interest within art history.

  • Curriculum vitae (resume) with your academic background and other educational experiences.

  • Academic writing sample (e.g., an undergraduate research paper) to show your most mature approach to research and writing.

  • Two letters of recommendation by professors or instructors who are familiar with your academic work and can speak to your ability to succeed in a rigorous academic program [submitted online separately by your evaluators].

Applicants who do not meet the minimum requirements of the Graduate School may, in some cases, be admitted to the program on a probationary basis.

The MA degree program is further described on the Program in Art History and Visual Studies website.

catalogFullDescription:
Asian Studies is a vibrant community of students, scholars, and faculty committed to a deep understanding of the peoples, politics, history, and languages of Asia. Through the rigorous study of languages, societal structures, and culture, students form a basis for understanding global issues and their impact within a region of Asia—Asia Pacific, China, Japan, Korea, Russia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia.

In this major, students gain descriptive, analytical, and methodological tools to help understand a region and culture of Asia. Coursework in our major and minor is grounded in language; students gain or expand on their proficiency in one of the Asian languages taught at the U—Chinese, Hindi-Urdu, Japanese, Korean, Russian, Samoan, Tongan, and Vietnamese. Alongside language, students select Asia focused classes from across campus. This interdisciplinary approach allows students the flexibility to pair their study with pre-health courses, a minor or second major, and exciting co-curricular activities related to their academic and career goals.

catalogFullDescription:
The Advanced Substance Use Disorder Counselor Training Certificate Program is an undergraduate program dedicated to helping students develop the solid knowledge base and treatment skills necessary to assist individuals and their families affected by substance use disorders. The overarching goal of the program is to enhance the quality of substance use disorder treatment and care delivery available in the state of Utah.

  • Available to all students and may be completed alongside a bachelor's degree or as a standalone certificate.

  • Completion of this program fulfills the educational requirements for individuals to become licensed in the state of Utah as substance use disorder counselors.

350-hour practicum is required in final semester.

Scope of Practice

  • Administer screening process by which a client is determined to need substance use disorder services which may include screening, brief intervention, and treatment referral

  • Conducts assessment procedures to gather information related to an individual's strengths, weaknesses, needs, and substance use disorder symptoms for the development of a treatment plan

  • Participation in the process of treatment planning including recommending specific interventions to support existing treatment goals and objectives

  • Other activities as outlined in Utah Code 58-60-502(10)(b)

  • Practice under general supervision of qualified mental health therapist (MHT)

  • Identify substance use disorder symptoms and behaviors and co-occurring health issues

  • Treatment planning for substance use disorders diagnosed by MHT

  • Qualified to supervise SUDC as they gather hrs. of supervised experience.

catalogFullDescription:
The allied health care profession of Athletic Training encompasses the prevention, examination, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of acute or chronic injuries and medical conditions. Athletic trainers (ATs) require multiple health care related skills to perform a wide-range of duties and care for various types of injuries and medical conditions.

Athletic trainers work under the direction of a physician as prescribed by state licensure or other regulation statutes. Traditionally, athletic trainers provide health care services for high school, collegiate, and professional athletes. In addition to professional, recreational and/or occupational athletes, today athletic trainers' are employed in a variety of other settings including military, public-service professions (police and fire departments), physician offices, sports medicine specialty clinics, and commercial occupational health departments (e.g. Amazon warehouses).

Athletic training professional education has chosen to move to a graduate level degree to align better with other allied health care professionals provide students with better clinical and inter-professional education experiences. Didactic and clinical learning within this program will focus on the primary domains of the AT profession: 1) injury and illness prevention, 2) examination, assessment and diagnosis, 3) immediate and emergency care, 4) therapeutic intervention, and 5) health care administration and professional responsibility. This professional program is required by the Commission on Accreditation of Athletic Training Education (CAATE) and prepares students to become nationally certified athletic trainers (ATC) able to obtain state licensure and begin a successful athletic training career.

catalogFullDescription:
Atmospheric Sciences seeks to understand the behavior and predictability of the Earth's atmosphere and requires a good foundation in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and computer science. The undergraduate Atmospheric Sciences major combines required courses in these areas with advanced courses in meteorology, climate, and related disciplines to develop an academic background that is appropriate for a variety of employment opportunities. Our program encourages the development of technical skills (written, oral, computer) that will lead to productive careers and prepares students for the pursuit of advanced degrees in atmospheric or related sciences. Students have the option to specialize in one of three Tracks that adds flexibility to their academic studies: Environmental Sciences, Professional Meteorology, and Snow and Water Sciences.

Environmental Sciences: Designed for students interested in applying knowledge of the atmosphere to related environmental fields, for example, air quality monitoring and modeling; remote sensing; hydrology and snow science; or public policy. This Track will prepare a student directly for a career as an environmental scientist or for continuing their education in an Earth Science graduate program. This option is intended to provide each graduate with a strong foundation in meteorology and providing skills in environmental monitoring, analysis of environmental data, and written and oral communications.

Professional Meteorology: Satisfies the requirements of the federal government for employment as a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. Other government agencies and private firms expect graduates to have completed course work similar to that required by the Professional Meteorology Track. This option is intended to provide each graduate with a solid foundation in meteorology and enable the student to become conversant in related fields such as hydrology, air pollution, data science, and communications. Students who excel academically will be prepared to attend graduate school in an Atmospheric Science or Meteorology program.

Snow and Water Sciences: Emphasizes a broad, interdisciplinary education involving the atmospheric sciences, hydrometeorology, hydrology, snow dynamics and avalanche studies, and mountain weather and climate issues. This Track prepares students for careers related to water resources and operational and research positions related to mountain environments.

  1. Total credit hours lowered to 120 per Navigate U requirements

  2. In lower-division required courses section 1, PHYS2110 was replaced with PHYS2210. This corrects an error.

  3. In upper-division required courses section 3, ATMOS3670 was deleted as it is now inactive. Several upper-division CW courses have been added to give students and advisors more options.

  4. Updating Environmental Science Emphasis Required Courses to delete inactive courses and add more potential course options.

  8. Same as 3, 4, and 5 except for Snow and Water Emphasis.

Updates to degree plans to reflect these changes, Navigate U requirements (we are aiming for as close to 15 credits per semester as possible and no more than 16), and new University GE and BD requirements. These plans were also improved in some areas where students have been confused. One issue here is that Atmos5050 will be 3 credits next year whereas it is listed as 2 still in coursedog, although we have overridden that in the "Details" section so the math otherwise works out.

These changes should greatly aid advising, student selection of emphasis electives, and student planning, reducing stress and advising loads.

The changes in terms of program requirements are actually quite minimal. Advisors have been guiding students through most of the items above already. Updating and expanding the required courses options in each of the emphases will be a major assist for the advisors and students. Communications of these updates will take place in regular meetings with advisors.

These updates were also motivated by recent advisor turnover in the College of Science. The updates provide updated and easier to follow program requirements and plans that will greatly aid new advisor orientation.

The former College of Science advisor tasked to the atmospheric sciences program, Isaac Reyes, was consulted on these changes (he has since departed for another position), as well as the College of Sciences Director of Academic Advising Cyri Dixon.

These changes do not require any special equipment or supplies, including computer lab time or specialized software.

The minimum GPA requirement for admission is a 3.0. Prospective graduate students must apply for admission through the University of Utah Graduate Admissions Office.

Application for Admission includes:

  • Submission of undergraduate transcripts. Please upload official transcripts to the online application.

  • GRE scores: Send your GRE scores to the institution code 4853.

  • Statement of purpose cover letter (i.e., why you want to be an audiologist; 1 - 2 pages)

  • Sample of scholarly writing (2 - 10 pages). Clinical reports will not be accepted. Collaborative works are not permitted.

  • Three letters of recommendation.

Our AuD degree is approved for the Western Regional Graduate Program. If you reside in a selected state determined by the WRGP program, you may be eligible to apply for in-state tuition. For more information see the WRGP website.

If English is not the applicant's native language, the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL) and Test of Spoken English (TSE) will also be required.

We will weigh the entire application to determine the ability of the student to complete the program successfully.

Prerequisite Information for Graduate Students. An undergraduate degree in Speech and Hearing Sciences is not a prerequisite for admission into our graduate program. Those who apply to our graduate program from other fields are required to complete a series of prerequisite undergraduate classes before full admittance to the graduate program. The CSD prerequisite requirements are mandated by the American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA). The prerequisites and example courses from the undergraduate curriculum are listed below. While it is intended that the majority of these prerequisites courses be completed prior to application to the graduate program, students may complete up to three courses as deficiency requirements after acceptance into the graduate program.

I. 15 credit hours of “Normal Communication:”

CSD 3100 - Phonetics, CSD 3120 - Anatomy of Speech and Hearing, CSD 4400 - Language Science, CSD 5380 - Speech and Language Development, CSD 4200 - Hearing Science (for AuD students) or CSD 4300 - Speech Science (for Speech-Language Pathology students)

II. Courses in hearing disorders and rehabilitation:

CSD 4500 - Introduction to Audiology CSD 5520 - Aural Habilitation and Rehabilitation

III. Twelve allied course credits: Allied courses must include three credits in each of the following four areas:

  • Statistics (e.g., upper division level of statistics, for example; FCS 3210, PSY 3000, SOC 3112, Statistics for the behavioral sciences, etc.)

  • Physical Science ( Physics or Chemistry)

  • Biological Science (Biology or Nutrition)

  • Social and Behavioral Science (e.g., Psychology, Sociology, Cultural Anthropology, etc.)

customFields.nHBHl:
The School of Dance (SOD) has a relatively small graduate program, admitting 3-6 incoming students each year, with an average of 7-10 total students at any given time. We have been working for the past few years to streamline curricular offerings for our graduate programs to alleviate faculty workload pressures and increase synergies across the two MFA degrees (Ballet & Modern Dance).

For the past several years, much of the curriculum between the two MFA degrees has overlapped with a few distinctions to ensure the degrees are indeed discrete. This proposal, in part, makes these overlaps (“meets with”) more official by consolidating courses and content. The proposed revised curricular plan also creates a course rotation to support enrollment management and alleviate faculty workload, while ensuring that all graduate students can complete the MFA degree in two years.

For currently enrolled students, a plan has already been implemented to ensure they will complete their degrees on time. (See the SOD MFA Bridge Plan for details). The SOD DOGS and Director have been in close communication with current students who are aware of the pending shifts. These changes will not negatively impact any students or slow time to graduation.

(Total credits for the degree will remain 60. Current discrepancies showing in Coursedog are because proposed course changes are pending.)

customFields.ztYeO:
Year after year, Utah ranks among one of the top states for business and careers, personal income growth, family prosperity, and quality of life. Despite this and promises of a great future, many individuals, families, and communities across the state experience hardship, notably around behavioral health. Utahns experience particularly high rates of mental illness. The use of illicit opioids, specifically fentanyl, is increasing among adults in Utah. In 2020, suicide was the leading cause of death for individuals ages 10-24, and the second leading cause of death for those ages 25-34. Compounding these behavioral health issues, there is a shortage of behavioral healthcare professionals throughout the state. A majority (97%) of counties in Utah are designated as Health Professional Shortage Areas (UMEC, 2021). Without an adequate supply of behavioral healthcare professionals, rates of mental illness, substance use, and suicide may increase.

In response to these issues, educators, practitioners, administrators, and policymakers across the state have recommended that additional opportunities (e.g., expand existing certification programs, create a one-year behavioral health technician voluntary state certification programs, create a bachelor's level generalist behavioral health license) be made for individuals to enter the behavioral health workforce sooner rather than later. Understanding these recommendations, not to mention the broader issues, the Utah System of Higher Education (USHE), through the Talent Ready Utah Program, has allotted funding (~$800,000) to degree-granting institutions or technical colleges within the USHE to develop and implement a Behavioral Health Technician certification program for undergraduate-level students. Currently, Utah's behavioral health workforce consists of 27% undergraduate-level behavioral health workers, versus 73% graduate-level behavioral health clinicians. In an effort to alleviate the behavioral healthcare professional workforce shortage, a sufficient supply of behavioral healthcare workers, including BHT's, who are rigorously educated and trained is necessary to meet the behavioral healthcare needs of thousands of Utah adults and children.

The College of Social Work Academic Advising team provides responsive and comprehensive academic advising to prospective and current CSW students each semester. Current students create a comprehensive graduation plan with their academic advisor and are expected to meet with their academic advisor at least once a semester to ensure progress and timely program completion.

Academic advisors provide proactive outreach to students who may be struggling in classes; track students' progress toward degree completion; and refer students to academic and social support resources. Academic advising is available to current and prospective students in person and via video conference as well as by appointment and during drop-in advising hours. Students enrolled in the BHC program will be assigned to a specific advisor who has been trained in the program curriculum and plan of study.

The College of Social Work Admissions and Advising team participates in recruitment events and presentations throughout the year. These events include tabling sessions focused on providing program information to community members; high school students; community college students; and current undergraduate students. The Admissions and Advising team also provides live and video presentations throughout the year to community college classes and undergraduate classes. The Admissions and Advising team regularly provides live and virtual Q&A sessions for prospective students interested in certificate programs, undergraduate, and graduate programs.

The College of Social Work (CSW) also has an embedded marketing/public relations team. This team is instrumental in developing advertising materials for the CSW and will be tasked with developing new recruitment materials for the BHC program.
customFields.qeWTW: One of the top priorities of Governor Cox and the State of Utah is to increase the number of behavioral healthcare workers in Utah. Implementation of the BHC program will help to contribute to the educational training of this future workforce. Students completing the BCH program will be employable in relevant occupational fields within 12 months of beginning the program. According to the US Bureau of Labor and Statistics, the overall employment of psychiatric technicians and aides (which is comparable to the Behavioral Health Technician) is projected to grow nine percent from 2022 to 2032, much faster than the average for all occupations. There is a growing demand for Behavioral Health Technicians and this certificate will lead to gainful employment upon completion.
customFields.wFFLu: The mission of USHE, University of Utah, and College of Social Work are in alignment with one another, provide accessible, valuable, innovative, and affordable higher education opportunities for students to improve their overall quality of life, expand their wellbeing and mobility, and enhance their cultural awareness. The BHT certificate can lead to gainful employment as a stand-alone certificate, but it is also a pathway to all levels of higher education. customFields.cJsXu:
The BHC program will be offered through the College of Social Work and will provide an educational pathway to the BSW program. The BHC program includes five courses providing 17 credit hours of didactic instruction. These 17 credit hours consist of required courses already in the BSW program. Students enrolled in the BSW program have the opportunity to complete the certificate program for no additional cost in 12-18 months prior to finishing their BSW degree. Most, if not all, of these credit hours could be transferred to a BSW program at a different institution as well.

In addition, students in the certificate program will be required to take a crisis intervention course. This course was developed in collaboration with the Utah Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), and students who successfully complete the course are eligible for crisis intervention certification through the State. This provides an additional, no-cost, professional certification as part of the BHC program.

Completing the BHC program will provide 3 credit hours towards the requirements for the State Social Service Worker (SSW) license.

Completing the BHC program will also strengthen future applications to a Master of Social Work (MSW) degree program. The additional 5 non-didactic credit hours in professional development and experiential clinical simulations may be important considerations in the MSW application review process; thus, these students will have additional education and experience to support their applications. Successful attainment of a MSW degree is a requisite for the State Certified Social Worker (CSW) license and the State Licensed Clinical Social Work (LCSW) license.

USHE's call for proposals for this grant was not limited to schools of social work, but at this time, it appears mainly social work programs applied. The CSW application built the certificate around CSW course work and was funded as such. The long-term intent is to work with interested programs on campus to develop a map of complementary courses that meet the learning objectives and are available in students home departments.

catalogFullDescription:
Biomedical Engineering (BME) is the application of the principles and tools of engineering to the enhancement of scientific research and problem solving in the biological, pharmacological, and medical fields. In addition to receiving a firm and comprehensive foundation in the physical sciences and engineering, students in Utah’s undergraduate Biomedical Engineering program obtain a strong background in biology and physiology as well as the physical sciences and mathematics. This foundation serves as the the source for ideas, inspiration, and concepts to solve engineering problems in modern healthcare. The program requires four full-time years to complete for students with a complete high school mathematics and science background.

Biomedical Engineering is of particular relevance and benefit to students with interests in the application and relationship of biology, mathematics, chemistry, and physics to medicine and health. An undergraduate degree in Biomedical Engineering is also particularly effective preparation for studies in medicine, dentistry, and veterinary medicine

catalogFullDescription:
The Biological Chemistry Program is a collaborative program between seven basic science departments. The Program serves the students and faculty of the University of Utah by providing excellence in graduate education. The Program coordinates relevant activities and provides interdisciplinary training during the first year of graduate school that is designed to equip students with a strong foundation for a career at the interface of biology and chemistry. The Program coordinates activities such as student recruiting and admissions, academic advising, career development, curriculum, and social events.

Following the first year, students leave the Program and formally enter one of the seven science departments to continue thesis research in one of the laboratories of the Program faculty. MS students defend their thesis research in a public forum. The public defense is followed by an oral comprehensive examination administered by the thesis committee. Copies of the thesis must be given to the advisor, each member of the supervisory committee and to the bioengineering graduate program coordinator at least two weeks prior to the defense. The committee can pass the candidate, pass the candidate contingent upon the candidate’s successfully responding to issues raised at the defense, or fail the candidate. learningOutcomes.name: Students will be able to apply the principles of natural selection and mechanisms of genetic change, including trait variation and heritability, to explain the observed diversity of life that has arisen over long-term as well as recent evolutionary time frames.

Students will be able to apply a knowledge of genetics, gene expression, growth and development, signal perception and transduction, and physiological regulation to explain how information is stored, transmitted and utilized in biological contexts.

Students will be able to apply knowledge of molecular, cellular, and organismal structures to explain the diverse set of functions - ranging from the sub cellular to behavioral to ecological - that underlie the remarkable diversity of individual organisms as well as communities of organisms.

Students will be able to explain how biological units interact to give rise to emergent properties at multiple levels of biological organization. These interactions range from the cycling of matter and energy at the subcellular to organismal to biogeochemical scales to the interaction and interdependency of organisms, including humans, with their environment.

Students will be able to apply the process of science to identify knowledge gaps, formulate hypotheses, and test them against experimental and observational data to advance an understanding of the natural world.

Students will be able to use mathematical and computational methods and tools to describe living systems and be able to apply quantitative approaches, such as statistics, quantitative analysis of dynamic systems, or mathematical modeling.

Students will be able to apply concepts and subdisciplinary knowledge from within and outside of biology in order to interpret biological phenomena, communicate with clear written and oral arguments, and work collaboratively to solve problems.

Students will be able to evaluate the interactions between biology and society, including the societal impacts of biological research as well as public perception and decision-making about science, and clearly communicate biological concepts and their implications to broad audiences.
Students will be able to apply biological concepts around environmental and human health to develop informed opinions on economic and societal issues.

catalogFullDescription: The Master of Statistics program is an interdepartmental, interdisciplinary program at the University of Utah. Begun in 1976, this is arguably the oldest program of its kind still on campus. The program awards an MStat, which is a professional, non-thesis degree in statistics. It is administered by the University Statistics Committee, by agreement with the chairs of participating departments. Current tracks (participating departments) are biostatistics (Family and Preventive Medicine), econometrics (Economics), educational psychology, mathematic and sociology. Graduates of the Master of Statistics program have gone on to doctoral study and faculty roles at this and other universities, positions such as vice-presidents of health care corporations and pharmaceutical company leadership, as well as roles as statistical analysts and consultants at this university and elsewhere. The MStat in Biostatistics is housed within the Division of Public Health at the Department of Family and Preventive Medicine in the School of Medicine. The goal of this track is to provide the student with a good foundation in the basics of applied statistics, the fundamentals of numerous problems in the areas of health, an ability to apply statistical knowledge to health-related data, an ability to understand the problems and deal with the personalities of health care personnel and an ability to use computers to good advantage. For well-prepared students, this is a two and a half year program. Students with less preparation will need to extend their time in the program. In addition many MStat students are part-time, as they also have a full-time job or family responsibilities. As a track in an interdepartmental program, the track leadership is rotated among track faculty, approximately annually. There is a biostatistics director in the Division of Public Health, who assists coordination between the public health programs and the biostatistics track. Graduates of the biostatistics track of the MStat program are prepared to assume biostatistical consulting positions in which study design, project management and data analysis and reporting skills are required. Typically, these include state and local public health organizations, health care delivery systems, universities and medical schools, governmental health agencies and the pharmaceutical industry. The track's graduates have pursued careers in the pharmaceutical and health care industries, as well as going on to PhD programs. While applications from students with varied backgrounds will be considered, the MStat-Biostatistics is primarily intended to enhance the skills and career development of those with a bachelor's in mathematics, statistics or a related field, with coursework in calculus, statistics, programming, matrix algebra and biology.

customFields.QvDbS:
Consistency with Institutional Mission and Goals

University of Utah Mission

The University of Utah’s mission emphasizes student success, innovative research, and improving health and quality of life. This program is consistent with these goals by:

  1. Student Success and Workforce Development:

    • The program prepares students for high-demand careers in healthcare data analytics, clinical informatics, and biomedical AI, aligning with the university’s focus on fostering career-ready graduates.

    • The program emphasizes hands-on training with real-world applications, ensuring graduates are equipped with the competencies to succeed in competitive job markets both locally and nationally​.

  2. Advancing Research and Innovation:

    • The focus on translational bioinformatics and biomedical AI encourages groundbreaking research in genomics, precision medicine, and AI-driven healthcare solutions, advancing knowledge and innovation​​.

    • Interdisciplinary collaboration with community and industry partners like Intermountain Health and ARUP Laboratories enhances research opportunities, supporting the university’s strategic goals.

  3. Improving Health and Quality of Life:

    • By educating professionals capable of implementing data-driven solutions in healthcare systems, the program addresses key challenges in improving health outcomes and reducing disparities​.

Alignment with Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine (SFESOM) Mission

The SFESOM mission centers around improving individual and community health outcomes through excellence in education, research, and equitable patient care. This program aligns by:

  1. Educating Future Professionals:

    • Tracks such as Applied Clinical Informatics, Biomedical AI and Data Science, and Translational Bioinformatics emphasize patient-centered care, equity, and advanced research, fostering professionals who can address pressing healthcare needs​​.

  2. Serving Underserved Communities:

    • The program’s emphasis on addressing healthcare disparities through informatics tools supports SFESOM’s priority of serving rural and underserved communities. Graduates are equipped to develop innovative solutions that improve access to quality healthcare​​.

  3. Fostering Professionalism and Respect:

    • The program promotes respect and accountability in collaborative, interdisciplinary learning environments, consistent with SFESOM’s values of professionalism and teamwork​.

Discussion with Other USHE Institutions

  1. Utah Tech and BYU Bioinformatics Programs:

    • Programs like the BS in Bioinformatics at Utah Tech and BYU focus primarily on undergraduate-level training in genomics, computational biology, and related fields​​. While these programs lay the groundwork, they lack advanced degrees in biomedical informatics, positioning the University of Utah’s program as the critical next step for students seeking to further their education and career.

  2. Collaboration and Complementarity:

    • The new Bioinformatics BS at the University of Utah’s Math Department complements the master’s program in Biomedical Informatics, creating a natural pipeline for students transitioning to graduate studies​.

    • These developments highlight the program’s role in fostering collaboration and ensuring a seamless educational pathway for students across institutions.

Local and State Focus (Utah)

  1. Health Informatics and Technologists:

    • Utah’s projected annual growth for health technologists is robust, supported by the shift to electronic health records (EHRs) and data-driven healthcare solutions (DWS)​​.

  2. Data Scientists and Analysts:

    • Data science roles in Utah are expanding, particularly in Salt Lake and Provo-Orem metro areas, with a high annual growth rate of 5.79% and competitive median wages of $46.87/hour (DWS)​​.

  3. Healthcare Managers and Administrators:

    • Local growth is driven by healthcare expansion and administrative needs. The salary benchmark exceeds $100,000 annually, making this a lucrative career path (DWS)​​.

National Data

  1. Health Informatics Careers:

    • National growth for health information technologists is projected at 16%, far outpacing many other fields, with median wages of $33.78/hour. This highlights strong demand for advanced degrees in this area (OOH)​​.

    • A Master’s Degree in Health Informatics leads to roles such as clinical informatics manager, with salaries reaching $130,000 annually (Forbes)​.

  2. Data Science and Machine Learning:

    • These fields are among the fastest-growing nationwide, with expanding opportunities due to AI and data science adoption. A Master of Science in Machine Learning is particularly lucrative for leadership roles (OOH and Forbes)​​.

  3. Database-Related Occupations:

    • Database administrators and architects nationally earn median wages of $48.80/hour and $64.76/hour, respectively. The demand is bolstered by the rise of big data and analytics (OOH)​​.

  4. Healthcare Management Roles:

    • Healthcare management roles, such as Medical and Health Services Managers, are projected to grow 29% from 2023 to 2033, with salaries exceeding $110,000 annually (OOH)​.

catalogFullDescription:
Full-Time MBA Minimum Hours: 62

The primary objective of Full-time MBA program is to develop leaders who are effective in a range of responsible managerial positions in business firms, nonprofit institutions, or government agencies. Emphasis is placed upon clear definition of problem situations, analysis, and decision making. The teaching method employs a balanced mix of case analysis, student projects and presentations, computer simulations, lectures, and seminar discussions. Written and oral communication skills are stressed throughout the curriculum. The programs serve graduates from liberal arts, science, engineering, or other fields, as well as graduates form recognized colleges of business who want to study business administration. The Full-time MBA program requires two academic years of study (four semesters) and a summer internship for full-time students.

Executive MBA Minimum Hours: 48

The Executive MBA is designed to provide working executives with 6+ years work experience, the management skills to handle today's rapidly changing business environment. By creating a dynamic learning environment with advanced technology resources, the program offers opportunities for meaningful exchange between faculty experts, business leaders and executive level program participants. This program's unique curriculum and schedule allows executives to continue managing their business affairs with minimal disruption to work schedules.

The degree program is a 21-month program that meets one full day a week on alternating Fridays/Saturdays from 8:00 am to 5:00 pm. In addition to regular class work, there are two intensive week sessions at the beginning of each year and a two-week international field study at the end of the program. All Executive MBA students are admitted only for fall semester.

Executive MBA Admission Requirements: Degree requirements for students entering the Executive MBA program include a bachelor's degree from an accredited university or college, college algebra with a grade of B or better within the last ten years, six years work experience, and official report of GMAT score (unless waived by department in select cases). The following items should be submitted directly to the Executive Education Department of the David Eccles School of Business: EMBA Application, Resume, Essay, and Nomination Form and Letter from the applicant's employer. Transcripts, graduate application, and applicable fee should be submitted to the University's Admission Office.

Professional MBA Minimum Hours: 48

The Professional MBA is designed to accommodate the schedules of working professionals, this part-time option is to develop leaders who are effective in a range of responsible managerial positions in business firms, nonprofit institutions, or government agencies. Emphasis is placed upon clear definition of problem situations, analysis, and decision making. The teaching method employs a balanced mix of case analysis, student projects and presentations, computer simulations, lectures, and seminar discussions. Written and oral communication skills are stressed throughout the curriculum. The programs serve graduates from liberal arts, science, engineering, or other fields, as well as graduates form recognized colleges of business who want to study business administration.

Online MBA Program Minimum Hours: 48

The online program is designed to provide the same rigorous content from our world-renowned faculty in a convenient, high-quality, interactive, on-demand format. Our program allows for in-depth discussions between team members and with faculty using web conferencing, online forums, and multimedia. While all content in the online courses is available 24/7, students have the opportunity to interact with faculty and other students in a weekly live web-conferencing session.

customFields.qeWTW:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has pioneered remarkable advancements in the field of technology, most notably visible in the development and deployment of self-driving cars (Gulen, 2022). Companies like Tesla and Waymo have successfully implemented AI algorithms to navigate vehicles, manage traffic scenarios, and make real-time decisions, thus partially or fully automating the driving experience. Moreover, virtual assistants like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant have become integral parts of our daily lives, assisting with tasks ranging from setting reminders to providing weather updates (Rubin, 2023). These virtual assistants utilize sophisticated AI algorithms to comprehend and respond to user commands, showcasing the practical application of AI in enhancing user interactions with technology.

In healthcare, AI has made striking contributions, particularly in diagnostics and drug discovery (Qureshi, 2023). Google's DeepMind, for instance, has developed an AI that can identify eye diseases in scans, facilitating early detection and intervention for conditions that might otherwise go unnoticed until later stages. Similarly, AI is being utilized to expedite the traditionally lengthy and complex drug discovery process. Companies like Atomwise employ AI to predict the efficacy of drug formulations, significantly reducing the time and resources required to bring effective therapeutic solutions to market.

AI has also revolutionized the financial sector, particularly in areas like algorithmic trading and fraud detection (Grosu, 2023). Many trading firms leverage AI algorithms to execute trades at speeds and frequencies that are unattainable for human traders, thus optimizing trading strategies and maximizing profits. On the other hand, AI plays a crucial role in safeguarding financial transactions and protecting users against fraud. For instance, Mastercard employs AI systems to monitor card usage patterns and promptly identify and flag potentially fraudulent activities, thereby enhancing the security of digital transactions.

In the retail industry, AI has been instrumental in enhancing customer service and personalizing the user experience (Zia, 2023). Many retailers deploy chatbots, powered by AI, to interact with customers, answer inquiries, and provide assistance, ensuring that users have access to instant support. Furthermore, AI algorithms analyze customer data to personalize marketing strategies, tailoring product recommendations and promotional offers to individual preferences and shopping habits. This not only optimizes marketing efficacy but also enhances the customer shopping experience by making it more personalized and user-friendly.

These examples provide tangible evidence of AI's impact across various sectors, demonstrating its practical applications and the substantial benefits it brings to different industries. While the historical achievements of Artificial Intelligence (AI) are noteworthy, envisioning its future trajectories presents a separate and equally compelling consideration, as outlined in the following points:

• AI will power 95% of all customer interactions by 2025 including live conversations (Lauder, 2017)

• According to a PWC report, 38% of U.S. jobs are at risk of automation by the early 2030s (Nelson, 2017).

• As per The NY Times article, 47 percent of U.S. jobs could be replaced by robots, automated technology and automated intelligence (AI) in 20 years (Kessler, 2023)

• Gartner expects that by 2024, organizations will lower operational costs by 30% by combining hyper-automation technologies with redesigned operational processes (Rimol, 2021).

• Open AI states that 19% of jobs have at least 50% of their tasks exposed to LLMs (just one form of AI) (Elondou et al., 2023)

• Open AI states that higher-wage occupations generally present more tasks with high exposure to LLMs (Elondou et al., 2023)

• According to McKinsey & Co., AI & related tech will increase productivity by 0.2 to 3.3 percent PER YEAR from 2023 to 2040 (Chui & Yee, 2023).

• According to McKinsey & Co., total economic impact of AI is estimated at: $6.1 trillion to $7.9 trillion annually (Chui et al., 2023). That is the equivalent of the entire GDP of Japan and the UK, the #3 and #5 economies in the world.

Clearly, the demand for professionals with AI and business expertise is on the rise, making the AI Business Minor a valuable asset in the job market. Graduates of this program will have a competitive edge and a wide range of career opportunities available to them. Emerging fields such as data science, machine learning engineering, and AI consulting are experiencing rapid growth, and students who possess expertise in these areas will be well-positioned for success in the evolving landscape of AI technology.

According to a report by Burning Glass Technologies, AI/ML skills are among the top 4 fastest growing (The other three are Cloud Computing, Product Management and social media), highest demand skills disrupting the US job market in 2022 (Glassdoor, 2023). Additionally, a survey by LinkedIn found that AI was one of the top 15 emerging jobs for 2023 (Faraut, 2023). In addition,

• The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects that employment in computer and information technology occupations, which includes roles related to AI, is expected to grow by 11% from 2019 to 2029, which is much faster than the average for all occupations (BLS, 2023).

• According to a report by Gartner, AI will create 2.3 million jobs by 2022 (Rimol, 2021).

• A report by CNBC revealed that jobs mentioning AI skills have more than doubled in the past year 2022-2023 (Kiderlin, 2023).

• A report by Glassdoor found that machine learning engineer was among top 10 bests job in the US in 2022, based on factors such as job satisfaction, median base salary, and the number of job openings (Glassdoor, 2023).

In terms of job roles, there are a wide range of opportunities for individuals with AI skills in the tech industry, including data scientists, machine learning engineers, AI developers, and AI consultants. These roles often require a combination of technical and business skills, making a Minor in Business AI particularly relevant.

Eccles students are also fully aware of the prominence and relevance of AI. An April 2023 survey conducted among 74 predominantly freshman and sophomore business students revealed that all of them are familiar with AI, not surprising yet a staggering figure. On a scale of 1-5, the average interest level in enrolling in an AI minor program was moderately high at 3.51. When asked about the importance of AI education, the average response was slightly higher at 3.72, indicating a moderate to high perceived importance. Regarding the significance of AI skills for future careers, students rated this very high, with an average response of 4.26 out of 5, suggesting that students perceive AI skills as crucial for their professional future. Topics of interest are Strategy and AI, and Machine Learning.

Overall, there is strong demand for individuals with AI skills in the tech industry, and a Minor in Business AI can provide a competitive edge in the job market by demonstrating a strong understanding of both the technical and business applications of AI.

catalogFullDescription:
The CVP program is designed to educate students and prepare them with the knowledge, skills, and expertise necessary to graduate as licensed cardiovascular perfusionists. These individuals are vital members of the cardiovascular surgical team as they are responsible for running the heart-lung (cardiopulmonary bypass) machine and are heavily relied on by surgeons. During surgery, they utilize the appropriate equipment to maintain blood flow to the body’s tissues and regulate levels of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood. Perfusionists are also responsible for measuring selected laboratory values and monitoring circulation. They also administer medicines through the cardiopulmonary bypass circuit, among other responsibilities in the surgical setting. Our program graduates will meet the requirements necessary to succeed in a field where surgical techniques, cardiopulmonary bypass techniques, and new technologies are constantly changing the way we practice medicine.

The CVP program is intended to attract current allied health professionals, recent baccalaureate graduates, and qualified individuals to learn the advanced perfusion techniques needed for successful careers in cardiovascular surgery. The CVP is a 24-month (6 semester) post-baccalaureate degree that begins with three semesters (48 credit hours) of full time didactic and laboratory education, with students also doing clinical observations at the University of Utah hospital. The didactic portion of the curriculum for this program includes: Master’s level anatomy, physiology, pharmacology, perfusion technology, laboratory, research methods, and a masters project. The last three semesters (34 credit hours) will comprise of a clinical phase which includes full-time clinical rotations under the direct supervision of a preceptor at top notch hospitals throughout the United States.

Academic Advising:

Angela Rasmussen is currently the ECE Undergraduate curriculum chair along with being the Director of Mentoring and Advising for the ECE department. Therefore, all changes considered academic advising impact along with the curricular impact. Once approval is completed for proposals, the advising team is ready to communicate the changes with students. A communication plan has already been discussed and will be sent out this Spring semester to inform students of these changes. Additionally, advisors are prepared to discuss changes and their impact with students during meetings.

USHE:

Angela Rasmussen is also the USHE Electrical Engineering Chair currently and has discussed both the CE and EE changes with all Utah state school representatives. She is also working with Steve Hood and Cyd Grua to update the changes in the articulation guides to ease the transition for transfer students. Meetings have already been initiated to coordinate efforts with SLCC to also implement these changes.

catalogFullDescription: Ever since we could ponder, humans have inquired about the mind. How does the mind work? What kind of a thing is a mind? How do our thoughts tell us about the world around us? Are these thoughts accurate? These questions have been asked for thousands of years. With twentieth century developments in mathematics, logic, computing, and attempts to build artificial intelligence, theorists from a variety of scientific and theoretical fields began to develop an intriguing thesis: The mind is a kind of computer. Most simply, when new information comes in to the mind, that information is processed according to a set of rules and by drawing upon relevant information from stored memory, all to deliver some kind of output, for example a decision or an action. These were the basics of early modern computing, and applying them to the study of mind has proved a fruitful and exciting research agenda. Today"s cognitive scientists don"t all commit to the thesis that the mind is a computer. But they do all commit to the same pursuit as early human thinkers, namely, figuring out how the mind works. Cognitive science today is a richly interdisciplinary pursuit of knowledge, involving anthropologists, computer scientists, engineers, linguists, philosophers, psychologists, roboticists, and others. As a cognitive science minor, you will have the opportunity to engage this exciting new field, taking a variety of courses from each of the contributing disciplines. And because this research is so young, not only will you learn the latest developments, you will have the rare opportunity to contribute to those developments!

catalogFullDescription:
Chemistry is the study of matter, what it is made of, how it changes, and how it can be turned into new substances. Chemistry is central to our search for answers as we explore our world. "What is it?" "How much is there?" "How does this work?" "Why does it do that?" If you’ve ever asked any of these questions, consider studying chemistry to find the solutions. The Chemistry major offers ten emphasis areas to choose from, and can declare up to two emphases from the following areas:

  • ACS Professional Chemistry

  • Atmospheric & Environmental Chemistry

  • Biology

  • Business

  • Chemical Engineering

  • Geology

  • Material Sciences and Engineering

  • Mathematics

  • Physics

  • Teaching

As a graduate of the U’s chemistry program, a number of job opportunities are available to you. You could become a chemist in private industry, government, or education; pursue professional training in medicine, dentistry, pharmacy or other health-related fields; or work in areas such as environmental science and engineering, forensics, business, and law. Some alumni have been employed as educators, software developers, and chemical engineers. Careers in higher education, as professors, researchers, and administrators, are also possible with additional schooling.

catalogFullDescription:
Research programs leading to the Chemistry Doctor of Philosophy degree are offered in the areas of analytical, biological, inorganic, materials, organic, and physical chemistry and in chemical physics. Please refer to our website www.chem.utah.edu to learn about the research interests of our faculty members.

All graduate students are encouraged to select a research director and to begin their thesis research no later than the end of the second semester in residence. The graduate program is flexible in order to meet the specific objectives of the candidate. It is possible to work on a problem involving collaborations with more than one faculty member.

At the beginning of the third year, all students must pass an informal oral examination designed to assure that significant progress has been made in the design and execution of the Ph.D. research project. Students are required to give a seminar in the Department. The Ph.D. course of study typically requires 4-5 years. The final requirement for graduation is an oral defense of a thesis written by the candidate as a formal exposition of his or her research accomplishments.

The Graduate Education Committee monitors the progress of students. This committee handles all problems students might have with degree requirements and is the place to go to seek clarification and consideration.

catalogFullDescription:
It is the versatility of chemical engineers that makes them attractive to so many industries and professions. The current state of the profession is being transformed by the needs of increasingly diverse industries. The companies that have recently hired our undergraduates make diverse products and provide a range of services: medical devices, cement, combustion engineering, energy engineering, semiconductors, personal care products, mineral processing, petroleum refining, oil services, energy production, water purification, environmental engineering, natural gas pipelines, and petrochemicals. A number of recent graduates have been admitted to graduate school, law school, and medical school.

The undergraduate program prepares students in fundamentals while providing exposure in diverse areas of chemical engineering. The core subjects in chemical engineering include fluid mechanics, heat transfer, chemical thermodynamics, reaction engineering, mass transfer, and separations. An Emphasis in Energy Engineering is available.

The Department has a strong record of involving students in research and cooperative education experiences. Roughly 80 % of our graduating seniors have had co-op or research experience and many have had both.

customFields.rfMyo:
These new emphases were initiated by a separate push from our Student Advisory Committee (SAC) and our Industrial Advisory Board (IAB). Over this year our SAC has held monthly student "town halls" and we have used our undergraduate seminar to gather student input. One of the most common request from the students was the addition of new emphases in these four areas. They have reasoned that they would be more competitive for specific chemical engineering areas that match their passions, if they can demonstrate an emphasis on their transcript in that area. Separately, our industrial advisory board, at our latest meeting, expressed a need for students with elevated skills in the emphasis areas proposed herein. Each emphasis was modeled after the structure of our existing Energy Engineering Emphasis, but the technical electives were selected by the Undergraduate Committee of the Chemical Engineering Department with the input of our SAC. The new emphases were also introduced to the entire faculty at faculty meeting with no objections.

All of our students will be eligible to benefit from the proposed emphases. However, engineering education research has demonstrated that engineering disciplines that are perceived as "helping professions" have a greater chance to attract students who are traditionally underrepresented in engineering fields, such as women and ethnic minorities. We believe the benefit to the environment and human health inherent in the Environmental and Biochemical emphases will both help inform students about the "helping profession" nature of chemical engineering.

Only 40% of our students are interested in going into biochemical engineering and about 5-10% of our graduates end up working in that area. This is consistent with recent trends in chemical engineering industry (about 5% of members of the national chemical engineering organization, AIChE, work in biochemical engineering). Our students who are aiming to enter other fields of chemical engineering, such as battery technology or semiconductors, do not benefit as much from this course; these credit hours could be better spent on technical electives that are more relevant to their careers.

This change has been discussed for years in our department but it was put to the forefront by a proposal from our student advisory committee. It was then discussed by our undergraduate subcommittee and given unanimous support. It was then approved unanimously by the entire faculty.
customFields.QvDbS:
All new emphases will give greater guidance and recognition to our students wishing to target specific industries in which chemical engineers may work. By aiding them match their passions and goals to specific courses, and giving them recognition as having an expertise in that area, we will boost engagement and facilitate their success. These students will also position themselves well to conduct UROP research and be hired by faculty research programs that focus on each emphasis area.

This set of emphases will cater to the variety of student interests we see in our incoming students. Further, engineering education research has shown that emphasizing the "helping profession" aspect of engineering is more likely to attract populations who have been traditionally discouraged from engineering spaces. Both the new Environmental & Sustainability and Biochemical & Bioprocessing emphasis demonstrate the "helping profession" aspects of chemical engineering. Each emphases will contribute to the general ideal of chemical engineering professional ethics to design processes that are efficient and without negative impact on the environment. customFields.7nJtQ:
According to the Occupation Outlook Handbook "Employment of chemical engineers is projected to grow 14 percent from 2021 to 2031, much faster than the average for all occupations." The last two initial placement surveys of chemical engineers by the American Institute of Chemical Engineers (AIChE), show the percentage of chemical engineers entering Environmental Engineering Services, Electronics & Semiconductors, and Biotechnology all increased, attesting to the fact that these area are growth areas for chemical engineers. While Data Science was not a tracked category in the latest AIChE survey (2017), according to the Utah DWS Economic Data site, data science is the top growth area in the state, which we see in the jobs being offered to our students. Recently, Texas Instruments has announced an $11 billion investment in Utah semiconductor processing operations. Many of our students already enter the semiconductor processing field, with this new investment in our state, we will need to increase our output of students who have specialized in semiconductor processing to meet the demand. The semiconductor field also relies heavily on chemical engineers with environmental experience to manage hazardous waste from these processes. Students with data science and computational expertise are also needed to support the automation and experimental design needed to create semiconductor devices economically.

By converting the required credits for biochemical engineering into technical electives, we will give our students more paths to graduation and more opportunities to target chemical engineering industries in which they wish to work. This change will also allow them to focus more on emerging chemical engineering technologies. Furthermore, with the new general education requirements from USHE, a life science course will be a part of every student's college experience. Removing this biochemical engineering course, will not leave our students without instruction on biology.
