catalogFullDescription:
The MS in Clinical Investigation (MSCI) is a post-graduate program that provides classroom and mentored experience in clinical research and innovation, preparing its trainees for careers in academic medicine, the allied health sciences, and global health related fields. The Program welcomes trainees who have or are pursuing graduate degrees in clinical and translational science (medicine, dentistry, nursing, physical therapy, pharmacy, and the biosciences) and trainees with engineering or business degrees who are involved in health care systems. The MSCI Program prepares trainees to be competitive investigators and team members working broadly within the clinical and translational science realm. Candidates for the MSCI degree elect to complete one of three tracks of study: Track 1 (Med into Grad) emphasizes the inherited basis of human disease, mechanism-oriented clinical research, and bench-to-bedside translational research. Track 2 (Clinician Scientist) emphasizes epidemiology, health services research, and bedside-to-community translational research. Emphasis (Global Health Innovation and Technology) emphasizes human-centered design, principles of innovation, and global translational research.

The curriculum for the MSCI program begins in July for Track 2 candidates with a four-week intensive introductory session and in August for Emphasis candidates with a six-week intensive introductory session.

The Clinical Pharmacology graduate program at the University Of Utah School Of Medicine is an innovative, interdisciplinary program that trains students to conduct research encompassing methodology from clinical pharmacology perspectives. The program was designed specifically for students who are interested in clinical pharmacology and translational research and share our goal of advancing the science of pharmacology and
therapeutics to improve the safe and effective use of drugs by patients. In our program, students will study clinical pharmacology of various drugs prescribed to adult patient as well as to pregnant women, neonates, children, adolescent, and elderly patients. Students will focus on new routes of drug administration, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of newly discovered drugs, optimization of dosing of drugs requiring therapeutic drug monitoring, pharmacometrics, developmental pharmacology, pharmacogenomics, immunotherapy, and translational research in a highly individualized course of study that will be chosen in close consultation with their advisors.

The student will be required to perform an oral dissertation defense. customFields.ztYeO:
While the Certificate in Scoring for Film and Games-BMus Composition Emphasis meets the needs

of composition students who are interested in composing music with visual media, the Certificate in Composing Music for Film and Games meets the needs of students who are interested in composing music with visual media but are not pursuing a degree in music composition. While the certificate

is open to all university students, it is likely that most of the students in the certificate will be music majors or students double majoring in Film & Media Arts and Music. This certificate would

provide opportunities for these students to pursue more rigorous and structured instruction in this interdisciplinary field than either major is able to provide on its own. It would also provide a way for students in our B.A. in Music to focus their electives into a structured interdisciplinary field focusing of film and music. Students in the B.A. in Music could pursue this certificate and count most of its credits as part of their B.A. in Music degree.

Additionally, there are quite a few film students in our music technology courses already. At this point, film students take these courses as electives, and they use the technical skills they learn in these courses to create soundtracks to their film projects. However, there is no incentive for film students to pursue further studies in music that would provide the sort of instructional background needed to actually compose music with any awareness of aesthetic and technical composition practices. With the certificate in place, there would be a stronger incentive for film students to consider pursuing more music courses, and perhaps even a B.A. in Music, along with their undergraduate bachelor degree in Film.

Similarly, this certificate could appeal to students majoring in Entertainment Arts & Engineering. It could also interest students in other majors with or without previous musical experience. Only one of the certificate's required courses has a pre-requisite (FILM 1500 must be completed before taking FILM 2500). Many of the elective options do not have pre-requisites either. This makes the certificate very accessible for students of all majors and backgrounds.

catalogFullDescription: How does the mind work? How do our thoughts tell us about the world around us, and are these thoughts accurate? These questions have been asked for thousands of years, and it is against this background that the field of cognitive science emerged 35 years ago. With twentieth century developments in mathematics, logic, computing, and artificial intelligence, theorists from a variety of scientific and theoretical fields began to develop an intriguing thesis: the mind is a kind of computer. Most simply, when new information comes in to the mind, that information is processed according to a set of rules and by drawing upon relevant information from stored memory, all to deliver some kind of output. This was the basis of early modern computing, and applying these concepts to the study of the mind has proved a fruitful and exciting research agenda. Today's cognitive scientists don't all commit to the thesis that the mind is a computer, but they do all commit to the same pursuit as early human thinkers, namely, figuring out how the mind works. Cognitive science today is a richly interdisciplinary pursuit of knowledge, involving anthropologists, computer scientists, engineers, linguists, philosophers, psychologists, roboticists, and others.

catalogFullDescription: The Graduate Certificate in Community-Engaged Practices prepares future leaders in architecture, community development, design, sustainability, urban planning, public policy and other domains of social change to engage and work with currently underserved populations through sustainable, human-centered, participatory practices. Activities within the Certificate program aim to co-create applicable knowledge and build capacity among all stakeholders. Community engagement requires collaborative, reciprocal processes that recognize, respect, and value the knowledge, perspective, and resources shared among partners. Through academic studies and hands-on experience in the field, students work directly with communities that have been affected by systemic inequalities. Challenges addressed by the College in the past have included inadequate shelter, food and water scarcity, disaster preparedness and recovery, cultural resilience, and economic well-being. The Certificate focuses on critiquing theories of change and leadership models while developing the specialized skills to build community capacity through dialogue and collaborative processes.

Communication is a diverse discipline and offers a variety of training to prepare students for their careers. Students are able to focus on technical skills along with theoretically geared courses to develop a comprehensive portfolio to market themselves to industry. Students are encouraged to personalize their curricular choices to help meet professional/personal goals. For example, students often take elective courses that are outside of their specific emphasis to develop additional skills to be able to access different careers.

The Department of Communication offers a B.A. or B.S. in Communication with four emphases: Strategic Communication (public relations, advertising, integrated marketing); Journalism (digital, broadcast, print); Communication Studies; or Science, Health, Environmental, and Risk Communication. Regardless of your emphasis, a major in communication will provide you with knowledge on ethical communication, persuasion, social influence and social responsibility. Paired with improved skills in writing and speaking, you will be highly competitive in the job market.

Many students also look at the Communication Department to complement another major. Business, Sociology, Economics, and even Music majors often find a home in the Communication Department. These students look to supplement their education with a degree in Communication, leaving the U of U with a more complete set of skills.

Major Declaration

Students can declare their major in Communication upon admission to the University of Utah. Declaration can be completed by submitting our online declaration form here: https://communication.utah.edu/undergraduate/major-declaration.php

Requirements

17 Communication courses required, 51 minimum credits. Students will complete the major core (4 COMM courses) and one of the four emphasis options (13 COMM courses).

Transfer Students

Transfer students interested in a Communication major should contact the department. Certain courses may articulate between a previous school and the department. Transfer students may apply up to six articulated or equivalent courses from other institutions toward the major. Students with transfer Communication courses should meet with an advisor to discuss how their courses may be applied in the major.

learningOutcomes.name: Thinking analytically about the history, culture, and practice of digital technology requires a special kind of critical distance. If the history of technology teaches us anything, it is that it is very difficult to see the cultural and social stakes when one is surrounded by or naturalized to technological innovation and practice. In our current age of "ubiquitous computing," especially, new platforms, mobile devices, and networks seem to emerge daily, adding to an already crowded thicket; in other words, it is difficult to view the forest when we are surrounded by the trees. Understanding the relation of emerging technology to past, present, and shifting epistemes will be crucial to the Digital Cultural Studies Certificate Program. Critical thinking is therefore at its core.

Although the past decade has seen an enormous surge in interest surrounding "information technology," there has been a less than enormous surge to understand the precise meaning of that term, resulting in an uneven information literacy among even very skilled users of digital technology. The Digital Culture Studies Certificate Program aims to address this by considering important theoretical frameworks for understanding what information technology is, as well as the manner in which it relates to cultural production, aesthetic expression, and prior media forms.

Faculties and Resources

The University of Utah School of Dentistry (UUSOD) is administratively housed in the University of Utah Health

Sciences, providing direct academic and clinical connections with the U of U Healthcare Services program as well as health-related colleges (pharmacy and nursing), schools (medicine, including the physicians' assis- tants program), and related department personnel requisite for successful interdisciplinary substance use disorder (SUD) prevention program development and implementation. The main UUSOD facilities include the Ray and Tye Noorda Oral Health Sciences Building (~80,000 square feet) with ~80 dental operatories, ~20,000 square feet of administrative office space (~50 individual offices), 110-seat auditorium with distance-learning teleconferencing capacity, 7 classrooms and conference rooms (ranging from 60-10 person capacities)

and an attached covered parking structure (~200 parking spaces) to support large continuing education events with internet teleconferencing ability. The UUSOD is located in a relatively new (2015 completion), readily accessible structure ADA compliant building on the University of Utah campus. The conference rooms have the capacity to hold virtual meetings, trainings, and conferences. The UUSOD has access to

all technology, equipment, and instructional campus resources to include print services, video services, and website design. University Information Technology (UIT) provides all information technology services to the UUSOD, thus maintaining and securing information compliant with federal law and regulation. The UUSOD also has the capacity to conduct instructional telehealth clinics (V-TECH), web-based/on-demand events, using UUSOD-accessible existing equipment and software. The UUSOD now has eight clinical sites; (1) University Hospital, a six-chair clinic fully integrated with a major medical center (2) Wakara Way, a 82 chair stand-alone (non-integrated) clinic (3) Greenwood, a ten chair clinic physically contiguous with medical primary care and specialty clinics in a community setting, but separately administered (4) South Main, an oral health service using four dental operatories fully integrated administratively and financially within U Health's Department of Pediatrics-run family health clinic in a community setting (5) Liberty School, a four chair dental stand-alone clinic in a community setting (6) St. George, an six chair clinic contiguous with the Utah Technical University dental hygiene program in St. George, Utah (7) Rose Park, a twelve-chair clinic physically contiguous with an equal-dimension medical primary care clinic, the latter now in the process of being transferred by the State of Utah to UHealth, creating the opportunity for unique collaborative care, and (8) Ogden, a four chair stand-alone dental clinic in a community setting.

The SOD also manages a mobile dental service to underserved areas in rural, remote and frontier Utah, which like the fixed sites (7) and (8) above was formerly managed by the State of Utah. Oral health services are planned to be included in a new, U Health mental health crisis receiving center, and within a large outpatient and low-acuity inpatient community health center in an area of high social need.

The current personnel employed by the UUSOD serve 200 dental students and 11 general practice residents and include ~40 full-time and 100 part-time clinical/didactic faculty members and ~40 full-time administrative staff most of whom would be available to contribute and support, with an ~ annual budget of $28,000,000. The involvement of the dental profession in health initiatives relating to the prevention of substance abuse is of high priority for the UUSOD. It is extremely concerned about the devastating impact of substance abuse on oral health of the communities and is committed to developing effective solutions to these challenges.

The UUSOD worked closely with the Region 8 Central Rockies Addiction Technology Transfer Center (2012 - 2017) and is currently working with the Region 8 Mountain Plains Technology Transfer Center (beginning 2018) to establish innovative dental-related substance abuse prevention, intervention, and treatment pro- grams in the State of Utah such as: providing dental care to persons undergoing SUD treatment as part

of the FLOSS (Facilitating a Lifetime of Oral health Sustainability for Substance use disorder patients and families); implementing SBIRT (Screening, Brief Intervention and Referral to Treatment) training for healthcare pre-doctoral and post-graduate student; and programs to facilitate training of rural health care providers

in substance abuse prevention. Such programs have established the UUSOD as a pioneer in the creation and implementation of programs in the area of substance abuse prevention. The UUSOD has the capacity to provide culturally appropriate, state of the art, evidence-based training and technical assistance to the substance abuse prevention field.

Background Certificate in Digital Dentistry Program

The Certificate in Digital Dentistry was considered in the School of Dentistry Curriculum Committee. The Cur- riculum Committee voted unanimously to recommend approval of the program to the Executive Committee for its consideration. The Executive Committee considered the Curriculum Committees recommendation and voted unanimously to approve the Certificate in Digital Dentistry program.

As outlined in the Memorandum of Understanding, University Connected Learning has partnered with the School of Dentistry to provide program management services to enable the development of the online Digital Dentistry program. University Connected Learning will provide course development services, program marketing, recruitment coordination, and student success. The School of Dentistry will provide course content through faculty authors identified by the Digital Dentistry program.

Certificate in Digital Dentistry Structure

The Certificate in Foundational Digital Dentistry is administered by the Digital Dentistry Program Director who coordinates the Digital Dentistry program with course faculty.

1. Digital Modalities (Fall Semester): Students learn about digital modalities and additive/subtractive manufacturing.

2. Radiology & Fixed Prosthodontics (Fall Semester): Under the guidance of course faculty, students develop skills and knowledge in digital dentistry radiology and fixed prosthodontics.

3. Digital Restorative Dentistry I (Spring Semester): Under the guidance of course faculty, students develop skills and knowledge in digital dentistry in fixed prosthodontics, operative dentistry, and removable prostho- dontics dentistry.

4. Digital Restorative Dentistry II (Spring Semester): Under the guidance of the requisite course director, students develop skills and knowledge in digital dentistry fixed prosthodontics, operative dentistry, and removeable prosthetic dentistry. The content of this course builds on the content from Digital Restorative Dentistry I.

5. Digital Implant Dentistry & the Business of Digital Dentistry (Summer Semester): Under the guidance of the requisite course director, students develop skills and knowledge in digital dentistry implant surgery, implant prosthetics, and the business of digital dentistry.

The Digital Dentistry program is set up as a certificate program (15 credits) that builds into a master's program with an additional 21 credits to earn a Master of Digital Dentistry. Students will be taught in group settings with substantial on-line and experiential components. Course structure is determined by the Course Directors and may include mentoring, shared learning experiences, presentations, portfolios/projects, hands-on experience with digital software, off-site learning experiences, and independent projects. The Digital Dentistry program is designed for dental professionals who desire to learn about cutting age technologies. The Digital Dentistry program is intended to assist dental professionals in the expertise and adoption of in-office digital dentist equipment to meet the needs of patients. Students will gain the skills required to operate this equipment and become successful in the adoption of this new technology. The Digital Dentistry program is a part-time on-line higher education program that is conducive to dentists who are already in practice.

The program utilizes a sequencing and stackable model where student's complete coursework for a Cer- tificate in Foundational Digital Dentistry with an option to transitioning to a full Masters of Digital Dentistry which focuses on specialized procedures and advanced manufacturing in digital dentistry. Completion of the Certificate counts toward the Master of Digital Dentistry.

The UUSOD worked closely with the Region 8 Central Rockies Addiction Technology Transfer Center (2012 - 2017) and is currently working with the Region 8 Mountain Plains Technology Transfer Center (beginning 2018) to establish innovative dental-related substance abuse prevention, intervention, and treatment pro- grams in the State of Utah such as: providing dental care to persons undergoing SUD treatment as part

of the FLOSS (Facilitating a Lifetime of Oral health Sustainability for Substance use disorder patients and families); implementing SBIRT (Screening, Brief Intervention and Referral to Treatment) training for healthcare pre-doctoral and post-graduate student; and programs to facilitate training of rural health care providers

in substance abuse prevention. Such programs have established the UUSOD as a pioneer in the creation and implementation of programs in the area of substance abuse prevention. The UUSOD has the capacity to provide culturally appropriate, state of the art, evidence-based training and technical assistance to the substance abuse prevention field.

A proforma income statement has been established for both the low enrollment/high tuition and high enrollment/low tuition scenarios. We predict that the Digital Dentistry program will generate revenue sometime between 2024 and 2027, respective to enrollment. Strategic investment funds will be provided through University Connected Learning to enable work with designated faculty authors on course development projects. Tuition revenue from the Digital Dentistry program classes will be distributed with 70% of the revenue to the School of Dentistry and 30% to the university general fund. The revenue to the college is intended to cover instructor costs, student academic support costs, and any marketing activities beyond the foundational University Connected Learning provided services.

The net program income will be firstly used to recoup the costs of establishing the new program. It is estimated that those costs will be recouped in 2025-2026. Program expansion will become the next step for the program, seeking a body of international students and increased accessibility for students in the United States. Income will be used to establish and maintain national partnerships with technology distributors and to keep course materials and instruction current. Funds will also be used to increase availability of digital dentistry technology at the School of Dentistry, which will allow students and faculty to practice and research using these tools. The School of Dentistry has additional goals of increasing offerings in graduate degrees and certificates. The income and success of the Digital Dentistry program will establish the foundations of those programs.

It is expected that these programs will exclusively enroll practicing dentists. Exact enrollment targets have not been determined. Current available programs are targeted towards full-time students which is not conducive to dentists already in practice. Other courses have been offered through continuing education programs and vendor education. High interest in these non-academic programs indicates that there is strong demand for formalized and accredited degrees and certificates.

learningOutcomes.name: Students will be able to identify theories and approaches to disability as these intersect with gender, sexuality, class, ethnicity, race, religion, indigeneity, colonialism, and other social forces.

Students will be able to use disability and other theories of identity and injustice to evaluate how ableism, racism, sexism, and other social forces construct our worlds and to reveal power inequities within them.

Students will be able to understand the history of disability and related social movements, connect social movements of the past with those of the present, and articulate the theoretical implications of both.

Students will develop information literacy, assessing and evaluating the validity, reliability, and appropriateness of sources, including attending to the knowledge and perspectives of disabled people
Students will cogently synthesize, employ, and communicate theories and key concepts related to disability in analytical essays, creative projects, and research papers.
Students will communicate effectively and accessibly in written, oral, and online formats in an audience-appropriate manner.

Students will use knowledge of the historic and contemporary role and differential effects of ableism and disability on local and global systems to develop or advocate for informed action to solve complex problems in society.
Students will be able to identify their own cultural patterns and values in relation to disability, understanding how they shape attitudes to difference and relationships to power.

Students will be able to engage ethically with others in class and in the larger community; they will attend to and be accountable to diverse ways of being, thinking, seeing, and acting; and they will understand their positionality within interdependent communities.

catalogFullDescription: The Diplomacy major prepares students to work on some of the most consequential issues of the present. The field of Diplomacy is wide-ranging and interdisciplinary. Wherever competing interests and perspectives collide, the craft of diplomacy is critical. This major combines the study of the structural causes of conflict with the practice of real-world negotiation and consensus-building. It emphasizes technical, cultural, and communicational competencies alike. The program builds on key research strengths from across the University of Utah. It has four focus areas: 1) Tribal Sovereignty and Cultural Heritage; 2) Conflict, Displacement, and Humanitarian Affairs; 3) Health, Climate, and Sustainability; and 4) Science, Technology, and Society.

rules.description:
Students select one of four focus areas and then complete the additional requirements and electives as specified. Each of the focus areas are internally scaffolded with requirements of their own. These focus area requirements combine courses from Philosophy and History. A Philosophy course familiarizes students with some of the fundamental ethical and analytical dimensions of the themes or issues in question. A History course allows students to understand the specific, localized, and highly particular conditions that have produced the issues and conditioned the perspectives at stake, and which are necessary to envision productive responses to them.

While the particular course in Philosophy is issue-specific and can therefore be specified as one of the focus area requirements, the most appropriate History course(s) depend(s) upon the time and place of interest to the student and therefore cannot be specified quite so easily. The most appropriate History course(s) are to be selected in conversation with relevant faculty and especially the student’s major advisor. Any of the History courses identified under each focus area as relevant electives may be taken to satisfy the focus area requirement. However, the history courses listed do not exhaust all possible options; rather, the courses listed from History are only those that may bear on the topic in ways that may not be immediately apparent to non-specialists. These are specified for the sake of clarity rather than priority. Hence, also, the list of relevant History courses is not comprehensive.

customFields.rfMyo:
Launched in 2012, Peace and Conflict Studies (PCS) is an interdisciplinary undergraduate degree program consisting of a major and a minor. Students in the major may choose between one of two thematic focus areas: “Social Justice” and “Global Perspectives.” Although the program has so far remained quite small—and despite its seemingly innocuous name and somewhat amorphous focus areas—the distinctive strength of the PCS major is a curriculum focused on teaching students to prevent or to resolve conflict, and to understand its fundamental causes in a systematic way. This is what the new title, Diplomacy, captures and reflects much more precisely. Diplomacy is a wide-ranging and interdisciplinary domain of real-world practice. Wherever competing interests and perspectives collide—and especially where they have devolved into disfunction or erupted into violence—the craft of diplomacy is critical.

Like the old PCS program, the new Diplomacy major is designed to be compact and to facilitate a double-major for those students interested in pursuing it. Indeed, the major is designed to point students to a range of counterpart areas of specialization that would make for ideal double-majors. Diplomacy majors would be encouraged to pursue such pairings. The inclusion of upper-division elective courses across disciplines and, where appropriate, across Colleges also facilitates double-majors. Opportunities for community engaged learning in the reformulated Diplomacy major abound through interdisciplinary course offerings and through Hinckley Institute internships.

While interdisciplinarity remains a signal strength of the reconfigured major, no less than 70% of its total required coursework, including no less than 40% of the major’s upper-division electives, are drawn exclusively from within the College of Humanities. These come from the College’s singular strengths in communication, language and culture, philosophy of science, history, and area studies programs focused on Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East. The Department of Communication is a top-ten program with particular strengths in cultural studies, media and technology, and in science communication. The Department of World Languages & Cultures (WLC) is a nationally-distinguished destination for language learning—renowned for its tight integration with Utah’s best-in-the-country public school language immersion programs, and for its programs in Less Commonly Taught Languages, which are explicitly identified as high priority by the US Agency for International Development, the Department of State, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Education and the Peace Corps.

Through International and Area Studies (IAS)—the unit that would house the Diplomacy major—the College of Humanities is home to one of the most robust Culture and Languages Across the Curriculum (CLAC) programs in the country. The combination of the Middle East Center and the two Department of Education-funded National Resource Centers (NRCs)—the Asia Center and the Center for Latin American Studies—distinguishes the University of Utah nationally and internationally. The NRCs provide students with some of the nation’s most extensive support for language study abroad through Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships. Both the Asia Center and the Center for Latin American Studies have long supported curriculum innovation in the culture-, history-, and language-specific coursework that would constitute much of the substance of the Diplomacy major.

The Department of History—which is home to internationally award-winning faculty with particular and relevant strengths in modern history, including in Asia, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East—already provides much of the foundational curriculum for undergraduates in all four extant IAS programs, and would do the same for Diplomacy as well.
customFields.QvDbS:
This major is concordant with the University’s stated mission to foster student success by preparing those from diverse backgrounds to have impact as leaders and citizens, to engage local and global communities, and to work towards a more sustainable world. The Diplomacy major combines an analysis of the dynamics of conflict and peacemaking with a consideration of the structural causes of violence, conflict, and displacement, and it does so at both regional and global scales. It places the University in a position of knowledge production which speaks to other similar programs across the country, increasing opportunities for students to engage in international study, research, and service. In addition to BYU, which has an “International Strategy and Diplomacy” concentration, two neighboring USHE institutions have degree programs that are similar enough to the reconfigured Diplomacy major to promote seamless transferability without the proposed program being duplicative. Weber State University has an International Studies major; USU has an International Studies major and, separately, a certificate in Leadership and Diplomacy (which, rather than international issues, is focused on developing leadership skills across varied career paths). In this ecosystem, the Diplomacy major is at once unique but also complementary.

The reconfigured Diplomacy major at the University of Utah would be a first-of-its kind program in the Mountain West and among the few such innovative undergraduate programs nationally, distinguishing Utah among peer research universities. No university in the Mountain West can lay claim to the particular and relevant strengths of Utah. The University of Denver’s Korbel School is perhaps the closest comparison. But Denver is a private institution, is costly to attend, and its program is heavily focused on the social sciences. The University of Utah is significantly more affordable ($23,000/year in-state; $45,000 out-of-state vs. $80,000/year at Denver) and is therefore better positioned to serve the widest possible range of students throughout the Mountain West and beyond. These are key considerations given the demographic transformations underway in the state of Utah and especially among the University’s student body, where many students are first-generation college students, transfer students from area community colleges, or from underserved communities throughout the region. The proposed program will broaden access to the interdisciplinary study of Diplomacy for students both within the Mountain West and nationally. Data from both US News and World Reports and Academic Analytics suggest that the University of Utah has unparalleled regional strengths across areas of study pertinent to the proposed Diplomacy program. These include a top-ten Department of Communication, a Department of World Languages & Cultures that is a nationally-distinguished destination for language learning, the combined expertise of the two Department of Education-funded National Resource Centers (the Asia Center and the Center for Latin American Studies), a leading program in the Philosophy of Science, and a Department of History that is home to internationally award-winning faculty with particular and relevant strengths in modern history, including in Asia, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

According to The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2023 and the nonpartisan Partnership for Public Service, both public- and private-sector employers see greater cultural and historical awareness, as well as greater attunement to such challenges as those posed by climate change and disruptive digital and communication technologies as essential to effective diplomacy.

According to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, diplomacy and related career paths are growing faster than the national average. And according to the American Academy of Diplomacy, students with degrees linked to diplomacy especially in such areas as sustainability, conflict resolution, human trafficking, technology and governance, and the preservation of cultural property have an expanding range of opportunities among both public- and private-sector employers—including within the American diplomatic corps, as the number of test takers for the Foreign Service exam have dropped precipitously since 2016. The professional networking site Linked-In regularly lists over 11,000 open positions related to diplomacy and international affairs. Relief Web, a site specializing in humanitarian careers, also regularly lists some 2500 open positions globally. Idealist, a key career site for non-profit specialists, listed almost 4000 jobs in diplomacy or related areas in the Mountain West alone—including (earlier this fall) the Directorship of the University of Utah’s own Go-Learn program. Salaries for such positions vary widely, of course, especially when comparing disparate positions globally. But domestically, among those with 4-year degrees, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, entry-level salaries in areas related to diplomacy average approximately $85,000/year.

The renamed and refocused Diplomacy major offers a revised curriculum designed to meet demand in precisely the areas identified in recent research and in which the College of Humanities has a distinguished national and international reputation: history, communication, language and culture, and area studies.

STUDENT DEMAND

International Studies, Global Studies, and Diplomacy are high-demand majors and areas of recent growth at major research universities around the country, including at UC-Berkeley, UC Irvine, Johns Hopkins University, the University of Wisconsin, the University of Washington, Seton Hall University, and the nearby University of Denver. At the University of Utah, majors in International Studies (IS)—the undergraduate degree most similar to Diplomacy (both are Humanities-based, interdisciplinary, present-oriented, and thematically focused)—appear to reflect the national trend. IS has consistently ranked among the most heavily subscribed majors in the College of Humanities. While pandemic disruptions appear to have led to a decline in major numbers (a national trend for programs in International and Global Studies), they remain very healthy. Presently there are over 250 declared IS majors and, for the first time since its introduction in spring of 2020, there is a wait list for students enrolling in the major’s core course (INTL 3000).
customFields.BFkjq:
The Diplomacy major is a scaffolded major with four Focus Areas that represent key convergences between some of the most consequential issues of our time, the research strengths of the College of Humanities, student interest, and labor market demand.

The four Focus Areas are as follows:

1. Tribal Sovereignty and Cultural Heritage
2. Conflict, Displacement, and Humanitarian Affairs
3. Health, Climate, and Sustainability
4. Science, Technology, and Society

The proposal is for both a BA and BS degree. Language and culture coursework requirements distinguish them. The BA is a slightly longer degree (43 credit hours of coursework in the major) and requires both advanced proficiency in a second language (or in a language other than English) and basic proficiency in a third language (as indicated by completion of a fourth-semester language course). The BS is a shorter degree (39 credit hours of coursework in the major) and requires the completion of at least two upper-division courses focused on a particular culture or world region.

There are five sets of requirements for the bachelor’s degree (whether the BA or BS) in Diplomacy. These are as follows:

1. Introductory Requirements [3 courses / 9 credits]
2. International Studies Core Curriculum Requirement [1 course / 3 credits]
3. Communication Requirement [2 courses / 6 credits]
4. Language (BA) or Culture (BS) Requirements [2 courses / 6 credits]
5. Focus Area Electives [5 courses / 15 credits]

The focus areas are scaffolded. Each has its own set of two (2) required upper-division courses and then allows students to select an additional three (3) upper-division electives that suit their particular interests and priorities. The upper-division required courses within each focus area establish the historical context for the issues in question, and then explore analytical approaches pertinent to those issues. The additional electives allow students to deepen their substantive understanding of the issue area.

While the old PCS curriculum did not include an assessment mechanism, the restructured Diplomacy major will have a robust procedure. Every second year, faculty drawn from the Faculty Advisory Committees for International and Area Studies will constitute an Undergraduate Assessment Committee (UAC) to undertake learning outcomes assessment. UAC assessments will be based on completed student assignments (“artifacts”) selected at random from required courses spread across the Diplomacy curriculum using the Learning Outcomes Associator Tool in Canvas. For learning outcomes 1 and 2 (Linguistic and Cultural Competence, and Communicational Competence), artifacts will be drawn from the required coursework of Diplomacy students in the World Language and Culture courses and in the Communication courses. The UAC will base learning outcomes 3 and 4 (Interdisciplinary Analytical Skills, and Global and Comparative Perspective) on artifacts similarly selected from the IAS core course, INTL 3000: Foundations for International Studies. Assignments in the core course are keyed specifically to cultivate and measure students’ growing familiarity with region-specific cultural and historical dynamics that correspond to the thematic focus areas of the Diplomacy major.

The UAC scores the evidence for each learning outcome on a scale of 0 to 4 as follows, with each assignment in the sample set for each outcome read by at least two committee members:

4 Excellent mastery
3 Good mastery
2 Some mastery
1 Minimal mastery
0 No mastery

The UAC then provides the data generated through this process to the director for analysis and the writing of a report that reflects UAC findings.

catalogFullDescription: The Deep Learning Certificate Program will provide working knowledge of the use of state-of-the-art deep learning technology as a graduate student certificate program. Deep learning allows the identification of objects in images, translating languages and driving cars autonomously. Deep Learning is rapidly gaining application across all industries due to the availability of adequate computing power (e.g., GPUs) and large data sets to train with. This is true from sensor data processing to database analytics to fraud detection in banks. Utah currently has a large number of unfilled well-paying jobs in this area. Student enrollment in the program is achieved as a stackable certificate on top of a regular graduate degree. Students with appropriate background may be allowed into the program as non-matriculated students. The successful award of the certificate in Deep Learning results from the completion of 15 student credit hours of work at the graduate level. This program provides education in this area to engineering and science graduate students beyond those with computing background. In addition, the certificate program requires a graduate internship project with programs industry partners.

catalogFullDescription: Dark Sky Studies is an emerging transdisciplinary field that explores the impacts of artificial light at night and the loss of our night skies through a broad range of disciplines. Light pollution excessive use of artificial light at night poses environmental and safety threats, and it also prevents us from seeing the starry sky at night. Utah is unique, globally, in both its protection of natural dark-sky places and its intense urban light pollution generating urban core; combined, Utah's rural starry skies and urban over-lighting are an ideal living laboratory for place-based exploration. The Dark Sky Studies (DSS) Minor Program includes courses and faculty from multiple disciplines at the University of Utah: anthropology, architecture, astronomy, atmospheric sciences, design, engineering, English, history, philosophy, physics, public health, pulmonary medicine, religion, urban planning and more. The Minor program is housed in the Department of City & Metropolitan Planning (College of Architecture + Planning) but is designed to include undergraduate students from across campus. DSS students will explore issues through scientific, humanist and public policy lenses, particularly the negative impacts of artificial light, as well as endeavor to characterize community needs and innovation opportunities inherent in the effort of protecting natural night.

The undergraduate Bachelor of Science in Design welcomes makers, researchers, and creative practitioners from a range of disciplinary perspectives into a collective environment that prepares students to imagine, develop, and enact design interventions. The program approaches design in three categories: Physical Product, Digital Product, and Open Investigation, and offers students two pathways through the curriculum: Design Studies and Studio Practice.  

Studio Practice foregrounds in-depth making and experiential learning in a studio environment.  Design Studies offers a hands-on platform for the interdisciplinary study of design management and product development, as well as an understanding of material culture through design history, theory, and criticism. Students also pursue a primary focus in methods that pertain to physical and digital products, experiences, and spatial investigations at multiple scales.

Both paths prepare students to leverage design skills and processes for careers in a wide variety of disciplines—in creative fields and beyond. Students in both Design Studies and Studio Practice begin their coursework together in a coordinated Sophomore year with the option of pursuing either a Physical or Digital Product emphasis. Those who wish to craft a course of study that doesn’t fall under the Physical or Digital Product trajectories have the option of curating their own set of courses in the Open Investigation emphasis. 

The MDD program invites students to develop their own practice and approach to design supported by rigorous craft, critical research methods, and ethical framing, reinforced by industry partnerships, community engaged scholarship, and diverse media and fabrication techniques.

Graduates go on to professional careers in a wide variety of design disciplines in the private sector, as well as government or non-profit organizations. Students have also gone on to graduate studies in diverse fields such as interaction design, architecture, landscape architecture, creative writing, systems and service design, business, and entrepreneurship.

Our proposed edits to the B.S. Degree meet two major objectives: (1) to create a “Design Studies” pathway through the degree, and (2) to formalize existing tracks (Physical Product, Digital Product, Open Investigation) in both pathways to graduation—“Design Studies” and “Studio Practice”.  

Design Studies Justification 
The MDD program averages between 60-90 applications a year but can only accept 30 students to the Design Major due to current space constraints in a studio teaching model. At the same time, we have seen there are students who could be better served with a pathway through the degree that doesn’t rely on as many studio credits, focusing on other aspects of the discipline such as design management, design studies, and design development. The new Design Studies emphases create a pathway to graduation in the current B.S. Design that better serves the unique needs of design students, while also allowing MDD to increase admissions and serve a greater number of students interested in pursuing a design degree.  

Affected students are currently declared as Design Foundations majors in the College of Architecture + Planning. These students will be notified through the Student Success Center with guidance from our in-major design advisor, who is also on our curriculum committee. The updated options will be presented to students in town halls and published in the course catalog. Because the edits create new, additional pathways in our degree without changing the existing options, students declared to the major prior to the changed catalog year are not affected by these changes. We will continue to maintain an active catalog going back five academic years as required.  

The updates to our degree do not require any special equipment or supplies; in fact, they are less demanding on our college’s studio facilities. Internally, we have projected a four-year implementation plan to strategize when and how new courses will be brought online to ensure a smooth transition for all current and future students.

customFields.QvDbS:
The B.S. Design degree has a track record of fostering student success in alignment with University core values and goals, particularly thanks to the integration of creativity, innovation, community engagement, sustainability, and research-led discovery. The proposed new pathways within the degree continue to strengthen this.   

By offering more pathways into our major, we contribute to the U’s goal to “Promote Student Success to Transform Lives” by growing the student body to 40,000 institution-wide. According to the University’s mission, “The U is committed to providing the financial assistance, personalized support, and engaged learning experiences that increase access to the university and facilitate persistence through degree completion.” Introducing new emphases within Multi-disciplinary Design (MDD) supports student persistence by providing more personalized pathways to completion. Currently MDD has one structured degree path to completion, with “tracks” distinguishing between digital or physical product design specializations alongside a studio-practice sequence of credits; as noted in the rationale section above, this limits enrollment capacity. This new emphasis structure facilitates greater persistence by removing the cap obstacle in our proposed new emphases, while allowing greater flexibility and choice of courses within and beyond the design disciplines. The “open investigation” emphasis is intentionally designed to allow students to incorporate minors into their degree while not increasing the time or cost of achieving this. At present, MDD students who complete a minor to complement their multi-disciplinary learning experience—for example, in entrepreneurship or fine arts—typically take longer to do so (or struggle to complete the minor at all); this proposal serves the increasing interest in, and need for, more cross-disciplinary experiences and degree pathways that can also be achieved in a reasonable time.  

MDD students contribute to the institutional goal of “unsurpassed societal impact” through their engagement in place-based, real-world design solutions, and the proposed degree changes will enhance opportunities for such impact. Design students participate in community-engaged learning that embed social and environmental sustainability as core values, and the proposed pathways continue to embed these values. From the requisite community-engagement designated course “Introduction to Design Thinking” onwards, MDD courses enable students to work directly with local communities to generate creative solutions to pressing social and environmental problems such as improving refugee experiences, researching rural community needs, and communicating the importance of socio-ecological systems. In this way, the program directly fulfills two related institutional missions as it “cultivates meaningful university, neighborhood, city, region, state, and global partnerships” and “contributes to a more sustainable world through research, teaching, and demonstrating best practices in protecting and enhancing the natural and built environment on the campus and environs” (University of Utah mission). The addition of courses in Advanced Design Communication, Advanced Research Methods, as well as a Design Studies Capstone, will support students to complete project-based learning which engages specific communities and current issues.

A new faculty hire ($100k) will be supported by increased student fee revenue generated from the new program. Based on our current program fee and incentive fund budget model, MDD will generate enough additional fees to support a full-time, tenure-line faculty member by Year 2 of the new curriculum (noting the first year of increased enrollment will add two sophomore Studio course sections, but current seminar courses will accommodate the additional students without further resource need). By Year 3, we will generate excess revenue which can be utilized to support additional faculty and staff recruitment, space needs, and operational costs.  

These initial budget estimates are a conservative minimum; we expect to generate greater revenue over subsequent years for two reasons. First, we will cap enrollment at 60 students in Year 1 of the new structure to enable a phased transition and development of new courses. But following Year 1, we expect to attract more enrollments, and revenue will increase accordingly. (Per the chart below, 2030–31 projections show a total revenue if MDD admits 75 students per year as a stable annual intake: i.e., our current intake of 30 students in Studio Practice, plus an increase to 45 students in Design Studies, per year.)   

Second, we intend to shift from a program fee and incentive fund budget model to a differential tuition model. Given that we will increase caps in several of our design electives and design emphases courses to accommodate Design Studies students—with potential seats open to non-majors—this will increase our overall revenue, while being cost-neutral to individual students.

We will require one new additional studio space per 15 new students that are admitted to sophomore level (i.e., 2 studio spaces in Year 1, 2025–26). customFields.Pp7N4:
The proposed updates were drafted with valuable guidance and input from the in-major advisor for design, Emi Ata’ata, who is also on the MDD Curriculum Committee. We reviewed the proposal and impacts with Assistant Dean for Student Belonging, Portia Anderson, and our MDD Student Advisory Council representatives.  

Impacts: 

  1. Pre-major/Design Foundations Advising: The advising process stays the same, with information updated for new curriculum paths/emphases.  

  2. Studio Practice application: Students who want to apply to the Studio Practice pathway will have a new, second application process in the spring of Sophomore year. This will be handled in MDD by staff and faculty.  

  3. Advisors will have the added task of declaring emphases once students are determined in-major. 

  4. Increased student-to-advisor ratio: Currently MDD has one in-major advisor on the College Student Success Team. This is a ratio of 1:30 for each incoming cohort. This would increase to 1:60. We are working on this with the Student Success Center and the Dean to address the increased load.  

  5. The MDD faculty and Chair have confirmed a commitment to supporting increased advising needs: we are not assuming the entire increased advising workload would automatically be covered by advising. These additional needs are noted in the resource analysis of our internal process.  

  6. The new emphases will provide additional opportunities to build a sense of belonging for students within their cohorts. MDD faculty will work with the Student Success team to strengthen this.  

The Division of Multi-disciplinary Design is primarily responsible for communicating and marketing the proposal to students and will do so in close coordination with the College Student Success Team and College administrators.
customFields.JKHAJ: This proposal was developed by a Curriculum Committee comprised of 4 of our 6 full-time faculty members. The program update and course updates were drafted collaboratively by the committee. It was also presented to the broader MDD faculty at several faculty meetings. We visited faculty meetings in the other units (Games, SMP, SOA) in our college several times each to update and get feedback in addition to an informational meeting at the College Council prior to calling for a vote of approval. The response from faculty has been positive, with helpful suggestions regarding the nuances in credit, admissions, advising, and most importantly cross-unit collaboration. Internally the vote in favor to approve this update was unanimous. Faculty in other units have expressed interest in the potential for collaboration across shared courses and curriculum.
customFields.7nJtQ:
The design field is evolving rapidly, becoming an essential skill across a broad range of industries. According to the Utah Department of Workforce Services, 58 occupations directly cite design as a core job function. The global landscape, however, is facing tectonic shifts. In AIGA’s report (1) of the current landscape, designers see increasingly digital, multi-disciplinary, data-driven and human-oriented work applications to take center stage in the future. Skilled workers with high resilience will be necessary to navigate these new frontiers. Challenges like sustainability goals, systems thinking, and utilizing AI technologies will require future leaders who can continuously innovate. The proposed Design Studies track is uniquely positioned to prepare these leaders by providing advanced design education around theory, history, and communication[. 

While Multi-disciplinary Design (MDD) has broad applicability, it is particularly relevant to a few key fields, such as Web and Digital Interface Design (2). According to Utah’s Department of Workforce Services, this field is projected to grow much faster than average in the coming years. Entry-level positions requiring an associate’s degree are expected to grow by 3.27% annually in Utah, with 10,700 nationwide job openings in the next year. It is rated as a 5-star occupation, with a median annual salary of $101,060 in Utah. The Design Studies track, with its emphasis on design theory and communication, will help fill high-level roles in this field, such as researcher, analyst, director, and manager. As the field becomes increasingly integrated with AI tools, graduates who have developed adaptability and self-direction through their studies will be well-equipped to lead and innovate. 

Design Studies graduates are well-suited for a range of other fast-growing fields. Producers and Directors, another related field, are expected to see "much faster-than-average" employment growth (3). The gaming industry also offers significant opportunities for Design Studies students. With a U.S. consumer base of 191 million (9) and a rapidly expanding job market (2), gaming presents similar growth prospects to Web and Digital Interface Design. Design Studies graduates will be well-suited to pursue positions within architecture—a fast-growing occupation which projects 3.87% growth statewide and an annual median income of $76,120 for bachelor’s degree holders (4). Graduates will be particularly well-suited to pursue advanced academic studies in design or architecture, building on the self-directed learning emphasized in the Design Studies track. High level roles in manufacturing processes will cater well to Design Studies students, whose analytical tools will serve in joining operational processes with quality outcomes. Manufacturing is projected to see steady statewide growth across a range of positions (5), and remains a top industry in the United States with 12,751,685 current roles filled (8).  

Although the demand for design skills is robust in many sectors, some career paths experience slower growth. For instance, craft artists are projected to see a modest 1.12% statewide growth, with an average annual income of $18,670 (6). Fine artists, on the other hand, are expected to experience a 3.48% growth in employment, with an average annual salary of $53,180 (7). These figures underscore the diversity in potential career paths, but also highlight the relative stability of higher-demand fields for Design Studies graduates. 

Additional career opportunities include roles such as project designer, project manager, art director, set and exhibit designer, special effects artist, animator, industrial designer, design researcher, design analyst, information architect, fashion designer, interior designer, and design instructor. These positions span across industries, further underscoring the versatility and demand for advanced design knowledge.

customFields.arvvH:
The update adds a new pathway, but it doesn’t remove any current options to complete the B.S. Design degree. Students who were declared to the Design Major up to five years prior to catalog year 2025/26 will still be able to complete their degree requirements as before. They will have the additional option of declaring an emphasis in the track they have chosen to pursue; this doesn’t change the classes they are taking or need to take, it only updates how the transcript reads. This will be communicated through both formal channels (such as email and advising) and informal channels (such as program Teams updates and studio announcements).  

Updated edits to the pathways will affect the students who are admitted to the program in Fall 2025 onward (declared by the 2025/26 catalog year). These students will complete a coordinated sophomore year that includes multiple touchpoints for advising. There will be an increased administrative role in communicating the new emphasis options, and we are working with faculty, staff, and advisors to create a plan for accomplishing this.  

In coordination with MDD faculty and academic advisors, the admissions process will remain the same for the first year, with the added option to apply to the studio practice pathway in the spring of the Sophomore year. This will minimize confusion with current students (who are already familiar with this process) and any students who are planning on re-applying. This will allow the faculty, advisors, and admissions committee to review the process and make recommendations going forward in a timeline that gives the most possible notice to future students.
customFields.fsS6S:
Applications for seats in our current MDD program far exceed our current capacity to accommodate them. Students compete for limited spaces: we cap admissions at 30 sophomores into our program each year due to limitations on physical space (specifically studio space) and limited faculty to deliver instruction. Applications are typically more than double this intake, and demand has steadily risen since MDD began in 2011.  

This proposal accommodates current and future student demand by offering more diverse on-ramps into our program. We will maintain the 30-student cap of our existing Studio Practice curriculum emphases (where many of the resource constraints limit our growth), while at the same time open new pathway options via Design Studies. This allows us to utilize other forms of instruction to deliver learning outcomes for a diversifying range of career opportunities, including design practice and graduate studies. 

We note that in the College of Architecture + Planning (CA+P), all students are currently admitted as pre-majors before proceeding to the current B.S. Design, or degrees in Architecture or Urban Ecologies. By implementing this proposal, we will provide a clear and functional four-year plan for students who enter the Design Foundations program and want to graduate with a degree in design.

learningOutcomes.name: DESIGN PROCESS: Students gain a nuanced understanding of contemporary design processes through observation, iteration, and implementation. We build upon and practice these processes to attend to complex issues in a wide range of societal settings.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Students' understanding of design process is assessed in multiple design foundation pre-requisite courses i.e. DES2615, DES2630. This is subsequently assessed in each studio course and senior capstone, though mid-reviews and final reviews of student project presentations. Students submit final reports in each studio that summarize their projects and can be collected as an archive of student work that can be reviewed for assessment purposes.

learningOutcomes.name: PERSONAL PRACTICE: Students develop a variety of techniques and sensibilities in order to identify design opportunities and advocate for contextually significant responses.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This is assessed in each studio course and senior capstone, though mid-reviews and final reviews of student project presentations. Students submit final reports in each studio that summarize their projects and can be collected as an archive of student work that can be reviewed for assessment purposes. Required courses regularly include assessment of a student’s ability to reflect on their own learning and practice.

learningOutcomes.name: COMMUNITY / ENGAGEMENT: We nurture a space of collaboration that prepares students to align compelling design artifacts and proposals with coherent conceptual arguments. Students foster relationships with community partners across various sectors, practices, and services.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This is assessed directly through review of student work in the studio and seminars. It can be indirectly assessed by course evaluations and post project reflections with community partners, and the assessment of group work collaboration.

learningOutcomes.name: SKILLS / APPLICATION: We learn an array of design communication methods that integrate cognition, craft, and technical innovation. Students acquire skills in representation, computation, and fabrication, moving back and forth between physical and digital spaces and technologies.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This is assessed in the coursework completed in both studios and seminars. All studios have public mid and final reviews that include presentations demonstrating this learning outcome. Many seminars have coursework that address this as well, and feature in class or public presentations.

learningOutcomes.name: DESIGN RESEARCH: Students develop an aptitude in, and an attitude about, qualitative and quantitative design research methods and their applications.
learningOutcomes.assessment: This is assessed in the design research courses as well as in the studio through coursework and project presentations. It can also be assessed in the program archive of student final project reports. Studios and capstones also have specific research phases with deliverables that can be assessed in reviews and in project submission documents.

The Entertainment Arts and Engineering: Master Games Studio (EAE:MGS) is an interdisciplinary master's level graduate program at the University of Utah. The Masters of Entertainment Art and Engineering degree (MEAE) was jointly developed with the College of Engineering and the College of Fine Arts, and our aim is to produce graduates ready to design, develop, create assets, and provide leadership for the video games of today and tomorrow.

The program consists of four semesters. There are four tracks you may choose for the masters program: Game Arts, Game Engineering, Technical Art, and Game Production. Students in the Game Arts Track focus on the tools and techniques used in creating art assets for games. This includes animation, modeling, texturing, lighting, visual design, narrative, and concept art for games. Students will expand their visual skills as they create interactive worlds, cut scenes, and designs that are integrated into cutting edge games. This will be done with cutting-edge industry tools (Maya, ZBrush, Unreal Development Kit, Mixamo, Unity, Marmoset Toolbag, Adobe, etc.) using the latest equipment in a true entrepreneurial game development environment. A number of the courses are taught by industry professionals and share the latest techniques used in the game industry.

Students work both individually and in teams as they create visual work for games in conjunction with our computer science and production students. Students develop a focused concentration in specific creative and technical areas, as they integrate individual portfolio development with team-based projects. Students will also take courses in game design and are instrumental to the final look and play of the game.

catalogFullDescription:
The M.F.A. program in creative writing is small and selective. Creative Writing students have the opportunity to study literature, take part in a series of intensive writing workshops, and work within a close community of writers. They may focus their literature coursework in any area of English or American literature.

During their residence M.F.A. students are expected to work closely with members of the writing staff. M.F.A. students will take nine courses: four workshops; a Form and Theory course in the chosen genre; and four literature courses.

The thesis is to be a book-length piece of writing of publishable quality--a novel, a collection of stories, or a collection of poems. The application deadline for entry into the M.F.A. program with or without financial aid is December 15 for the following fall semester.

The English MFA gives students the opportunity to study literature, participate in intensive writing workshops, and work in a close community of writers. Studies may focus their literature coursework in any area of English or American literature. During their residence, MFA students are expected to work closely with members of the creative writing faculty and write book-length thesis of publishable quality-a novel, a collection of stories, or a collection of poems.

Students will take a minimum of nine courses of at least three credit hours each and may take up to two courses at the 5000-level for graduate credit. (Students must register for 5000-level courses as English 6910: Independent Study, and enrollment in 5000-level courses for graduate credit requires the prior approval of the Director of Graduate Studies.) Teaching colloquia do not count toward the ten courses required for the degree, nor does English 6910 (unless approved in advance by the Graduate Director). MFA students must also complete at least 6 hours of Thesis Research (English 6970).

Eligibility

Students applying for the M.A., M.F.A., or Ph.D. degree programs must hold a B.A or B.S. degree from an accredited college or university, and have a cumulative grade-point average of 3.2 or higher. Students holding an M.A. or M.F.A. in English are eligible for admission into the Ph.D. program.

The B.A. to Ph.D. direct track option is available to applicants to any program who do not hold a master's degree in the field. A candidate with a B.A. will submit application materials at the same time as other candidates (December 15). If accepted, the student receives a teaching assistantship for the first year. Those denied admission into the B.A. to Ph.D. direct-track program may instead be offered admission into the M.A. or M.F.A. program.

Instructions for Application Submission

Please read the following instructions carefully and submit a complete application by the deadline of December 15 each year for the following fall semester. Please be sure to indicate in the appropriate places your name, address, and the specific program to which you are applying. If you are applying for admission to our doctoral program but will not have a master's degree in the field of English upon entering our program, please choose "English-PHD," and in the section labeled "Additional Information" indicate that you are applying for the B.A. to Ph.D. track.

IMPORTANT NOTE: You may only apply to one program. Please indicate the program to which you are applying. With the exception of those applying to the B.A. to Ph.D. track (who will be considered for admission to the M.A. or M.F.A. programs if they are not admitted to the Ph.D. program), applicants will not be considered for admission to a more than one program.

Applications that are not submitted by the department deadline date of December 15 will not be considered. Student portions of applications that are not complete by the appropriate deadline, or that are filled out incorrectly, will also not be considered. Please be sure to put your name on all application materials.

  • All applications must include a completed electronic University of Utah Graduate Application Form; there is no separate English Department application.

All application materials must be submitted and/or uploaded via the online application system: https://app.applyyourself.com//?id=utahgrad. The English Department will not accept application materials by mail.

  • All applications must include a critical writing sample of at least six pages. The critical sample should demonstrate your ability to elucidate the critical issues pertinent to a text and to conduct a sustained reading of a text or texts.

  • Applications for creative writing must include, in addition to the critical sample, a creative writing sample, either poetry, fiction, or non-fiction of approximately 10 pages. For the poetry sample, a small collection of poems is acceptable. For fiction or non-fiction samples, a short story, or a chapter or selection from a novel, memoir, or essay is acceptable. If your fiction or non-fiction samples are short, you can submit more than one piece. Creative writing samples should reflect the genre of the program to which you are applying.

  • Writing samples must be uploaded into your electronic online application: https://app.applyyourself.com//?id=utahgrad.

IMPORTANT NOTE: Applicants submitting both creative and critical writing samples, please note that the application software allows applicants to submit two files. Upload one critical and one creative file. If your creative sample, for example, consists of a few short pieces, you should incorporate them into one file.

  • All applications must include three academic letters of recommendation from faculty who can assess your ability to do English graduate work; most recommendations, therefore, should come from faculty who know your work. You must submit the email addresses of your three recommenders via the online application: https://app.applyyourself.com//?id=utahgrad.

  • STATEMENT OF PURPOSE: All applicants must include a statement of purpose explaining their professional interests and goals. Please address those aspects of the study of literature or creative writing that have influenced your decision to pursue a graduate degree in English.

  • International applicants who are not native speakers of English should note that they must demonstrate proficiency in English before they can receive financial assistance that involves teaching English Composition. Proficiency is partly demonstrated by a score of 26 or higher on the Speaking section of the iBL exam or a score of 7 or higher on the Speaking band of the IELTS exam. In addition, the graduate admissions committee will carefully assess applicants' writing samples when considering international students for financial aid.

  • The University must receive GRE SCORES directly from ETS. There is no minimum cut-off score on this exam. Instead, we are interested in applicants' overall performance overall and their performance on the verbal portion of the general exam in particular. Please note that GRE scores tend to arrive approximately three weeks after the date of the exam. Therefore, the exam should be taken by the middle of November at the latest to meet the December 15 deadline. To expedite the arrival of your GRE scores, please use the University of Utah institution code (#4853) and the English Department code (#2501 for literature programs or #2503 for creative writing tracks).

International applicants must upload the appropriate fee, one official set of transcripts, and TOEFL results to: https://app.applyyourself.com//?id=utahgrad.

Applications will be distributed to members of the English Department graduate admissions committee soon after the application deadline. The English Department generally informs applicants of its decisions via email in the second week of March. The University of Utah Graduate Admissions Office will send official confirmation of this decision later.

Deadlines for Application Submission:

The following deadlines may differ from the general University admission deadlines. Please follow the deadlines listed below if you are applying to the English graduate program.

All application materials must have been entered into the Apply Yourself system no later than December 15 for admission the following Fall (https://app.applyyourself.com//?id=utahgrad). All applications will be considered for funding. Applications for admission to all programs will be reviewed only once each year. Note: If a deadline falls on a holiday or weekend, applications will be accepted through the following business day.

Please note that there is NO Spring Semester admission to the English Department.

rules.name: Program Structure
rules.description: The M.Ed. in ECS is structured to provide students with one core course (3 credit hours). M.Ed. students then select their area of emphasis (interdisciplinary inquiry or reflexive praxis with or without ESL endorsement). Based on their selected area of emphasis, students select the remainder of their courses as outlined below (24-25 credit hours). To complete the M.Ed. program, students are required to register for the M.Ed. Comprehensive Exam (3 hours, ECS 6961). The M.Ed. program consists of a total of 30 credit hours. For those seeking an ESL endorsement, the M.Ed. program will consist of a total of 31 credit hours. Those seeking to continue studies towards a Ph.D. after obtaining a M.Ed. must consult the Director of Graduate Studies after they have completed 18 credit hours of coursework.

rules.name: Comprehensive Exam
rules.description: All M.Ed. students must complete a final comprehensive exam in order to graduate. The comprehensive exam is an open book, take home exam consisting of three questions. This examination will be based on your course work. You will be asked to review, synthesize, and analyze critically the content of your course work. Comprehensive exams are scheduled at the end of the Fall and Spring semesters. Students must be registered for three hours the semester they take the exam. Contact the Academic Program Specialist the semester before the semester you wish to take the exam. They will help you complete the paperwork you need to register for the exam and to receive your degree. (ECS 6961)

catalogFullDescription: The BA/BS degree in Educational Psychology will provide students with training and expertise in behavioral and mental health, services desperately needed locally and nationally. The degree differs from other human service degrees in that the course work and work-based learning experiences lead directly to competitive, high demand employment opportunities including certification as an assistant behavior analyst. Other human service degrees focus on the general theory of counseling and mental health; this degree teaches specific individual and group counseling interventions so that students leave with theory and skills. Students will not only be prepared to enter the job market upon graduation, but will also have the knowledge and skills to enter graduate programs within the behavioral and mental health field.
