catalogFullDescription:
The Bachelor of Science in Kinesiology is a versatile degree.  Defined as “the study of physical activity and its impact on health, society, and quality of life” (www.AmericanKinesiology.org), Kinesiology offers students opportunities to explore physical movement and human health and experience from multiple perspectives.  Three emphases, each with unique capstone options, allow students to tailor the degree to suit their professional interests and aspirations.  All three emphases engage students in courses that reinforce skills (such as critical thinking, problem solving, oral and written communication) transferable to many career paths.  Kinesiology is designated a STEM degree, which is helpful to those interested in health sciences careers.

Pre-Health Professions Emphasis. 
Students in the Pre-Health Professions emphasis will gain essential content in Kinesiology, addressing complex physiological, mechanical, sociological, psychological, and behavioral content through the lens of human movement.  The emphasis affords scheduling flexibility for students planning to pursue careers in healthcare, such as medicine, dentistry, nursing, occupational therapy, physical therapy, dietetics, pharmacology, audiology, speech and language pathology, and recreational therapy.

Exercise in Health and Disease Emphasis. 
Students in the Exercise in Health and Disease Emphasis will gain the necessary content knowledge, critical thinking skills, and exercise programming skillset necessary to become a successful exercise professional, both in the applied and research contexts. Students will gain competence in working with all individuals (e.g., across the lifespan, apparently healthy, and individuals living with chronic disease). The skillset and knowledge attained from this emphasis are transferrable to other areas and positions in healthcare and health-related research.

Movement Science Emphasis.
Students in the Movement Science Emphasis will gain a deeper, more structured understanding of how humans move, from neural control to mechanics, and how to assess movement in healthy and clinical populations. Students will gain transferable knowledge and skills in neurophysiology, neuroscience, biomechanics, and the analysis of human movement using new and emerging technology. These areas will enable students to pursue a wide range of future opportunities, including medical school, multidisciplinary graduate school programs, and industry.

The B.S. in Kinesiology aligns with the values and strategic priorities of the College of Health that aims to prepare future leaders in challenging educational and occupational settings with a goal to improve the human healthspan.

catalogFullDescription: Students must complete 30 credit hours, including eight 3-credit courses (for a total of 24 credits of coursework) and 6 thesis hours.

rules.name: Foreign Language
rules.notes:
All students must demonstrate third-year proficiency in one of the two major Latin American languages (Spanish or Portuguese) and first-year proficiency in a second language spoken in Latin America. Language proficiency can be demonstrated by successful completion of relevant language courses with a grade of B or better as indicated by an undergraduate transcript, as part of the program of study for the MA, or by providing other evidence of proficiency that is certified by the Second Language Teaching and Research Center at the University of Utah.

Language courses do not count toward the minimum of 30 credit hours required for the degree unless they are taken at the 6000 level or higher.

Typically students will satisfy the field or disciplinary concentration requirement by taking a minimum of four classes (12 credits) in a specific discipline or an interdisciplinary area of study (e.g. Environmental Studies).

The concentration can be based in any department or academic program at the university including professional programs (e.g. Social Work, Nursing, Urban Planning, Public Administration), or involve creative and practical interdisciplinary combinations of courses that fit with the students’ career goals (e.g. Gender Studies or Environmental Studies).
rules.name: Disciplinary Concentration
Methods Requirement
rules.notes: Students must take at least one core methods course or research seminar appropriate to their discipline or field of concentration. This course should be chosen in consultation with their faculty advisor.

rules.name: Breadth Requirement
rules.notes: Students will be required to take classes or write a thesis that examines at least two of four broad regions in Latin America. The regions are defined as Mexico and Central America, South America (not Brazil), Brazil, and the Caribbean.

rules.name: Latin American Content Requirement
rules.notes:
• Overall at least 15 credit hours (five courses) must come from the approved list of LAS content courses.

  • To qualify for the MA, courses must be taken at the 6000-level or higher. 6000-level courses may include advanced undergraduate courses in which students complete appropriate additional assignments and readings for graduate credit.

rules.name: MA Essay Requirement
rules.notes:
• Students must complete an MA essay and have it approved by their supervisory committee. An MA essay is a substantial research paper on an issue or topic related to Latin America.

  • Typically, students will register for 6 thesis credits during their second year in the MA program in order to complete their essay. These credits count toward the overall credit requirement. The course is LAS 6971, which the student will set up with the program advisor.

  • We encourage students to do the MA essay, although a thesis option is also available upon request.

catalogFullDescription:
The Master of Legal Studies degree is a one-year program which provides a foundation for working with and understanding the law and regulation. Students learn how to think and communicate broadly about legal issues affecting various careers and industries, understand contemporary legal issues, and know the practical implications of the law.

The MLS degree is available in three convenient formats: In-Person MLS Program, MLS Distance Program at the St. George Graduate Center, and Online MLS Program. All programs last one year (three semesters) and students need 30 credits to graduate.

Our curriculum provides students with a deeper understanding of the legal system, with an emphasis on law’s role in the modern world. Courses focus on areas of law most commonly encountered by executives and working professionals, including contracts, intellectual property, litigation, regulation, conflict resolution, employment, and compliance.

We offer the MLS degree in three convenient formats: In-Person MLS Program, MLS Distance Program and the St. George Graduate Center, and Online MLS Program. All programs last one year (three semesters) and students need 30 credits to graduate.

In-Person MLS Program: Our in-person program meets every other weekend, Friday and Saturday from 8a.m. to 5p.m. Classes are held at the S.J. Quinney College of Law on the University of Utah campus in Salt Lake City, Utah.

MLS Distance Program: Students living in and around Washington County can attend classes with our in-person cohort via remote technology at the University of Utah’s St. George Graduate Center. Classes are held simultaneously with our Salt Lake in-person students every other weekend, Friday and Saturday from 8a.m. to 5p.m.

Online MLS Program: Students can obtain their MLS degree in an entirely online format. Online classes include the same content (and often the same instructor) as the live version of the class. Content is delivered “asynchronously,” meaning students can generally complete the work on their own time, without the need to attend scheduled classes or meetings.

The MLS program uses a cohort system, and students come from a variety of backgrounds and professions, including human resources, compliance and risk management, education, paralegals and other legal paraprofessionals, mediation, real estate, and social work, to name just a few.

For more information, visit https://sjquinney.utah.edu/mls/.

customFields.nHBHl:
The first change we are making is removing the Conflict requirement and moving the courses that were in that requirement (LAW6320 and LAW6510) to electives.

Rationale

  1. Diverse Career Pathways:

    • Students in the MLS program pursue various career paths, not all of which necessitate expertise in crisis management. By making Conflicts an elective, students can choose to take those courses if they align with their career goals.

  2. Flexibility in Curriculum:

    • Removing this requirement would create room for additional electives that could cover emerging legal topics, such as AI in the Law and Healthcare Law. This flexibility would allow students to tailor their studies to their interests and the evolving legal landscape.

  3. Program Alignment with Other Specialized Legal Topic Courses:

    • This requirement centers on alternative dispute resolution, making it more appropriately categorized as a specialized legal topic. This classification would correctly align with other elective courses in our current curriculum, which include the specialized legal topics of property law, contract law, comparative legal studies, labor and employment law, criminal law, and family law.

The second program change is that we are adding three heath care courses (LAW 6610, LAW 6615, and LAW6620) as a concentration to better equip health care professionals with the understanding of the industry’s governing laws and regulations.

The final program change is to make the online program mirror the in person program with the same core requirements and the same elective choices.

All of these changes are being made to increase student enrollment. We will use the S.J. Quinney College of Law Master of Legal Studies website (which is regularly updated) to communicate the program standards to the public and to affected students. We will also use a comprehensive media marketing campaign to announce the addition of the health care courses to encourage a new audience to apply to the program.

learningOutcomes.name: Students should demonstrate fundamental knowledge and comprehension of the basic structure, function, operation, and role of the U.S. legal system. Students should demonstrate an understanding of the different branches of government; the relationship between federal, state, and local governments; the ways in which individuals and businesses interact with the legal system; and sources of U.S. law. Formative assessment measures, in the form of class assignments and quizzes, will measure this expected learning outcome in a variety of program courses, including Business Law; Comparative Legal Studies; Contracts in the Modern Economy; Conflict and Legal Crisis Management; Criminal Law for MLS Students; Government, Private Property, and Land Use; Lawsuits and Litigation; Labor and Employment; Legal Ethics in the Provision and Management of Legal Services; Legal Research and Writing for Non-Lawyers; The Regulatory System; Understanding Cases, Statutes, and Legislation, AI and the Law for MLS; Conflicts and Legal Crisis Management; Basic Mediation; Health Law for Non-Lawyers; Health Care Fraud and Abuse;  and Health Care Compliance. Summative assessments, in the form of final exams, will also be used in a number of these courses.

Students should demonstrate the ability to apply their understanding of the legal system to their chosen professional field. Students will be able to apply the skills they have learned in the context of their studies to applications in the real world. Assessment measures related to this learning outcome will take place mostly outside the context of the classroom. Students will receive oral and written feedback from College of Law faculty and from the staff as they progress through the program. Feedback will include insight on developing meaningful professional direction for life after graduation. Post-graduation surveys may also be used to measure achievement of this learning outcome.

customFields.ztYeO:
After consultation with faculty, staff, students, law alumni, local and regional industry representatives and thought leaders in the evolving fields of legally-related jobs where a JD is not required, the senior administrative team at the College determined that a degree in Legal Studies would serve future students, the College of Law, the University and our local and state communities.

The rationale for this new degree is multi-faceted:

First, people in a wide range of careers encounter legal issues on a regular basis. By gaining an understanding of basic legal principles, the functional areas of law, and their application in an interdisciplinary context, students will have a competitive advantage in the marketplace regardless of whatever career students elect. For example, human resource professionals routinely encounter issues regarding employment, labor and contract law. Business executives often deal with matters involving corporate law, risk management and regulatory compliance. Employees in creative industries encounter intellectual property issues. Health care workers often involve regulatory and privacy issues and government employees may be responsible for complying with administrative regulations or constitutional limitations. These and other professionals may not be required to practice in a court of law, but having familiarity with the law will help them understand the legal requirements imposed on them, recognize potential legal issues and prepare them to work with legal professionals when the need arises. In general, the knowledge and skills learned in the degree will be valuable to any student who obtains a job that involves writing, problem solving, research and critical thinking. The unique combination of courses offered in this degree are not found in any other major, either at the University of Utah or any other USHE institution.

Second, students with an in-depth understanding of the law will become better informed citizens and future leaders who will be able to utilize critical thinking skills in applying various legal concepts in their interaction with real-world societal issues. locally, nationally and globally. No other single major will offer such a broad based and comprehensive understanding of the law and combine that understanding with other disciplines.

Third, the degree will advance the University's goal of becoming a top public University in terms of societal impact by producing more graduates who enter society with a good understanding of the role of law in modern society and who are equipped with the skills necessary to be impactful in their communities.

The new degree enjoys universal support from across the campus and the larger community as shown by the multiple attached letters of support.

The intention is to monitor the results of that association and then either (a) expand the participation in the Hub to include the major when it becomes effective in the Fall of 2026 or (b) hire a dedicated academic advisor(s) for the degree who will work in cooperation with the existing JD academic advisors at the COL.

catalogFullDescription: The Linguistics BA and BS degrees provide a broad foundation in the scientific study of language. Students study the structural properties of languages, including the sounds of languages, their sentence structure, and meaning. They also explore how languages can vary, how they are used in different contexts, and how they are acquired by children and adults. Advanced courses offer deeper examination of these topics, and students have the opportunity to pursue research through their coursework, in independent studies, or by participating in research groups in the Linguistics Department.

catalogFullDescription: Designed to provide students with the skills and expertise to become leaders in an increasingly globalized job market by providing a formalized certification of regional competency and language skills within their chosen field of study. The Graduate Certificate in Latin American Studies will be available to all graduate students across the university, including MA and PhD students, and students in professional programs such as Law, MPA, Social Work, etc. The new certificate will provide graduate students from all disciplines opportunities to deepen their expertise in Latin America and its languages, while still allowing them to complete requirements in their primary discipline with minimal or no delay in their progress towards graduation. With the Certificate, graduates will be able to clearly signal to prospective employers that they have relevant language skills and expertise in Latin America.

rules.description:
• Complete at least 15 credits from the following types of courses:

    Coursework related to Latin America selected from at least two different academic programs or departments. Up to 9 credits of directed readings or a significant field research/study experience abroad may be used to fulfill this requirement. Practicum and internship experiences can also be used to fulfill this requirement with prior approval. Demonstrate intermediate-high reading and speaking proficiency in Spanish, Portuguese, Nahuatl or Quechua/Kichwa by passing an oral exam or completing a language course at the 3000 level or higher. Complete a graduate project (e.g. dissertation, master’s paper or thesis, internship, practicum, etc.) related to Latin America. In lieu of a graduate project, a student may complete an additional 3 credits of Latin America-related coursework There are no required classes. Students may choose elective classes from the full list of approved graduate classes taught across the university.

customFields.XwfIO:
Written Qualifying Examinations

The written qualifying examinations are given twice a year, in January and August, just before the start of the Spring and Fall semesters. A Ph.D. candidate is required to pass three written qualifying examinations chosen from the following set of subjects (corresponding course numbers are included in parenthesis):

  • algebra (6310-6320)

  • applied mathematics (6710-6720)

  • differential equations (6410-6420)

  • numerical analysis (6610-6620)

  • probability (6040)

  • real and complex analysis (6210-6220)

  • statistics (6070)

  • topology and geometry (6510-6520)

Each exam lasts three hours and is written at a first-year graduate level. Entering students are recommended to take the 6000-level course corresponding to a particular exam and use the course materials to prepare for the exams. Students with particularly strong backgrounds can choose to take the exams without taking the courses. Copies of past exams from the last ten years can be obtained by contacting the Graduate Coordinator.

Oral Qualifying Examination

This exam is conducted by the student’s supervisory committee and it can take one of the following two formats: a general exam to measure the student’s overall mathematical maturity and breadth, or a presentation of the proposed dissertation project. The exam also evaluates the student’s skill at chalkboard exposition and verbal exchange.

Teaching Requirement

Each Ph.D. candidate is required to teach a minimum of two courses or equivalent tutorials, or supervise laboratory sessions.

Final Oral Examination

This examination consists of a public thesis defense that summarizes the candidate’s thesis work.

catalogDescription: Master of City and Metropolitan Planning
catalogFullDescription: The Master of City and Metropolitan Planning (MCMP) is an accredited professional degree that prepares students to achieve excellence in guiding the growth and development of towns, cities, and regions. The core courses emphasize ecological resiliency, smart growth, and social justice through effective communication, collaboration, and innovation. The curriculum allows students to specialize in a variety of areas including affordable housing, community development, disaster recovery planning, ecological planning, geographical information systems, historic preservation, land-use, sustainability, real estate development, rural and small-town planning, transportation, and urban design. The program blends core knowledge and skills with specializations to prepare students for professional leadership roles in public sector agencies at local, regional, state, and federal levels as well as private consulting firms, and non profit organizations. Interdisciplinary work, drawing from fields outside of planning, is encouraged. The curriculum additionally features a community-based planning workshop and a capstone professional project.

customFields.9Nog3:
BA/BS Urban Ecology and Master of City & Metropolitan Planning

The BA/BS in Urban Ecology can be completed as a combined degree with a Master of City & Metropolitan Planning (MCMP). The BS/BA + MCMP is a “4+1” program through which eligible students complete both a Bachelor’s in Urban Ecology and a Master of City & Metropolitan Planning in five years. The 4+1 program combines the strengths of both programs, preparing students to think ecologically in guiding the growth and development of cities and regions both locally and globally. Please see our website for more information.

Dual Degrees

A student enrolled in a dual degree program will be able to earn two degrees in less time and with fewer overall credit requirements than if that student enrolled in each degree program independently. Completing a dual degree provides students with a competitive advantage in the job market.

Public Administration and City & Metropolitan Planning

The Department of City & Metropolitan Planning, together with the College of Social & Behavior Science, offers a dual degree program that enables students to earn a Master in City & Metropolitan Planning (MCMP) and a Master of Public Administration (MPA), simultaneously. This dual degree will prepare students for careers in local government, particularly in rapidly growing small towns and rural areas where administrators and planners wear many hats. Upon enrollment, students in the dual degree program will complete the core courses in both regular degree programs, totaling 60 credit hours. More information can be found here.

Public Policy and City & Metropolitan Planning

The Department of City & Metropolitan Planning, together with the College of Social & Behavior Science, offers a dual degree program that enables students to earn a Master in City & Metropolitan Planning (MCMP) and a Master of Public Policy (MPP), simultaneously. This dual degree will prepare students to be leaders in government, nonprofit and private sectors. Upon enrollment, students in the dual degree program will complete the core courses in both regular degree programs, totaling 61 credit hours. More information can be found here.

Juris Doctor and City & Metropolitan Planning

The Department of City & Metropolitan Planning, together with the S.J. Quinney College of Law, offers a dual degree program that enables students to earn a Master of City & Metropolitan Planning (MCMP) degree and a Juris Doctor (JD) degree, simultaneously. The subject of city and metropolitan planning in the United States can hardly be broached without directly incorporating some aspect of the American legal system. Similarly, a significant element of modern state and local government law involves topics and processes that are central to planning practices. Students enrolled in the dual degree program may count up to 12 credit hours of JD class work towards fulfilling the 48 credit-hour requirement of the MCMP degree and may count up to 12 credit hours of MCMP class work towards fulfilling the 88 credit-hour requirement of the JD degree. More information can be found here.

Real Estate Development and City & Metropolitan Planning

The Department of City & Metropolitan Planning, together with the David Eccles School of Business and the Department of Finance, offers a dual degree program that enables students to earn a Master of City & Metropolitan Planning (MCMP) degree and a Master of Real Estate Development (MRED) degree, simultaneously. The MCMP/MRED program is designed for those students seeking to combine the planning and real estate development professions. Upon enrollment, students in the dual degree program will complete the core courses in both regular degree programs, totaling 66 credit hours (30 MRED, 30 CMP plus 6 electives). More information can be found here.

catalogFullDescription:
The undergraduate MLS program is accredited by the National Accrediting Agency for Clinical Laboratory Sciences (NAACLS). 5600 N. River Rd. Suite 720, Rosemont, IL 60018-5119. (773-714-8880; http://www.naacls.org).

The performance of laboratory tests and analyses by medical laboratory scientists (MLS) aids in the diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of disease and the maintenance of health. Medical laboratory scientists perform diagnostic testing in clinical chemistry, microbiology, immunology, immunohematology, molecular diagnostics, hematology, and their related subspecialties. This NAACLS-accredited degree program provides students with the entry-level knowledge and technical skills necessary to work as a medical laboratory scientist in a modern diagnostic medical laboratory.

Students interested in learning more about the medical laboratory science profession can enroll in the program's introductory course, MD LB 1010: Survey of Medical Laboratory Sciences.

The School of Medicine offers the following tracks for students pursuing certification as a medical laboratory scientist:

  • Traditional 2+2 - two years of general education and preprofessional courses (prerequisites) followed by two years of professional coursework upon acceptance to the MLS program. Culminates in a Bachelor of Science degree. Students may declare as a Pre-MLS major at any time, but admission to the MLS major is not guaranteed.

  • Post-baccalaureate - graduates with a previous bachelor's degree (or higher) in a biological or chemical science complete 18-24 months of professional coursework once accepted into the MLS program. Post-baccalaureate applicants with a degree in other majors will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis for completion of prerequisite courses. Students on this track complete the same professional course requirements as the traditional (2+2) track. Students pursuing a second bachelor's degree on this track must also complete university requirements for general education and a bachelor of science degree.

  • Technologist (categorical) - individuals with a previous bachelor's degree (or higher) from a regionally or nationally accredited college/university may opt to further their education and pursue certification in a specific content area. The bachelor's degree must be in a biological or chemical science, or demonstrate a combination of 30 semester hours (45 quarter hours) in biology and chemistry obtained within, or in addition to, the degree. Students on this track complete the same professional course requirements as the traditional (2+2) track within the selected content area.

Students seeking their first bachelor's degree (2+2 track) typically apply to the program during their sophomore year and begin the professional coursework in their junior year. Students may declare as a Pre-MLS major at any time, but must apply and be accepted to the program before they will be declared in the full major. Applications for all tracks are accepted December 1 - February 15 for fall admission.

Once accepted to the program, full-time students complete three semesters of didactic coursework (fall, spring, summer) comprising the first professional year. Clinical experiences (rotations) at local laboratories are completed during the second or final year of study in addition to a capstone correlations course and didactic courses in management, education, and research design. The professional didactic courses for all tracks run concurrently and are only offered once per academic year.

After completing all professional MLS courses, students must successfully pass a comprehensive examination administered by the program.

After completing all of the requirements of the MLS program, students are eligible to take a national certification examination, but it is not a requirement for graduation.

Eligibility

  • Completion of all MLS prerequisite courses with a minimum grade of "C-" prior to beginning the program.

  • Minimum cumulative and math/science GPAs of 2.5 on a 4.0 scale. Note: At the time of application, a combined GPA from all institutions attended will be calculated.

  • Submission of a completed application portfolio.

  • Selection by the MLS Admissions Committee.

  • Note that completion of all general education and bachelor degree requirements prior to starting the MLS program is highly encouraged.

Prerequisites: Completion of all the prerequisite courses is required prior to starting the MLS Program. All prerequisite courses must have a minimum grade of "C-." It is the applicant's responsibility to submit updated transcripts to the University of Utah for all transfer work.

Application Requirements: Applications to the MLS program are accepted through an online application system accessible on the division's website. Application instructions are available on the division's website by Dec. 1. Complete application portfolios received between December 1 and February 15 will be reviewed for fall admission. The following is an overview of the application process:

Phase One - Application Portfolio Submission

  • Completion of the online application form by the deadline.

  • Completion or satisfactory plan for completion of all prerequisite courses prior to beginning the MLS program.

  • Completion or satisfactory plan for completion of all university general education and baccalaureate requirements.

  • Current transcripts from all colleges/universities attended on file with the University of Utah by the application deadline.

  • Cumulative and math/science GPAs of 2.5 or higher.

  • Responses to provided essay prompts received by the application deadline.

  • Updated resume highlighting work experience, community service involvement, and leadership experience received by the application deadline.

  • Two letters of professional reference received by the application deadline.

  • Submitted application to the University of Utah (if not currently an active student).

Only applicants who meet the minimum requirements including submission of all required documents by the application deadline will be advanced for Phase Two review.

Phase Two - Admissions Committee Review

Complete application portfolios are carefully reviewed by the MLS Admissions Committee on the basis of academic qualifications as well as promise for success in the program and potential contributions to the profession. The Medical Laboratory Sciences Division adheres to the University of Utah's policy of nondiscrimination and equal opportunity in admission decisions. A personal interview may be conducted by the MLS Admissions Committee, if needed, to further assess applicant qualifications.

All applicants will receive notification of the Admissions Committee's decision by email. Admission is contingent upon successful completion of the prerequisite and general education courses with a minimum grade of C minus.

Students conditionally accepted to the MLS program must:

  • Complete a one time, non-refundable acceptance fee.

  • Maintain a minimum cumulative and math/science GPA of 2.5.

  • Provide documentation of immunizations status and/or approved medical/religious exemption, completed health history and physical examination form and negative screening result for tuberculosis.

  • Attend a mandatory on-campus orientation held the week before the first week of fall semester classes.

  • Pass a comprehensive background check and urine drug test prior to beginning their clinical rotations.

Students completing the minor will also learn how to critically evaluate results from these analyses and explore how the results are used by other healthcare practitioners in the diagnosis, treatment, and management of disease. Upon admission, each student will be required to meet with one of the division’s academic advisors to confirm the practicality and appropriateness of their plan for completion of the minor’s program of study, including pre-requisites for each class, as applicable. Additional meetings with the advisor are encouraged when questions or changes in the student’s plan for completion arise. One semester before graduation, the undergraduate program director or designee will work with the academic advisors to confirm completion of the minor requirements.

The proposed curriculum for the minor is in line with that of the existing major. The division’s academic advisors and the Preprofessional Advising Director within the Academic Advising Center were asked to review and comment on the proposed curriculum. MLS faculty anticipate substantial interest in the minor from students pursuing education and training in healthcare, such as those planning to apply to medical school, physician assistant programs etc. As such, faculty felt it was important to consult with the Academic Advising Center on the curriculum to ensure the minor could be completed in a timely fashion alongside major requirements, university requirements, and any additional pre-professional courses needed for this specific group of students.

The MLS division currently has two full-time academic advisors supporting approximately 200 pre-MLS students. The undergraduate program director serves as the academic advisor for students with full major status, which is approximately 100 students. At this time, it is projected that the division’s current number of academic advisors will be able to manage the expected number of students pursuing this minor per NACADA standards for advising ratios; however, the division is prepared to add an additional advisor and program coordinator to manage the MLS minor as needed in the future.

The MLS division has one full-time staff member responsible for marketing, promotion, and recruitment of students so the academic advisors would not be expected to participate in these activities beyond notifying the Academic Advising Center of any pertinent updates.

customFields.qeWTW:
According to the most recent data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), there were 344,200 Medical Laboratory Scientists (MLS) and Medical Laboratory Technicians employed in the United States in 2023. The BLS projects a nationwide need for a 5% increase in MLS Professionals for 2023-2033, which is in line with other healthcare occupations requiring a bachelor's degree. Approximately 24,200 openings for medical laboratory professionals are projected each year, on average, over the next decade. Many of those openings are expected to result from the need to replace workers who transfer to different occupations or exit the labor force, such as to retire (Ref 1).

Additional data from the National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, US Department of Health and Human Services, Human Resources and Services Administration (HRSA), projects an increase of 19% in demand and growth for medical laboratory professionals through 2030 (Ref 2).

The American Society for Clinical Pathology (ASCP) conducts a Vacancy Survey every two years to determine the extent and distribution of workforce vacancies within the nation’s medical laboratories. Since its inception, the ASCP Vacancy Survey has served as the primary source of information about staffing of laboratories for academic, government, and industry labor analysts. Results from past surveys have shown that laboratory medicine is a rapidly evolving field, and the survey has evolved in response to changes within the profession. Laboratory managers across the country continue to report high vacancy rates, with significant delays encountered in identifying and hiring qualified new employees. According to the American Society for Clinical Pathology’s 2016-2017 Vacancy Survey of Laboratories in the United States, the nationwide average vacancy rate was approximately 7.2% across 17 different laboratory disciplines (Ref 3). The 2020 survey report revealed that the COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted the staffing of clinical laboratories and the training of graduates entering the workforce causing the vacancy rates for medical laboratory professionals to remain high (average vacancy rate of 8.3% across 17 laboratory disciplines) (Ref 4) . The most recent survey, conducted in 2022, revealed an average vacancy rate of 14.8% across the same 17 disciplines.

Though the curriculum for the proposed minor does not satisfy the eligibility requirements for national certification as a Medical Laboratory Scientist, as the MLS major does, it may draw additional student interest to this field of study. Students with a prior baccalaureate degree from a regionally or nationally accredited university can apply to complete the MLS professional coursework at the University of Utah as a post-baccalaureate student. After successfully completing their program of study, these students would be eligible to apply for national certification and seek employment as a Medical Laboratory Scientist. Students who complete the MLS minor as part of their undergraduate degrees in biology, chemistry, and other physical sciences would have already completed the majority of the program's pre-requisites and some of the required professional coursework. These students would be given preference during the admissions process to the major and may be able to complete the MLS professional coursework at an accelerated pace.

References

1)     Bureau of Labor Statistics, U.S. Department of Labor, Occupational Outlook Handbook, Clinical Laboratory Technologists and Technicians, at: https://www.bls.gov/ooh/healthcare/clinical-laboratory-technologists-and-technicians.htm (accessed October 3, 2024).

2)     HRSA Health Workforce Fact Sheet. Allied Health Workforce Projections, 2016-2030: Medical and Clinical Laboratory Technologists, at: https://bhw.hrsa.gov/sites/default/files/bureau-health-workforce/data-research/lab-technologists-2016-2030.pdf (accessed October 3, 2024).

3)     Garcia E, Kundu I, Ali A, Soles R. The American Society for Clinical Pathology's 2016-2017 Vacancy Survey of Medical Laboratories in the United States. Am J Clin Pathol. 2018 Mar 29;149(5):387-400. doi: 10.1093/ajcp/aqy005. PMID: 29522068.

4)     Garcia E, Kundu I, Kelly M, Soles R. The American Society for Clinical Pathology 2020 Vacancy Survey of Medical Laboratories in the United States. Am J Clin Pathol. 2022 Jun;157(6):874-889. doi: 10.1093/ajcp/aqab197. PMID: 34864855.

5)     Garcia E, Kundu I, Kelly M, Soles R. The American Society for Clinical Pathology 2022 Vacancy Survey of Medical Laboratories in the United States. Am J Clin Pathol. 2024 Mar;161(3):289-304. doi:10.1093/ajcp/aqad149. PMID: 34864855.

The proposed Minor in Medical Laboratory Science aligns with the University of Utah’s Institutional Mission and that of University of Utah Health by promoting interprofessional health education and guiding students to a potential career path that benefits the community, locally and nationally. The minor is designed to engage with students from diverse backgrounds and to sustain the University’s highest standards of professional and scholarly practice. It will be maintained at the high standard of academic and professional quality that is now present in the Medical Laboratory Science BS program. Outcome measures for the undergraduate MLS program are publicly available at: https://medicine.utah.edu/pathology/medical-laboratory-science/undergraduate (Program Outcomes).

The proposed minor will be inside the University of Utah’s designated service area, and is not anticipated to have any adverse impact on other institutions in the USHE system. None of the other USHE institutions with Medical Laboratory Science programs are currently offering a Minor in Medical Laboratory Science. If approved, the University of Utah would be the only institution in the intermountain region to offer a minor in medical laboratory science.

customFields.afMfd:
The main questions that will be used to assess the curriculum are:

  1. Are the identified learning objectives for the minor program in MD LB and PATH courses being achieved?

  2. How are students performing in the MD LB courses compared to full major students, where performance indicators include exam and course grade distribution?

  3. Are students satisfied with the curriculum, instructional support, course content, and resources for the MD LB and PATH courses?

  4. Are there any challenges or opportunities for improvements?

 Qualitative and quantitative methods will be employed to collect data needed to answer these questions. Qualitative methods will include collecting and analyzing course evaluations for each of the PATH and MD LB courses and responses to an anonymous exit survey (see Appendix A - Draft Exit Survey). The exit survey will be sent out at the end of each semester to students who completed their final requirements for the minor. This process will be tracked and managed by the undergraduate program director or faculty designee in concert with the surveys already being managed for the bachelor’s degree program. A summary of the responses will be compiled for review by the MLS Division Chief, undergraduate program officials, and the MLS faculty.

Quantitative methods will include collection and analysis of students’ course performance indicators (e.g., exam and course grades) and assessment of student performance on specific activities aligned with the program’s learning outcomes in each of the MD LB and PATH courses (see Appendix B - Example of Performance Indicators). Students completing MD LB or PATH courses as part of the minor will be enrolled in separate sections from students in the full MLS major to allow faculty to carefully monitor their progress throughout the semester. This will also allow faculty to compare the preparation and performance of students in the minor compared to full major students.

Individual faculty members will be responsible for collecting and analyzing data for their MD LB and/or PATH course(s) and submitting the following information at the end of each semester in which the course was offered and had students actively enrolled as part of the minor:

  1. Course syllabi

  2. Course evaluations

  3. Faculty Teaching Report (FTR)

The Faculty Teaching Report will include a summary of the teaching methods, learning objectives, students’ performance indicators (grades, grade distribution, quality of work), performance compared to full major students, and course evaluations. The faculty writing the FTR will also include a reflection on how well the program learning objectives and course outcomes were achieved and the impact of previous revisions to the course. The faculty will also include their thoughts on what improvements should be made to address any identified deficiencies (see Appendix C - Faculty Teaching Report Example Template).

The MLS undergraduate program officials and the faculty member with administrative oversight for the minor will conduct a comprehensive review of the FTRs annually and provide a summary report for the MLS Division Chief, MLS faculty, and the undergraduate program’s advisory committee. These findings, along with a summary of responses to the exit survey, will be discussed at the annual faculty retreat (summer) with the MLS Division Chief, undergraduate program officials and MLS faculty members to determine the efficacy of previous changes and to identify any necessary changes and improvements to the curriculum that must occur for the upcoming academic year. Following discussion and consensus of the faculty, the undergraduate program director or faculty designee will create a written assessment report to ensure continuous data collection, analysis, and implementation for curricular assessment and development.

customFields.ztYeO:
We are proposing to create a new Major in Medical Humanities at the University of Utah, with the option for students to complete this major as either a BS or BA degree.

Baccalaureate programs in medical/health humanities are proliferating rapidly. While there were only about a dozen such programs in the United States and Canada in 2000, that number has jumped twelvefold to over 170 in 2024 ( see Figure 1 ). The interdisciplinary mix of health sciences, arts, and humanities appeals to students who are drawn to issues of health and illness, and want to explore those profound issues through the lens of humanistic and artistic methods and insights.

[Figure 1 included at end of the USHE Proposal]

Figure 1. Total U.S. and Canada Baccalaureate Health Humanities Programs (Source: Health Humanities Baccalaureate Programs in the United States and Canada, 2024)

Medical/health humanities programs attract and produce exceptional students. They can create well-rounded professionals entering the health industry (broadly understood) who are patient­ centered creative thinkers, ethically intelligent, and committed to serving a broad population of patients with diverse backgrounds. They cultivate essential skills for healthcare and beyond: empathy, critical thinking, skilled communication, an understanding of and ability to thoughtfully engage basic science and biomedicine, appreciation of structural inequities and how they impact health and illness. Students in medical/health humanities programs are more likely to be interested in clinical research, more likely to earn academic honors, more likely to participate in leadership and service opportunities, and more likely to flourish in post ­baccalaureate professional health education.

The University of Utah is uniquely positioned to offer a Medical Humanities Major. It is the State of Utah's flagship research university--one of the premier academic research institutions in the United States, with a renowned academic medical center on the same campus. It hosts the Center for Health Ethics, Arts & Humanities, which includes members from the Department of Theater, the Department of Philosophy, the Department of Pediatrics, the College of Law, the Department of Psychiatry, and the Department of Pharmacy. It includes a College of Humanities, a College of Fine Arts, and a School for Cultural and Social Transformation that are replete with faculty conducting research and offering classes focused on the humanistic, artistic, and social issues in and implications of illness and healthcare.

Medical/health humanities programs at other academic institutions are administered in a variety of different units--arts programs, medical schools, bioethics centers, public health institutes, English departments. There is no "field standard" disciplinary location; rather, it is dependent on the unique make-up of each institution. The Philosophy Department will serve as the administrative home for the Medical Humanities Major, and it is a natural fit for the University of Utah. Faculty in Philosophy affiliated with the proposed major are internationally-recognized scholars in medical ethics and the philosophy of medicine--among the central pillars of medical/ health humanities; they are long-standing members of the Center for Health Ethics, Arts, & Humanities with adjunct appointments in the School of Medicine; they are regular collaborators with clinicians and scholars in the university's health sciences programs and hospitals; they frequently teach health science students. The Department of Philosophy routinely offers very popular courses that contribute vitally to medical/health humanities curricula, such as Introduction to Medical Humanities, Bioethics, Science & Society, and Philosophy of Medicine. While the university's existing Medical Humanities Minor was initially housed in the College of Humanities, it proved difficult to effectively administer at the college-level, and so the Department of Philosophy was handpicked to take on that responsibility and the further opportunity to develop and administer the proposed major.

customFields.cJsXu:
At least 51 credits are required to complete this major. The number and distribution of required credits to earn a major was purposefully selected for three reasons: (1) to optimize the ability of combining the major with other courses of study, (2) to accommodate transfer students coming to the major after already completing one or two years at a different academic institution, and (3) to combine in one place all the impressive, medical/health humanities-related courses offered by the University of Utah, while simultaneously maximizing the different ways that interested students can trace their own interests through that range of courses.

Required Courses (6 credit hours)

Two courses are required of all Medical Humanities Major students: (1) Introduction to Medical Humanities, and (2) Medical Humanities Capstone Course.

The 3-credit Introduction to Medical Humanities (HUM 2250) course already exists and will continue to be offered at least annually and, if in sufficient demand, every semester. This course is a prerequisite for many of the courses in the major and must be taken prior to, or during, the academic year that the major or minor is declared.

The 3-credit Medical Humanities Capstone Course will be a new, upper-level course developed by the Department of Philosophy, specially designed for the Medical Humanities Major. The major requires the successful completion of a final project or course that integrates much of what the student has learned--a "capstone." This course may be offered to groups or individual students, depending on interests and availability of resources. The capstone may be scholarly ( e.g., original research), clinical/practical ( e.g., shadowing a clinician, therapist, clinical ethicist), or creative (e.g., original artwork or arts-based healthcare interventions) but must include a formal presentation of the work.

Core Area Course Distribution (24 credit hours)

In addition to the two required courses, Medical Humanities Major students will take two 3-credit courses from each of four Core Areas. These Core Areas and the disciplinary domains that they represent were chosen to reflect the breadth of fields that bear on medical/health humanities and will thus give all students earning the degree exposure to a sample of those fields. The four Core Areas are:

  • Arts and Letters

  • Culture and Communication

  • Ethics and Epistemology

  • Gender, Ethnicity, and Disability

Targeted Course Distribution (21 credit hours)

Students will also take an additional 21 credit hours from a targeted selection of courses or degree programs that add to the interdisciplinary nature of the Medical Humanities BS/BA degrees. There is flexibility in how the students choose those allied courses.

One example, for instance, is to go into greater Depth with an associated discipline and earn a certificate, minor, or a second major that complements the Medical Humanities degree. That could be a minor in Disability Studies or a second major in Biology or Prehealth. 21 or more credits from any of the Departments/Programs represented in the Core Areas of the Program Plan or Departments/Programs from the College of Science or any of the Health Science Colleges will suffice. (The Degree Maps below showing how a student could double-major in Medical Humanities alongside either Biology or Prehealth are examples of this Depth route.)

Alternatively, students can opt for Breadth and earn at least 21 additional credit hours with a mix of courses from any of the Departments/Programs represented in the Core Areas of the Program Plan or Departments/Programs from the College of Science or any of the Health Science College. (The Degree Map below showing how a student could earn a BA in Medical Humanities is an example of this Breadth route.)

Students may also request approval of allied credit hours (be they of the Depth or Breadth sort) from another Department/Program not listed above; they will have to make the case for how training in that discipline appropriately complements their Medical Humanities degree.

Special Tracks (not built below - unsure how to display)

Students may propose a special track of their own that fulfills the Core Area requirements with courses that are not listed in the existing curriculum. As the Medical Humanities Major is designed to be interdisciplinary, requests for approval will be handled on a case-by-case basis. Any special track must fulfill all area requirements, including required courses, and show a convincing difference from what is offered in the major.

Mission Statement

The Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine at the University of Utah serves all people and communities of Utah and the Mountain West by intentionally working to improve individual and community health outcomes and quality of life. This is achieved through excellence in patient care, education, and research by:

  • Purposefully educating physicians, scientists, and health care professionals to ensure compassionate, patient-centered care to all.

  • Serving rural and underserved communities by addressing social determinants of health to decrease health disparities among all people.

  • Engaging in scholarly research to advance knowledge, innovation, well-being, and health for all people.

  • Fostering a culture of respect and community for students, trainees, staff, faculty, and community partners.

Vision

To create an exceptional learning experience for our students to promote their development into competent and caring professionals. To achieve our vision of exceptional learning, we value:

  • Relationships built on trust and mutual respect

  • Talents and ability of each member of the learning community to contribute according to their talents

  • Responsibility of each member of the community to one another

  • Accountability towards professional standards, attitudes, and behavior

  • Respect for all of perspectives and the spirit of teamwork

These requirements are subject to change, please review the Spencer Fox Eccles School of Medicine (SFESOM) Office of Admissions website for the most up-to-date admissions requirements and deadlines: medicine.utah.edu/admissions/.

Bachelor's Degree: Those who wish to apply to the SFESOM must have completed a bachelor's degree at a regionally accredited institution in the United States or Canada prior to matriculation at the SFESOM. If an applicant does not have a bachelor's degree but has earned a doctoral-level (terminal degree) from a regionally accredited U.S. or Canadian institution that did not require a bachelor's degree for entrance, they may apply if they will earn or have earned this degree by July 1 of the year they will begin medical school.

Undergraduate Majors: The SFESOM does not require any specific undergraduate academic major. The degree may be in the discipline of the applicant's choosing, as long as required premedical coursework has been completed. The SFESOM recommends that students choose a major field for which they have enthusiasm and interest.

Required Premedical Coursework: Prerequisite courses must be taken for credit at a regionally accredited institution in the United States or Canada prior to matriculation to medical school. Premedical coursework prior to Spring 2020 must have a letter grade. Due to online courses being mandatory at most colleges during the COVID-19 pandemic, applicants will not be required to earn a letter grade to meet our premedical coursework requirements beginning Spring 2020. Applicants are encouraged to earn a letter grade when possible to impact GPA. Courses completed through regionally accredited online institutions, two-year institutions, and/or community colleges are also accepted. Acceptance is conditional pending successful completion of prerequisite coursework requirements.

  • General Chemistry: 2 courses completing a general chemistry series (incorporating both quantitative and qualitative analysis), including all applicable labs.

  • Organic Chemistry: 2 courses completing an organic chemistry series, including all applicable labs. Advanced Placement Chemistry credit earned with a score of four or five satisfies one general chemistry course of this requirement. AP Chemistry credit must be posted on the official transcript in order to be counted.

  • Physics: 2 courses with all applicable laboratories.

  • Writing/Speech: 2 courses must emphasize written or verbal communication in the English language.

  • Biology: 2 courses (1 course must be in Cellular Biology or Biochemistry).

  • 1 Course: Psychology, Sociology, Anthropology, Economics, or Political Science

  • 1 Course: Art, Music, Dance, Theatre, History, Philosophy, Literature, or Communication.

Medical College Admission Test (MCAT) and Grade Point Average (GPA): The SFESOM employs a matrix, applicants with MCAT scores and undergraduate GPA within the following ranges are encouraged to apply to our program: An MCAT Total of 494- 497 and a GPA of 3.80 or higher An MCAT total of 498-499 and a GPA of 3.60 or higher An MCAT total of 500 and a GPA of 3.00 or higher

*SFESOM does not consider MCAT subsections and will use your highest overall MCAT score in the matrix.

All applicants are required to take the MCAT within four years of their matriculation to medical school. Visit the AAMC MCAT Testing Calendar for specific dates, deadlines, and testing information. students-residents.aamc.org/register-mcat-exam/register-mcat-exam

Post-Baccalaureate GPA is factored into the undergraduate GPA. Graduate GPA is not considered and is not factored into the undergraduate GPA. Undergraduate GPA is calculated by AMCAS. To learn more about how AMCAS calculates GPA, please visit AMCAS Application Guide.

American Medical College Application Service (AMCAS): All applications should be submitted to American Medical College Application Service (AMCAS). Applications must be submitted no later than October 1st at 11:50 EST.

Admissions Requirements & Recommendations: SFESOM employs a holistic review process, meaning all aspects of the application are considered. Applicants must meet a variety of academic and activity requirements, as the balance of activities and responsibilities with school or work can be an indicator of one's ability to navigate the personal and professional challenges they may face as a physician.

Secondary Application: Applicants invited to complete a Secondary Application will be required to submit the application fee and all application materials by the deadline provided at the time of invite.

Secondary Application Materials

Secondary Application:

  • If invited to complete a Secondary Application, applicants will be required to submit the non-refundable application fee of $110.00.

  • SFESOM does not offer fee waivers, though will honor fee waivers granted by the AAMC Fee Assistance Program AAMC Fee Assistance Program. Applicants applying for AAMC fee assistance should submit their secondary application after the AAMC waiver has been granted to guarantee eligibility for fee exception.

Letter of Recommendation Requirements

  • Three (3) letters of recommendation are required, but no more than four (4) will be considered.

  • All letters must be submitted to the hyperlink: AMCAS Letter Service

  • Please refer to the letter types accepted by AMCAS

Prerequisite Coursework

Activity Recommendations

Essays & Statements

Residency

  • Based on an applicant's legal state of residence as indicated on their AMCAS application, the secondary application may require additional residency documentation and will be communicated to the applicant by the SFESOM Admissions Office. Please refer to our website for the most up-to-date requirements for applicants by state/province.

MD-PhD Program

Website: medicine.utah.edu/programs/combined/md-phd

The school offers a combined MD-PhD training program to applicants with an outstanding record of achievement and a commitment to a career in biomedical science. At least 3 additional years beyond the standard 4-year curriculum is required to complete the M.D.-Ph.D. program.

All applications must be submitted to the American Medical College Application Services (AMCAS) between June 1 and October 1 at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Standard Time. Applications to the MD-PhD Program are available for US citizens or permanent US residents only. We encourage applications from qualified students nationwide.

Current University of Utah MD students who wish to apply must submit their application prior to June 30 after the second year of medical school and must have approval from the School of Medicine Associate Dean of Student Affairs.

MD-MSPH and MD-MPH Programs

Website: https://medicine.utah.edu/dfpm/public-health/education/degrees/master-science-public-health/admissions
Website: https://medicine.utah.edu/dfpm/public-health/education/degrees/master-public-health/admissions

The combined MD-MSPH (Master of Science in Public Health) or MD-MPH (Master of Public Health) degrees combine clinical training with the perspective and skills of public health and preventive medicine. The MSPH requires 45 credit hours of coursework and is a research-based degree. The MPH degree requires 45 credit hours of coursework.

Students who wish to apply for the combined MD-MSPH or MD-MPH degree after initial matriculation into medical school must have approval from the School of Medicine Associate Dean of Student Affairs prior to admission into the program.

Applications must be submitted by January 15 after the second year in the MD Program. Students are required to take a Leave of Absence from the MD Program to complete the degree requirement. The leave should be taken between the second and third years of the MD Program. It is expected that part of the fourth year of medical school will be used to conduct research and write a required thesis or publishable paper for the MSPH degree.

At least one additional year beyond the standard 4-year curriculum is required to complete the MD-MSPH and MD-MPH combined degree programs.

A formal application to the Graduate School is required. If a student is accepted to medical school, he or she may substitute the MCAT for the Graduate Record Examination (GRE) requirement.

MD-MBA Program

Website: https://eccles.utah.edu/programs/mba/full-time-mba/concentrations/

The combined MD-MBA (Master of Business Administration) degree is offered through a joint program with the David Eccles School of Business at the University of Utah. The dual degree MD-MBA program links the MD degree with intensive management education, providing graduates a full MBA with focus on the health sector. This five-year program is designed for students interested in both clinical medicine and the business aspects of medicine, and it is tailored for individuals seeking careers in clinical leadership in the for-profit and not-for-profit industries. One year beyond the standard four-year MD curriculum is required to complete the MD-MBA degree program. The MBA degree requires 50 credit hours of coursework which is concentrated in the fourth year with additional courses integrated into the fifth year.

MD-MBA graduate students are prepared for careers in:

  • Health Management

  • Medical Doctor

Students who wish to apply for the combined MD-MBA degree after initial matriculation into medical school must have approval from the School of Medicine Associate Dean of Student Affairs prior to application for the MBA program. A formal application to the David Eccles School of Business is required during the third year. Requirements include three short essays, two letters of recommendation, and the Graduate Management Admissions Test (GMAT) or Graduate Record Examination (GRE).

catalogFullDescription:
Mechanical engineers play a significant role in designing and manufacturing all of the products and systems essential to everyday modern life: recreational equipment, automobiles, aerospace systems, airplanes, medical devices, robots, industrial equipment, power generation, and sustainable energy systems. The field of mechanical engineering (ME) is concerned with the mechanical, thermal, and fluid-flow aspects of all of these systems, including computer and feedback control of complex systems. As a mechanical engineering student at the University of Utah, you will learn the professional, technical, critical thinking, and communication skills you need to be successful and make meaningful contributions to this exciting field.

The ME curriculum consists of courses throughout the broad disipline including: thermal-fluids, solid mechanics, robotics/mechatronics, and design and manufacturing. The major is built upon primarily math and physics prerequisites and culminates in a year long senior capstone design course. As the ME degree is a broad foundational engineering program, students also have the option to complete an emphasis, allowing them to tailor their program to best fit their strengths and interests.

customFields.9VKoN:
Major Status

Students who indicate Mechanical Engineering as their University of Utah admissions application are granted Major Status in Mechanical Engineering upon admission to the University.

Students with a different major declared who want to change their major to Mechanical Engineering must have a cumulative University of Utah GPA of 2.500 or higher and schedule a meeting with an ME Academic Advisor to initiate the change. Students who have previously been dismissed from the major can only regain ME Major Status if they are readmitted to the major via the process outlined on the department website: https://www.mech.utah.edu/academics/undergraduate/.

For all students with ME Major Status, catalog year will be updated according to the first semester that an ME EN course (excluding ME EN 1020) was completed for a letter grade.

Enrollment Requirements

In order to enroll in ME EN courses, a student must satisfy all of the following requirements:

  1. ME Major Status

  2. All course requisites met

  3. NOT in "ME Advising Hold" Student Group

  4. NOT in “ME Dismissed” Student Group

Additionally, in order to enroll in ME EN courses numbered higher than ME EN 2010 Statics, a student must be in the "ME EN 2-5XXX Eligible" Student Group.

ME EN 2-5XXX Eligible Student Group

Students with ME Major Status will be added to the “ME EN 2-5XXX Eligible” Student Group when they:

(1) enroll in ME EN 1000 or ME EN 1010 - OR - 

(2) matriculate at the University of Utah as a transfer student with ME EN 1000 and ME EN 1010 already completed 

if they satisfy one of the following:

  • Less than 30 college credits completed after high school

  • Weighted cumulative and major GPA of 3.0 or higher AND no failed major courses

  • Approved by ME Academic Standards Committee after providing additional information via an online form

Students who submit the online form but are not approved by the ME Academic Standards Committee will NOT be added to the “ME EN 2-5XXX Eligible” Student Group. These students may ask to be re-evaluated for a future semester.

Students who are dismissed from the ME Undergraduate Program (for example, through the department’s Academic Standards process or for academic misconduct) will be removed from the “ME EN 2-5XXX Eligible” Student Group and added to the “ME Dismissed” Student Group. They will also lose ME Major Status.

ME Advising Hold Student Group

Students with ME Major Status will be added to the “ME Advising Hold” Student Group if they:

  • Do not satisfy departmental advising requirements (for example, Academic Standards advising or mandatory transfer advising).

  • Do not enroll in any ME EN courses during a Fall or Spring semester (and are not on a Leave of Absence from the University).

Students will be removed from this group when advising requirements have been satisfied.

ME Dismissed Student Group

Students who are dismissed from the ME Undergraduate Program (for example, through the department’s Academic Standards process or for academic misconduct) will be added to the “ME Dismissed” Student Group. A student will only be removed from this group if they are readmitted to the major via the process outlined on the department website: https://www.mech.utah.edu/academics/undergraduate/.

Combined BS and MS Mechanical Engineering

Students must fill out a BS/MS pre-screening form and meet with a grad advisor to be screened for the combined B.S./M.S. program one year prior to the completion of all course work for the B.S. in Mechanical Engineering degree.

After meeting the screening requirements for the program, some graduate course work and research (if completing the thesis option) is undertaken during the last year in the B.S. program. Two of the four required technical electives for the undergraduate program are taken at the graduate level (6000-level and above) and an additional two graduate-level courses may be taken during the undergraduate program (that are not counting towards the four required technical electives) and applied towards the graduate degree. Both the B.S. and M.S. degrees are awarded upon completion of all M.S. degree requirements, which is expected to be approximately 12 months after the completion of all B.S. degree requirements.

customFields.nHBHl:
The Mechanical Engineering BS is currently at 128 credits, but by Fall 2026 we will be able to reduce to 123 credits by doing the following:

  1. Removing 4 credits from the Engineering Math Sequence

    1. The current sequence is MATH 1310 + 1320 + 2250 + 3140 = 16 credits.

    2. The new sequence will be MATH 1310 + MATH 1320 + MATH 2250 = 12 credits. However, this is not as simple as cutting ME EN 3140 from our program of study because our students need some of the content that is currently in MATH 3140. The plan is to remove some content from 1320 and then move some content from 3140 to 1320.

    3. The Math department is unable to make this change for Fall 2025 because it will require coordination with other engineering departments and changes to course descriptions. The plan is to make the course changes for Fall 2026.

  2. Removing 1 credit from the CHEM 1210/1215 course sequence (currently 5 total credits).

    1. The Chemistry department is willing to create a 4-credit Engineering Chemistry course (lecture + lab) with a slight reduction in the lecture content and around half of the existing CHEM 1215 labs.

    2. The Chemistry department is unable to make this change for Fall 2025 because they do not have an instructor available for the new course (they have faculty members on sabbatical or retiring early). The plan is to start offering the new Engineering Chemistry course in Fall 2026.

We would like to ask for an exception to be at 123 credits because very few of our students need to take WRTG 1010 (GE-WR1). Mining engineers design, develop, and manage systems for obtaining useful minerals from the Earth. Successful completion of the undergraduate mining engineering curriculum qualifies the student for a professional career in valuation and development of mineral properties, design and management of mine systems, as well as in research and consulting. Research and instruction facilities include laboratories for rock mechanics, ventilation, mine aerosols, mine reclamation, mine water, explosives, and computer applications.

Program Educational Objectives

  • Graduates will ethically and professionally practice mining engineering or other professions

  • Graduates will value sustainability, especially the economic, safety, and environmental interests of their employers, colleagues and society

  • Graduates will be leaders who foster inclusive work environments and demonstrate a curiosity about cultures and diversity

  • Graduates will be effective communicators, good collaborators, and lifelong learners

The Department of Pathology participates in two campus-wide interdepartmental graduate programs: Molecular Biology Program and Biological Chemistry Program. Students interested in pursuing a Ph.D. in Microbiology and Immunology are recommended to first apply and be admitted to one of those programs where they are supported financially while they complete the requirements for their first year of graduate study. At the end of the first year, students choose a thesis advisor from and affiliate with one of the participating departments. For more information, see Bioscience Ph.D. Programs.

In exceptional circumstances students can be directly admitted into the M&I Graduate Program via a specific lab. To be considered for admission, the student should submit the following documents to Kim Springer (kim.springer@path.utah.edu):

  • CV

  • Transcripts from undergraduate and, if applicable, any graduate degrees

  • Personal statement 1-2 pages in length outlining previous research experience and detailing the drive to undertake a PhD in the lab of choice

  • Letter of recommendation / commitment from the PI of the chosen lab

  • 3 other letters of recommendation outlining aptitude for research.

If Direct Admission is deemed appropriate, the student will be interviewed by the Executive Committee of the M&I Graduate Program. Applicants should have an undergraduate GPA of 3.0 or more. It takes anywhere from 2 months to 6 months to complete paperwork associated with admission. While admission is preferred for a Fall start, Summer admissions may be considered by the Executive Committee.
