customFields.rfMyo:
The Middle East Center proposes to restructure our Middle East Studies Major (B.A.) program. Founded in 1960, for more than half a century the University of Utah’s Middle East Center and its associated degree programs were among the most successful in the nation, consistently receiving Title VI National Resource Center (NRC) funding. In the late 2000s and 2010s, the Middle East Center experienced a series of unfortunate setbacks. Ultimately, the cumulative impact of this period led to a loss of Title VI funding, faculty retirements, attrition, and a decline in majors. Following this period, significant portions of the curriculum as presently constructed have lain fallow. Many of the courses in the present catalog either require updates to reflect the current state of the field or no longer reflect the expertise of the professors now on faculty. Prior to 2022-2023, a significant portion of the Middle East Studies Major’s core courses were being taught by adjunct or non-research active faculty. Likewise, many of the program’s most basic courses were no longer being offered on a consistent basis.

Following the July 2023 appointment of the Middle East Center’s current Director, Chris Low, the Middle East Center and Middle East Studies program have undertaken several steps to ameliorate this situation. In Fall 2023, we submitted a 5-Year Plan to the College of Humanities with the long-term goal of returning the center and its associated programs to their former nationally and internationally recognized status with the intention of competing for Title VI NRC funding by 2030. In Spring 2024, the Middle East Center also hosted an “informal” external review of our programs by Jennifer Derr (UC Santa Cruz) and Marc Lynch (George Washington). Building on both internal and external assessments of our strengths and weaknesses, the Middle East Center has worked closely with Dean Hollis Robbins and the College of Humanities to recruit a new generation of world-class faculty capable of leading our programs into the future.

In 2022, the Department of History hired Chris Low, an expert in Ottoman, Arab, and environmental histories. In 2023-2024, the Department of History hired two more tenure-track assistant professors: Edith Chen, a specialist of Mongol Iran and early Islamic history, and Annie Greene, an expert in Ottoman Iraq and Jews of the Islamic world. The Middle East Center and the College of Humanities also partnered with the College of Social and Behavioral Sciences to recruit a tenure-track assistant professor, Yuree Noh, who is an expert in authoritarian institutions and elections in the Middle East and North Africa. In World Languages and Cultures, we were able to add a post-doctoral fellow in Arabic, Rawad Wehbe, a specialist in Arabic poetry. And finally, in 2024-205, World Languages and Cultures will also be conducting a search for a new tenure-track assistant professor in Arabic language and/or literature. Collectively this group brings research expertise and archival fieldwork covering Algeria, Iran, Iraq, Israel-Palestine, Jordan, Kuwait, Lebanon, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, and Yemen.

Building on this substantial wave of new investments, the Middle East Center now has been able to hire the necessary faculty to offer an up-to-date and more stable curriculum to students. With this foundational cohort of new faculty members, we propose to adapt our curriculum to better promote research-informed teaching and remold our programing to reflect the substantially changed face of our faculty and student demand.

In addition to the new opportunities brought by this burst of reinvestment in Middle East Studies, we are also making additional changes to better reflect recent college and university guidance related to total credit hours and elective pathways for our program.
customFields.QvDbS:
While the Middle East Studies Major and Minor programs contribute to a variety of the University of Utah’s core values, most notably, our curriculum contributes to core value #5: Global Vision and Strategy: “The U thinks and acts globally by increasing opportunities for students and faculty to engage in international study, teaching, research, and service.”

As a member of the Association of American Universities, the University of Utah is recognized among an elite group of North America’s leading research universities. President Taylor Randall has set forward an ambitious goal to propel the University of Utah into the ranks of the top 10 public institutions in the country. Even the most cursory survey of these distinguished groupings sheds light on a simple commonality: Virtually all top 10 or even top 25 or 30 public universities in the United States feature robust Middle East centers. We strongly believe that further enhancing Utah’s strengths in International and Area Studies would allow the university to better match the profile of our peer public institutions, putting us in a category with schools like the University of Arizona, University of California-Santa Cruz, University of California-Davis, University of Illinois, Indiana University, University of Michigan, University of North Carolina, Ohio State University, University of Texas at Austin, and University of Wisconsin-Madison. Given the Asia Center and Center for Latin American Studies’ recent records of success in securing and maintaining Title VI NRC funding, it seems entirely reasonable to believe that the University of Utah is more than capable of rebuilding the Middle East Center to a level befitting our aspirational peer group’s standards.

When considering the impact of our programs on the more local USHE ecosystem, the University of Utah’s Middle East Studies program remains unique in the state of Utah. The only other Middle East Studies/Arabic Major in the state is housed at BYU, a non-USHE institution. Even BYU’s presence is a potential strength, providing a supply of potential transfer students. Likewise, BYU’s continued collaboration with the University of Utah’s International and Area Studies programs, offers our Middle East Center a potential partner for consortium applications for Title VI NRC status in the future.

Utah State offers Arabic courses and a Middle East Studies Minor. However, their programing is composed of just 3 faculty members. Again, this small program offers opportunities to attract and accommodate transfer students.

SLCC also offers Beginning and Intermediate Arabic. Here again, we have transfer agreements in place and our advising staff is experienced in accommodating the needs of SLCC transfer students.

Utah Valley University, Weber State, and Southern Utah University do not offer Arabic, Persian, or Middle East Studies. However, we believe that Weber State International Studies students or Utah Valley University students in National Security Studies might very well present transfer student opportunities or benefit from the content that we bring to University of Utah programs like International Studies and Diplomacy.
customFields.mZ2ZM: As with the existing Middle East Studies Major, these curriculum revisions will share the existing curricular and advising infrastructure of the International and Area Studies suite. This cross-program sharing with International Studies, Diplomacy, Asian Studies, and Latin American Studies saves countless resources (staff, office space, etc.). No new financial commitments are necessary for the proposed changes.

There is ample advising capacity to handle the changes required to update the Middle East Studies Major. Here, we have already received support from our most experienced Middle East Studies advisor, Amanda Jarvis. Advisors will not be expected to participate in any new marketing, promotion, or recruitment initiatives.
customFields.JKHAJ: Since the appointment of Chris Low as Director of the Middle East Center and Middle East Studies program in July 2023, Dean Hollis Robbins has worked closely with us on a revitalization plan. In Fall 2024, Low held a meeting of Middle East Center faculty affiliates to solicit suggestions for rebuilding plans. Low also submitted a 5-Year Plan to the College of Humanities. In March 2024, the Middle East Center hosted an “informal” external review. During the reviewers’ visit, meetings were held with affiliate faculty members to discuss both our programs’ strengths and weaknesses and to plan for future hiring and curricular revisions. In Summer and Fall 2024, Director Low met individually with core members of the affiliate faculty, especially our critical new hires, to discuss how best to revise the curriculum to highlight their respective strengths and continue to build the program. Likewise, feedback was solicited from partner departments, especially History, where the bulk of our recent hiring and required curricular changes will necessarily occur, including those reflected here and plans for further maintenance that we anticipate in the future. Feedback was also solicited from Mike Middleton, Associate Dean for Academic Affairs. In addition to recent individualized consultations with participating faculty, this proposal has been circulated to the chairs and directors of History, International Studies, Political Science, and World Languages and Cultures for their feedback and required letters of support. This proposal has also received unanimous support from the College of Humanities Curriculum Committee.
customFields.7nJtQ:
Job opportunities for Middle East Studies majors in the U.S. are diverse. Graduates often find roles in government, military, international relations, and non-profit organizations. Common career paths include roles in diplomacy, national security, intelligence analysis, and international development. Agencies such as the U.S. Department of State, CIA, and USAID are frequent employers of individuals with expertise in the Middle East. These roles often require additional skills in languages, research, and policy analysis.

Other promising fields include translation and interpretation, especially with the growing demand for global communication. Additionally, non-governmental organizations (NGOs) and think tanks, such as the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), offer internships and jobs in policy analysis and research focusing on Middle Eastern geopolitics. The demand for area specialists also extends into secondary education, academia, international business, and even media.

Salaries for such positions vary widely, of course, especially when comparing disparate positions globally. But domestically, among those with 4-year degrees, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, median salaries for graduates with adjacent degrees include: Foreign Languages ($60,000/year) and Culture and Gender Studies ($63,000). However, given the demand for national-security-related roles Middle East Studies majors are also competitive for similar jobs to Political Science majors with median earning potential of $123,000/year. Similarly, entry-level salaries in areas related to Diplomacy average approximately $85,000/year.

Beginning in 2025-2026, the entire International and Area Studies suite, including International Studies, Diplomacy, Middle East Studies, Asian Studies, and Latin American Studies, will be implementing a shared Foundational Core Curriculum, anchored by the creation of INTL: 3000: Foundations for International Studies.

Every second year, faculty drawn from the Faculty Advisory Committees for International and Area Studies will constitute an Undergraduate Assessment Committee (UAC) to undertake learning outcomes assessment. UAC assessments will be based on completed student assignments (“artifacts”) selected at random from required courses spread across the Middle East Studies curriculum using the Learning Outcomes Associator Tool in Canvas. For learning outcome 1, data will be drawn from the Arabic or Persian coursework (1010-2020) in World Languages and Cultures required to achieve Language Proficiency. In an ideal scenario, we would be equipped to assess the expansion of students’ language abilities through standardized, language-specific proficiency testing performed at the beginning and the completion of each student’s degree program. However, this is not practical due to the challenging logistics and significant costs of administering language proficiency tests. Accordingly, we must rely upon records of students’ language course completion and assessment of their performance in these courses. Since many language courses include achievement of proficiency goals as learning objectives within their syllabi, successful course completion is indicative of gains in language ability. Thus, degree audit documents will be used to assess learning outcome 1. This process mirrors procedures already followed by Asian Studies.

For learning outcomes 2 and 4: Global Awareness and International Career Readiness and Interdisciplinary Analytical Skills, artifacts will be drawn from INTL 3000.

For learning outcome 3: Cultural and Historical Competence, artifacts will be drawn from HIST 1450 and HIST 1460. Like INTL 3000, these required History courses will capture the full cross-section of Middle East Studies students.

The UAC scores the evidence for each learning outcome on a scale of 0 to 4 as follows, with each assignment in the sample set for each outcome read by at least two committee members:

  • 4 Excellent mastery

  • 3 Good mastery

  • 2 Some mastery 1 Minimal mastery

  • 0 No mastery

The UAC then provides the data generated through this process to the director for analysis and the writing of a report that reflects UAC findings.

catalogFullDescription: The Department of Molecular Pharmaceutics offers a Ph.D. degree program through the Graduate School of the University of Utah. The program seeks to prepare graduate students to function independently, competently and technically in a variety of settings including academic, research, administrative, business management, legal, regulatory and investment career tracks. This goal is accomplished through formal didactic courses, seminars and journal clubs, laboratory research rotations, and dissertation research. Every attempt is made by the faculty to help the student complete the program in a timely fashion. Typically, students graduate within 5 years of entering the program, although the nature of some projects and approaches requires a longer time commitment for full completion of the dissertation work.

All applicants are required to use the Apply Yourself online application system through the Admissions Office. Below is a list of materials you will need to complete the process.

  • Academic Transcripts. Official copies of transcripts from all colleges and universities attended should be sent directly by the institution (not the applicant). For foreign institutions, include official transcripts in the original language, plus official English translations if the original language is not English.

  • GRE Scores. An official report of scores from the General Test of the Graduate Record Exam (GRE) should be sent directly by the Educational Testing Service (ETS) to the Admissions Office. Use the institutional code for the University of Utah, 4853, and the department code for Pharmaceutical Chemistry, 0613.

  • Letters of Reference. We require at least three letters of personal reference from course instructors, research supervisors, or employers who are directly familiar with your abilities and performance. The recommender may use the Apply Yourself online system

  • Personal Statement. A two-page personal statement (approximately 500 words) outlining your background, research interests (including possible faculty research advisors), goals, and reasons for applying to our graduate program, even for specific areas of research.

  • Potential Areas of Research. Applicants should choose among the areas of research offered. See also our research page, and look up individual faculty members by areas of research here.

For international students only:

TOEFL scores. An official report of scores from the Test of English as a Foreign Language (TOEFL) is required and should be directly sent to the Admissions Office. You will need to use code 4853 for the International Admissions Office.

For students requesting an I-20 Certificate of Eligibility, the following will need to be provided by the applicant:

  1. A financial statement with supporting documents showing a minimum amount in U.S. dollars to cover the first year tuition and living expenses is required.

  2. A copy of the first page of applicant’s current passport or national ID card.

Admission Standards

Applicants must have received, prior to commencing graduate study, a bachelor’s degree from an accredited institute, college, or university.

Requirements include a B.S. degree in

  • Pharmacy

  • Chemistry

  • Biology

  • Chemical engineering

  • Related areas

Applicants are expected to have mastered basic material and fulfilled the prerequisites in the following areas:

  • One year of Organic chemistry with laboratories

  • One year of Physical chemistry

  • One year of Calculus

  • One semester of anatomy, cell biology, developmental biology, classical genetics, or physiology

All aspects of an application will be seriously considered during the evaluation process. However, students should have a grade point average equivalent to 3.0 or better on a 4-point scale. International students should have a minimum TOEFL score of 550 on the paper-based test, or a 100 (recommended) on the computer-based test out of a 120-point scale. Average GRE scores are approximately 158 (verbal), 160 (quantitative), 4.5 (analytical).

catalogFullDescription: The doctoral degree in Metropolitan Planning, Policy and Design helps meet society's need for researchers, scholars, teachers, and leaders to make our metropolitan areas sustainable and resilient. The planning challenge is to anticipate change and learn how best to manage it; the policy challenge is how to craft and implement policies needed to facilitate desired change, and the design challenge is how to shape the built environment to achieve desired outcomes. The degree program is managed by the Department of City & Metropolitan Planning and is designed to facilitate the interdisciplinary culture of the University of Utah. The doctoral degree includes core courses, electives, qualifying examination, proposal and dissertation benchmarks. The total number of credits needed to graduate is 55 with a master's degree in planning, 58 with a master's degree in another field and 76 without a master's degree.

customFields.9VKoN:
We have a selective doctoral program. Students entering the program will demonstrate a clear purpose in pursuing doctoral studies; this assures direction in students' doctoral work. In addition, students' interests will be highly correlated with several faculty members to assure a critical mass of mentoring. The objective is to assemble a group of highly motivated, self-directed, and talented students who show great promise to complete the degree and succeed in society after graduation.

Applicants are normally expected to have a master's degree in or related broadly to the fields of planning, policy, and/or design; but this will not be exclusive. The Doctoral Admissions Committee carefully screens all applications. At least one faculty member must agree to supervise an applicant whose record meets admissions requirements before they will receive a formal offer of admission.

For more information, go to the department's Ph.D. Admissions Page.
customFields.XwfIO:
Program of Study

Planning Foundation (0-24 credits): For students with an accredited planning master's degree from Utah or elsewhere, the planning foundation core is waived. For students with a master's degree in another area from Utah or elsewhere, the graduate planning core is waived except for CMP7100 - Urban & Planning Theory. For those without a graduate degree, the Master of City & Metropolitan Planning core is required. For most students, completing the core planning courses will require the equivalent of about one full academic year of study.

Doctoral Foundation (16 credits): The doctoral foundation is composed of 4 semester-long doctoral seminars: CMP7840 Advanced Planning Theory, CMP7401 Research Design, CMP7302 Qualitative Methods, CMP7022 Quantitative Methods in Planning. Students must also take 4 semesters of CMP7501 Ph.D. Research Seminar in the first two years of the program; however, students are expected to participate in the seminar as advanced students.

Electives (12 credits): Elective courses are selected in consultation with the Supervisory Committee and should be selected to deepen knowledge in substantive areas related to the dissertation project. While a minimum number of credits are expected, this may vary depending on the level of preparation by the student as determined by the Supervisory Committee. The courses can be taken inside or outside of the department and must be numbered 6000 and above.

Qualifying Examination (6 credits): Advancing to candidacy requires completing course work and passing the qualifying exam. The qualifying (or preliminary) examination requires the student to produce a scholarly piece of work that is of publishable quality. Students are required to take at least 6 credit hours of CMP7930 to prepare for the qualifying exam. The paper is the written portion of the exam. In the oral exam, the student presents the paper and responds to questions posed by the Supervisory Committee. Students must complete the qualifying exam by the end of the 4th year to remain in good academic standing, however, most students finish this exam by the 3rd year.

Dissertation Research Proposal (3 credits): Ph.D. candidates will prepare and defend their proposal for a dissertation based on the plan and format negotiated with the Supervisory Committee. The design for the proposal may begin at any time. Students are required to take at least 3 credit hours of CMP7940-Dissertation Research Proposal while they are writing the dissertation proposal. Students must pass the proposal exam by the end of the 4th year to remain in good academic standing, however, most students finish this exam by the 3rd year. Dissertation (18 credits) After a student defends the dissertation proposal the student is considered to be “all but dissertation” (ABD). Students must be ABD to enroll in CMP7970: Dissertation. A minimum of 18 credit hours is required. Students are required to write and defend their dissertation in order to graduate from the program. Typically, a dissertation is a written work on a singular topic, but a three discrete paper dissertation is also an option. All dissertations must conform to the formatting requirements outlined by the Graduate School Handbook for Theses and Dissertations. According to the policies of the University of Utah Graduate School, students must submit the defended dissertation to the Thesis Office.

Ph.D. Supervisory Committee: Ph.D. students should have their Supervisory Committee in place by the end of the second year which is the time it takes to complete the required foundational core and elective course work. Each Supervisory Committee consists of five faculty members. The committee chair and the majority of the committee must be tenure-line faculty in the student's department. One member of the committee must be appointed from outside the student's major department. The outside member is normally from another University of Utah department. The Supervisory Committee is responsible for approving the student's academic program, preparing and judging the qualifying examinations, approving the dissertation subject and final dissertation, and administering and judging the final oral examination (dissertation defense).

Continuous Registration: According to the Graduate School policy, “all graduate students must be registered for at least one course from the time of formal admission through completion of all requirements for the degree they are seeking unless granted an official leave of absence.”

catalogFullDescription: Materials Science and Engineering is an integrated discipline of chemistry, physics and engineering. This is reflected in our Program of Study. It is the one discipline within the College of Engineering that still gives the students the opportunity to study science while earning an engineering degree. Materials Scientists apply the principles of physics and chemistry to engineering problems, design and development of new materials. This application is a critical aspect of engineering, as virtually all technological advances are limited by the available materials. As a result of this challenge, Materials Scientists and Engineers are engaged in exploring the numerous ways that materials can enrich everyday lives.

customFields.nHBHl: We need to cut MUSC 2140 (Aural Skills IV) because it has a co-requisite of the 4th semester of Music theory (MUSC 3550 now but will be MUSC 2120 in F2025) which is not required for the BA, and it is not intended to function as an independent course, so we are eliminating it. We have decided to add MUSC 4486 (Global Music Ensemble) and MUSC 4436 (Electroacoustic Ensemble) to the Chamber Ensembles category to make it more inclusive and allow more variety. The changes to the Music Theory Elective are necessitated by the changes to the Music Theory sequence of the BM core. In addition to MUSC 2120 (Music Theory IV), we have decided to include both MUSC 1100 and 1460 as options that could be taken before starting the Music Theory core sequence, for students who do not have previous music experience, as well as adding “or instructor permission” to MUSC 4560 and 4565 for students who have the skills and want a more advanced theory offering. We also decided to cut 3670 (History of Jazz) from the Music Theory Elective category, because it is not a theory course, and instead add MUSC 4570 (Jazz Theory).

learningOutcomes.name: The ability to hear, identify, and work conceptually with the elements of music such as rhythm, melody, harmony, structure, timbre, texture.
An understanding of compositional processes, aesthetic properties of style, and the ways these shape and are shaped by artistic and cultural forces.
An acquaintance with a wide selection of musical literature, the principal eras, genres, and cultural sources.
The ability to develop and defend musical judgments.
Students will become knowledgeable in music history, music theory, basic conducting, and aural skills.
Students develop skills and knowledge in foreign languages and in the liberal arts that will enable them to function in an allied field.
Students will become competent performers (soloists and members of ensembles).

name: Music BA

catalogFullDescription: The Bachelor of Music (BM) degree is an accredited professional degree in music. Students participated in a variety of musical performing opportunities from solo performance to chamber music to large ensembles, that vary depending on individual interests and area of study.

BM Core Degree Requirements

MUSC 2120 will replace MUSC 3550 and 3560.

 

Rationale: The core curriculum of the BM degree currently includes a five-semester sequence of theory courses that guide students through rudimentary chordal analysis and part-writing through to complex analysis of atonal compositions and largescale forms. In order to respond to the request to reduce the total credit hours for all emphases in the Bachelor of Music to a maximum of 120-credits, the Theory Area has decided to compress and revise the material covered in the original five 3-credit courses of the Music Theory sequence into four 3-credit courses. We performed a survey of peer institutions and found that this was not an uncommon solution amongst a range of possibilities. The primary change is that the content of MUSC 3560 (Form and Analysis) will be integrated into the other 4 courses, which has some benefits because it will allow students to study the largescale impacts of tonal and harmonic techniques on the formal compositional characteristics of the repertoire they are studying and analyzing. All degrees and emphases in the School of Music will be impacted by this change.

Summary of changes:

·      MUSC 1110, 1120, 2110, and 2120 will need to have updated course descriptions,

·      Eventually MUSC 3560 and 3550 will both be retired from use (after a couple years) and removed from the BM core

·      MUSC 2120 needs to be added to the BM core,

MUSC 2140 (Aural Skills IV) will need to have the corequisite course updated.

BM Jazz Composition

Cut MUSC 1570 (Intro to Jazz Theory) and MUSC 4970 (Senior project).

 

Rationale: The content of MUSC 1570 is more effectively covered in other courses offered to students in the two BM Jazz emphases (Composition and Performance). MUSC 4970 is redundant to MUSC 4505, so we are removing it from this emphasis.

BM Jazz Performance

Cut MUSC 1570 (Intro to Jazz Theory) and change Lesson levels requirements for Jazz guitarists to “Jazz guitarists take MUSC 1230 & 1231 (Jazz Guitar Techniques I & II) then 2000, 3000, and 4000 level lessons.” 

 

Rationale: The content of MUSC 1570 is more effectively covered in other courses offered to students in the two BM Jazz emphases (Composition and Performance). Since Jazz guitarist’s substitute MUSC 1230 & 1231 for their private lessons during their first year of study, it makes sense for them to start lessons at the 2000-level during their second year. This change will also ensure that they have an adequate number of upper-division credits.

This is our only emphasis that is still over the 120-credit maximum at 123-credits. Dr. Jane Hatter is in the process of applying for a GE-HF designation for “Music History I: ca. 750 to Mid 18th Century” (MUSC 3635/2635) which is one of the BM Core courses. This GE designation will reduce all BM degrees by 3-credits, bringing the Jazz Performance emphasis down to 120.

BM Vocal Performance

 

Cut MUSC 1890 (Preperf. Vocal) and reduce the required number of Ensemble semesters from 10 to 8.

 

Rationale: The content of MUSC 1890 is more effectively covered in other diction and pedagogy courses offered to students when they are further along in their program of study. The reduction from 10 to 8 semesters of ensemble enrollment is in line with other emphases. Also, we are now asking student to enroll in choir and Opera workshop for a least a year but allowing students to choose from those options for the other two years of study, which should help students self-determine based on their own interests and goals.

BM Instrumental Performance

Add MUSC 4437 (Early Music Ensemble) and reduce the number of Music Electives from 5 to 4.

 

Rationale: The BM in Classical Guitar Performance includes MUSC 4437 in the Chamber Ensemble category, so it makes sense to make this option available to all students in the other instrumental areas. The Music Elective category currently allows string students to take 2 courses (String Pedagogy and Literature) for 4 credits. In the future we hope to make similar courses available to students studying other instruments, and they would all be 2-credits courses. Eliminating the 1 extra credit beyond the 4-credits should help students graduate and there is not clear pedagogical reason for it to be retained.

BM Classical Guitar Performance

Increase the number of Music Electives from 3 to 4.

 

Rationale: This is to align the elective category the emphasis in Classical Guitar Performance with those in the other instrumental performance areas, which will all now have a 4-credit Music Elective category.

BM Organ Performance

Change the “Large Ensemble” category to “Ensembles” and add Chamber Music (MUSC 4430) and New Music Ensemble (MUSC 4435).

 

Rationale: This new label reflects the reality that the options in this category already include both large and chamber ensembles. To allow our organ students to find opportunities to collaborate with other musicians, we are also adding two new chamber music options (MUSC 4430 and 4435) to the available ensembles they can take to fulfill this crucial aspect of all performance degrees.

BM Piano Pedagogy

Cut FCS 2570 from the “Education Elective.”

 

Rationale: The courses in this category were chosen because they were both relevant to the pedagogical goals of this elective and fulfilled the GE BF requirement. FCS 2570 no longer has this designation, so we are removing it from this category.

BM Music History and Literature

Retirement of this BM emphasis.

 

Rationale: As anyone who wishes to study musicology at a graduate level can easily be admitted to a MA or PhD program with an undergraduate degree in music performance or another similar emphasis, we had decided to retire this emphasis a few years ago and we did not seek reaccreditation for the program with NASM.

catalogFullDescription:
Neurotechnology is a rapidly emerging field of deep technology at the intersection of neuroscience, engineering, artificial intelligence, and medical devices. Example neurotechnologies include brain-machine interfaces for virtual/augmented reality, implanted biomedical devices for treating neurological disorders, brain-inspired artificial intelligence, thought-controlled robotic arms, and biophotonic nanointerfaces for treating psychiatric disorders. Utah has long been a hub for Neural Engineering research, and workforce demand is now growing rapidly.
The Neural Engineering Master of Science degree builds on undergraduate STEM bachelor's degrees and provides students with specialized skills and knowledge within the field of neural engineering suitable for more advanced roles with higher salaries. Graduates of the Neural Engineering MS are also highly qualified for PhD programs in neural engineering, neuroscience, or related fields.

Students interested in pursuing a Neural Engineering MS Degree should apply via the University of Utah Graduate School application and indicate "Neural Engineering MS" as their chosen program. Students must be admitted to the Graduate School of the University of Utah as well as the Neural Engineering MS degree program. Admissions requirements are as follows:

  • A bachelor's degree in a STEM related area. Applicants with degrees from other areas will be considered, but students may need to complete additional work (e.g., math, physics, programming, etc.) to be prepared to take required courses.

  • Graduate degree applications will be considered holistically; therefore, specific GRE scores and GPAs are not required for admission. An undergraduate GPA of at least 3.5 is recommended for admission (the university requires a minimum of 3.0). Some exceptions are available, so students with lower GPA's can apply and explain their individual circumstances in their personal statement.

  • GRE scores are currently not required but may be considered if they will strengthen the student's application. They are recommended for international students as another way to demonstrate English proficiency and academic preparation and for students with a GPA under 3.5.

    o Recommended for admission to this program: TOEFL 90+, IELTS 7.5, 125 Duolingo

Applicants should also provide:

  • Names and emails of three people that will provide recommendations.

  • A resume or curriculum vitae.

  • 1-2 page personal statement.

  • Unofficial transcripts from all institutions attended.

  • Writing sample of recent research or publication (optional; recommended for students wishing to complete the thesis option).

These are minimum requirements and do not guarantee admission. The graduate admissions committee reviews all aspects of the application package before determining acceptance into the Neural Engineering graduate program. customFields.XwfIO:
The MS degree has a coursework option, a project option and a thesis option (all are a minimum of 30 credits).

Coursework option graduation requirements:

  • Complete a minimum of 28 regular course credit hours with a grade of B- or better in each course.

  • Achieve a cumulative GPA greater than or equal to 3.0 in Program of Study.

  • Complete a minimum of 1-2 Seminar credit hours (two semesters of a .5 or 1 credit graduate research seminar)

  • Successfully complete the final examination requirement: pass an oral exam administered by the M.S. supervisory committee or the written portion of the Ph.D. qualifying examination.

Project option graduation requirements:

  • Complete a minimum of 22 regular course credit hours with a grade of B- or better in each course.

  • Achieve a cumulative GPA greater than or equal to 3.0 in Program of Study.

  • Complete 1-2 Seminar credit hours (two semesters of a .5 or 1 credit graduate research seminar)

  • Complete 3-6 project credit hours, or equivalent combination of independent project, internship, or project-intensive coursework

  • To reach 30 credit hours, students may complete an additional project, seminar, or course credit, if necessary.

  • Successfully complete an approved public presentation of project.

Thesis option graduation requirements:

  • Complete a minimum of 22 regular course credit hours with a grade of B- or better in each course.

  • Achieve a cumulative GPA greater than or equal to 3.0 in Program of Study.

  • Complete 1-2 Seminar credit hours

  • Complete a minimum of 6 thesis credit hours.

  • Successfully defend the master’s thesis before the supervisory committee.

The University of Utah, as a longstanding leader in Neural Engineering and with support from Utah-based industry leaders, is well poised to create first-of-its-kind Neural Engineering degrees and neurotechnology certificates. customFields.afMfd:
The Neurotechnology and Neural Engineering program shares similar core goals amongst all its credentials, but the breadth and depth of the goals increase starting from the undergraduate minor and progressing through the Neurotechnology undergraduate certificate, Neurotechnology graduate certificate, Neural Engineering Master’s degree, and Neural Engineering PhD. Students earning the graduate certificate will be assured to have higher levels of achievement than the undergraduate minor or certificate since they are enrolled in the graduate classes, which have additional content to distinguish them from the undergraduate credentials. Students earning the Neural Engineering Master’s degree will demonstrate proficiencies in all core areas 1-4 below, and numbers 5-7 below. Students completing the Neural Engineering Master’s degree will choose core courses from all 4 core areas, as well as 2 electives from the same core areas, 1 seminar credit, and 3 or more project or project-intensive course credits. Master’s students in Neural Engineering will demonstrate higher levels of achievement in numbers 6 and 7 as they will complete more projects (through courses or project credits) and more in-depth research if they complete a master's thesis (thesis option only) or exposure to current research through the seminar course (all master’s students).

Outcomes are closely tied to the work completed (homework, projects, exams) in select courses such that course grades are a good indicator as to whether the students have achieved the learning outcome. To be consistent with the degree requirements, the outcomes will be satisfied if a student achieves the minimum “B-” grade in each class. Each of the learning outcomes will be assessed as described below.

learningOutcomes.name: Neural Interfaces: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the design, development, and application of advanced neural interfaces. Upon completion of this degree, students will be able to critically evaluate various neural interface technologies and methodologies. Students will demonstrate proficiency in analyzing neural signals and comparing single-unit to population activity signals in both the central and peripheral nervous system. Students will gain an understanding of biocompatibility as it relates to neural interfaces and will be able to discuss biocompatibility issues and how they relate to neural interface performance, methods for testing biocompatibility, and possible optimizations to increase biocompatibility. Finally, students will gain hands-on experience in the fabrication and testing of neural electrodes, biosensors, and microelectronic devices tailored for interfacing with the nervous system.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neural Interfaces: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Neural Engineering Lab (BME 7155) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME7155

learningOutcomes.name: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the analysis of neural signals and the techniques used for neural modeling. Upon completion of this program, students will demonstrate proficiency in mathematical and computational techniques for modeling neural systems, including neural networks, neural circuits, and spiking neurons. Students will gain hands-on experience in computational neuroscience, enabling them to construct and analyze models that replicate neural behaviors and phenomena. Additionally, students will develop skills in data-driven modeling approaches, such as machine learning and statistical analysis, allowing them to extract meaningful insights from experimental neural data. Students will gain hands-on experience with simulation software and programming languages commonly used in neural analysis and modeling.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Computational Neuroscience (BME 6005) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6005

learningOutcomes.name: Neurophysiology: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the structure and function of the nervous system. Upon completion of this degree, students will demonstrate proficiency in the anatomy and physiology of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system, including the organization of neural systems and circuits and the mechanisms underlying neural signaling. Students will understand experimental techniques for studying neural activity, such as electrophysiology, optogenetics, and imaging methods like fMRI and PET. Through critical review and hands-on experience, students will gain expertise in applying basic physical and physiological principles to resolve questions related to systems or cellular processes in the nervous system.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neurophysiology: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430) or Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience (NEUSC 6040) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME 6430, NEUSC6040

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroprosthetics and Neurorobotics: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the design, development, and implementation of robotic and prosthetic systems interfacing with the nervous system. Upon completion of this degree, students will demonstrate proficiency in various principles of biomechanics, robotics, mechatronics, and control as they relate to neuroprosthetic devices and neurorobotic systems. Students will have an understanding of neuroprosthetic devices that are tailored to individuals with neurological impairments, as well as experience in programming and controlling neurorobotic platforms using neural signals. Additionally, students will develop various hands-on skills in human-machine interaction, neural decoding, and closed-loop control, enabling them to create prosthetic and robotic systems that restore function and enhance quality of life for individuals with neurological dysfunction.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neuroprosthetics and Neurorobotics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics (BME 6440 / ECE 6654) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6440, ECE 6654

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroethics: Understanding of the ethical, legal, and societal implications associated with advancements in neurotechnology and neural engineering. Upon completion of this degree, students will demonstrate proficiency in critically evaluating ethical dilemmas and issues arising from the use of neurotechnologies in research, clinical practice, and everyday life. Students will gain insights into topics such as cognitive enhancement, privacy concerns, informed consent, data bias, and equitable access to neurotechnological interventions. Additionally, students will develop skills in ethical decision-making, interdisciplinary collaboration, and effective communication, enabling them to navigate complex ethical challenges and contribute to the responsible development and implementation of neurotechnology. Through coursework, case studies, and discussions with experts in the field, graduates will be prepared to address ethical considerations at the forefront of neurotechnology, promoting ethical practices and ensuring that advancements in the field benefit society as a whole.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neuroethics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by a dedicated assignment in each core course. The Neural Engineering Lab (NTECH 7155) will include modules on the cost of neurotechnology, the required regulatory pathways, and the broader topic of neurotechnology access. Computational Neuroscience (BME 6005) will include a data privacy/bias assignment. Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430) will include case studies related to specific neurological conditions and discussions of accessibility and societal needs. Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics (BME 6440 / ECE 6654) already includes multiple discussions surrounding ethics, including accessibility, privacy, and enhancement. Another assignment in this course requires students to critically analyze existing product claims for accuracy and misleading information. Finally, the Neural Engineering Research Group (BME 6470) will invite a dedicated expert in Neuroethics to speak each year and will encourage all speakers to include a discussion (or slide or more) on ethics as it pertains to their research.
learningOutcomes.justification: NTECH7155, BME6005, BME6430, BME6440, ECE6654, BME6470

learningOutcomes.name: Hands-on Project Experience: Practical skills applying neurotechnology knowledge to a hands-on project experience. The project can be achieved through approved project-intensive coursework, faculty-directed projects, projects with student clubs, or approved industry projects or internships. Degree students will apply principles from neurotechnology to real problems or novel questions to provide tangible results such as software, hardware, or data analysis.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Hands-on Project Experience: Projects will be evaluated by the student’s homework, presentation, and final grade in BME 5930 or ECE 3950 by Neural Engineering Faculty in the BME or ECE departments, if they choose to complete an independent project or internship. Many of the core courses and electives are project-intensive (as indicated on the curriculum table with an asterisk), so most students will achieve this learning outcome even if they don’t enroll in one of the independent project courses.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME5930

learningOutcomes.name: Modern Research Topics: Understanding and knowledge of modern topics of research in neurotechnology. Students will engage in research presentations related to neurotechnology and neural engineering from faculty and advanced trainees in the seminar courses. Students will synthesize and discuss research presentations. Students can also participate in journal club discussions to engage in current research in neurotechnolgy. Students completing the thesis master’s will also engage in their own high-quality research work with rigorous scientific contributions to the existing body of knowledge.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Modern Research Topics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student's homework, reports, presentations, and final grade in the Neural Engineering Research Group (BME 6470), Frontiers in Neuroscience (NEUSC 6030) the Neuroscience Journal Club (NEUSC 6010), the Biomedical Engineering Seminar (BME 6090), or the Electrical Engineering Seminar (ECE 6900).
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6470, NEUSC6030, NEUSC6010, BME6090, ECE6900

learningOutcomes.name: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the analysis of neural signals and the techniques used for neural modeling. Upon completion of this program, students will demonstrate proficiency in mathematical and computational techniques for modeling neural systems, including neural networks, neural circuits, and spiking neurons. Students will gain hands-on experience in computational neuroscience, enabling them to construct and analyze models that replicate neural behaviors and phenomena. Additionally, students will develop skills in data-driven modeling approaches, such as machine learning and statistical analysis, allowing them to extract meaningful insights from experimental neural data. Students will gain hands-on experience with simulation software and programming languages commonly used in neural analysis and modeling.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Computational Neuroscience (BME 6005) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6005

learningOutcomes.name: Neurophysiology: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the structure and function of the nervous system. Upon completion of this PhD program, students will demonstrate proficiency in the anatomy and physiology of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system, including the organization of neural systems and circuits and the mechanisms underlying neural signaling. Students will understand experimental techniques for studying neural activity, such as electrophysiology, optogenetics, and imaging methods like fMRI and PET. Through critical review and hands-on experience, students will gain expertise in applying basic physical and physiological principles to resolve questions related to systems or cellular processes in the nervous system.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neurophysiology: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430) or Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience (NEUSC 6040) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME 6430, NEUSC6040

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroprosthetics and Neurorobotics: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the design, development, and implementation of robotic and prosthetic systems interfacing with the nervous system. Upon completion of this PhD program, students will demonstrate proficiency in various principles of biomechanics, robotics, mechatronics, and control as they relate to neuroprosthetic devices and neurorobotic systems. Students will have an understanding of neuroprosthetic devices that are tailored to individuals with neurological impairments, as well as experience in programming and controlling neurorobotic platforms using neural signals. Additionally, students will develop various hands-on skills in human-machine interaction, neural decoding, and closed-loop control, enabling them to create prosthetic and robotic systems that restore function and enhance quality of life for individuals with neurological dysfunction.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neuroprosthetics and Neurorobotics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics (BME 6440 / ECE 6654) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6440, ECE 6654

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroethics: Understanding of the ethical, legal, and societal implications associated with advancements in neurotechnology and neural engineering. Upon completion of this degree, students will demonstrate proficiency in critically evaluating ethical dilemmas and issues arising from the use of neurotechnologies in research, clinical practice, and everyday life. Students will gain insights into topics such as cognitive enhancement, privacy concerns, informed consent, data bias, and equitable access to neurotechnological interventions. Additionally, students will develop skills in ethical decision-making, interdisciplinary collaboration, and effective communication, enabling them to navigate complex ethical challenges and contribute to the responsible development and implementation of neurotechnology. Through coursework, case studies, and discussions with experts in the field, graduates will be prepared to address ethical considerations at the forefront of neurotechnology, promoting ethical practices and ensuring that advancements in the field benefit society as a whole.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neuroethics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by a dedicated assignment in each core course. The Neural Engineering Lab (NTECH 7155) will include modules on the cost of neurotechnology, the required regulatory pathways, and the broader topic of neurotechnology access. Computational Neuroscience (BME 6005) will include a data privacy/bias assignment. Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430) will include case studies related to specific neurological conditions and discussions of accessibility and societal needs. Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics (BME 6440 / ECE 6654) already includes multiple discussions surrounding ethics, including accessibility, privacy, and enhancement. Another assignment in this course requires students to critically analyze existing product claims for accuracy and misleading information. Finally, the Neural Engineering Research Group (BME 6470) will invite a dedicated expert in Neuroethics to speak each year and will encourage all speakers to include a discussion (or slide or more) on ethics as it pertains to their research.
learningOutcomes.justification: NTECH7155, BME6005, BME6430, BME6440, ECE6654, BME6470

learningOutcomes.name: Hands-on Project Experience: Practical skills applying neurotechnology knowledge to a hands-on project experience. The project can be achieved through approved project-intensive coursework for doctoral students, as they will not complete a separate project. PhD students will apply principles from neurotechnology to real problems or novel questions to provide tangible results such as software, hardware, or data analysis in project-intensive coursework. PhD students will also gain hands-on experience through their dissertation research.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Hands-on Project Experience: Doctoral students will not complete a separate project, but many courses are project-intensive so this learning outcome will be evaluated by the student’s homework, presentation, and final grade in courses designated with an asterisk on the curriculum table.

catalogFullDescription:
Neurotechnology is a rapidly emerging field of deep technology at the intersection of neuroscience, engineering, artificial intelligence, and medical devices. Example neurotechnologies include brain-machine interfaces for virtual/augmented reality, implanted biomedical devices for treating neurological disorders, brain-inspired artificial intelligence, thought-controlled robotic arms, and biophotonic nanointerfaces for treating psychiatric disorders. Utah has long been a hub for Neural Engineering research, and workforce demand is now growing rapidly.

The Neurotechnology Graduate Certificate builds on STEM bachelor's or master's degrees and is also available to non-degree seeking students in the workforce who desire additional specialized training in neurotechnology. A Neurotechnology Graduate Certificate provides students with specialized skills and knowledge within the field of neural engineering, suitable for more advanced roles with higher salaries. Recipients of the Neurotechnology Graduate Certificate are also highly qualified for PhD programs in neural engineering, neuroscience, or related fields.

customFields.ztYeO:
The University of Utah, as a longstanding leader in neural engineering and with support from Utah-based industry leaders, is well poised to create first-of-its-kind neural engineering degrees and neurotechnology certificates. These stackable credentials will: 1) provide hands-on interdisciplinary training to meet workforce demands, 2) create a recruiting and educational pipeline to fuel enrollment and to retain the top talent in Utah, and 3) ensure Utah maintains and capitalizes on its unique position as a leader in neurotechnology.

Over a decade ago, The University of Utah spun off several of the first neurotechnology companies. Today, the neurotechnology market is seeing unprecedented growth and these Utah-based companies have emerged as global leaders. These companies need more employees with a unique interdisciplinary education that does not presently exist. Neurotechnology companies require interdisciplinary education that encompasses life science knowledge and hands-on engineering skills. Traditional neuroscientists lack engineering fundamentals and traditional engineers lack extensive neuroscience knowledge. Neural Engineering merges neuroscience and engineering to provide engineering solutions, quantitative methodology, computational tools to treat neurological impairments and solve challenges in neuroscience.

The Graduate Certificate will serve students with B.S. or M.S. STEM degrees and can be completed as a non-degree seeking student, allowing industry workers to complete it, or in conjunction with an M.S. or Ph.D. degree. Demand for this program is evidenced by strong enrollment in the core courses in the past 2-3 years:

  • BME 6430 Systems Neuroscience Spring 2024=17 students; Spring 2023=11 students

  • ECE 6654/BME 6440 Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics Fall 2023=37 students; Fall 2022=45 students; Fall 2021=40 students

  • BME 5005/6005 Computational Neuroscience Spring 2023=20 students; Spring 2021=19 students

  • NEUSC 6040 Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience Fall 2023=31 students
customFields.yVI7x: A program coordinator will be hired to advise Neural Engineering and Neurotechnology students, but since most students will be in the Electrical & Computer Engineering and Biomedical Engineering Departments, the Graduate advisors in those departments will be trained on program details through a training webinar led by the PI (Jacob George) and either the program Administrator or the new lab course Instructor, so that students don’t necessarily need to go to a different advisor to receive information about completing the certificate. A program handbook that includes all program details, sample curriculum, and requirements will be disseminated to the graduate advisors and interested students for reference. The proposed curriculum aligns closely with current graduate “tracks” in both Biomedical Engineering and Electrical and Computer Engineering which will help the graduate student advisors’ understand the program requirements. We expect approximately 5-10 students for each advisor at the onset of the program. These initial students will be existing students of the advisors, which will ease the workload of the advisor. Advisors will be expected to promote and recruit students to the graduate certificate program through introduction of the certificate to students in related tracks during annual advising sessions .

customFields.qeWTW:
The prevalence and incidence of neurological disorders are rising, and growing funding from private and public entities is fueling workforce demand. According to Precedence Research, the neurotechnology market is expected to increase 198% over the next decade. At the forefront of this explosion are University of Utah spinoffs Blackrock Neurotech, Ripple Neuro, Ripple Neuromed, Iris Biomedical, Epitel, and Intan Technologies. Graduates of this program will be highly competitive for industry jobs.

Neuroengineers combine skills from Biomedical Engineering, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Neuroscience, Computer Science, and Mechanical Engineering. The following are a list of job titles from job posting websites and neurotechnology companies that students from our Neural Engineering Program would be well-qualified for:

  • Neural Engineering: neural engineer, neuroengineer, neural data engineer, neuroscientist

  • Medical Devices: medical device engineer, medical device developer, regulatory affairs engineer

  • Systems Engineering: embedded system engineer, electrical/electronics engineer, quality engineer, research support engineer, senior/principal scientist, engineering technical lead, principal materials engineer, director of product engineering, mechanical and process engineering manager, manufacturing process engineer, systems engineer, systems support manager

  • Research and Development: research and development engineer, research associate/assistant, research scientist, clinical research scientist, project manager, research fellow, postdoctoral researcher/fellow

  • Computing: software architect, software engineer, data engineer, data scientist, data analyst, machine learning scientist, computational scientist, computational neuroscientist, computational biologist

Analysis of Forecasted Industry Growth in Utah: Utah Workforce projected engineering job growth from 2016 to 2026 in the state of Utah is: Biomedical Engineers (180 positions), Electrical Engineers (540 positions), Software/Systems Software Programmers (1304 positions), and Mechanical Engineers (1240 positions). According to Precedence Research, the neurotechnology market is expected to increase 198% over the next decade, from $12.82 billion in 2022 to $38.17 billion in 2032. This proposal will help attract this growth to Utah.

Our graduate certificate easily stacks with STEM B.S., M.S. or Ph.D. degrees from other USHE universities (minimum of B.S. required). Qualified non-degree seeking students from industry and with degrees from other USHE institutions can be admitted to the Graduate Certificate Program, and if they wish to continue their education, they can pursue Master of Science or Doctorate (PhD) degrees in Neural Engineering or a related STEM field.

To strengthen our partnerships with other institutions of higher education in Utah, we have budgeted travel costs for University of Utah faculty to give annual neurotechnology demonstrations and seminar presentations at partner institutions, including Utah State University, Utah Valley University, Salt Lake Community College, Weber State University, Utah Tech University, and Westminster College, and Brigham Young University. Reciprocally, we will invite students and faculty from these partner institutions to attend the Neural Engineering Research Group Seminar Presentations, the Utah Biomedical Engineering Conference, and the Utah Conference on Undergraduate Research. These events will create a pipeline of students for the Graduate Neurotechnology Certificate at other universities and they may also decide to pursue further, stackable credentials (i.e., the Neural Engineering MS and PhD) that are only available at the University of Utah due to its prominence as an international leader in neurotechnology research.

learningOutcomes.justification: BME6440, ECE6654

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroethics: Understanding of the ethical, legal, and societal implications associated with advancements in neurotechnology and neural engineering. Upon completion of this certificate, students will demonstrate proficiency in critically evaluating ethical dilemmas and issues arising from the use of neurotechnologies in research, clinical practice, and everyday life. Students will gain insights into topics such as cognitive enhancement, privacy concerns, informed consent, data bias, and equitable access to neurotechnological interventions. Additionally, students will develop skills in ethical decision-making, interdisciplinary collaboration, and effective communication, enabling them to navigate complex ethical challenges and contribute to the responsible development and implementation of neurotechnology. Through coursework, case studies, and discussions with experts in the field, graduates will be prepared to address ethical considerations at the forefront of neurotechnology, promoting ethical practices and ensuring that advancements in the field benefit society as a whole.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neuroethics: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by a dedicated assignment in each core course. The Neural Engineering Lab (NTECH 7155) will include modules on the cost of neurotechnology, the required regulatory pathways, and the broader topic of neurotechnology access. Computational Neuroscience (BME 6005) will include a data privacy/bias assignment. Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430) will include case studies related to specific neurological conditions and discussions of accessibility and societal needs. Neural Engineering & NeuroRobotics (BME 6440 / ECE 6654) already includes multiple discussions surrounding ethics, including accessibility, privacy, and enhancement. Another assignment in this course requires students to critically analyze existing product claims for accuracy and misleading information. learningOutcomes.justification: NTECH7155, BME6005, BME6430, BME6440, ECE6654, BME6470

Neurotechnology is a rapidly emerging field of deep technology at the intersection of neuroscience, engineering, artificial intelligence, and medical devices. Example neurotechnologies include brain-machine interfaces for virtual/augmented reality, implanted biomedical devices for treating neurological disorders, brain-inspired artificial intelligence, thought-controlled robotic arms, and biophotonic nanointerfaces for treating psychiatric disorders.

The Neurotechnology undergraduate certificate prepares students for internships and entry-level careers in neurotechnology, the medical device industry, research and development jobs, or to enter graduate programs related to neural engineering, neuroscience, and related fields.

customFields.ztYeO:
The University of Utah, as a longstanding leader in neural engineering and with support from Utah-based industry leaders, is well poised to create first-of-its-kind neural engineering degrees, neurotechnology certificates and this minor. These stackable credentials will: 1) provide hands-on interdisciplinary training to meet workforce demands, 2) create a recruiting and educational pipeline to fuel enrollment and to retain the top talent in Utah, and 3) ensure Utah maintains and capitalizes on its unique position as a leader in neurotechnology.

Over a decade ago, The University of Utah spun off several of the first neurotechnology companies. Today, the neurotechnology market is seeing unprecedented growth and these Utah-based companies have emerged as global leaders. These companies need more employees with a unique interdisciplinary education that does not presently exist. Neurotechnology companies require interdisciplinary education that encompasses life science knowledge and hands-on engineering skills. Traditional neuroscientists lack engineering fundamentals and traditional engineers lack extensive neuroscience knowledge. Neural engineering merges neuroscience and engineering to provide engineering solutions, quantitative methodology, computational tools to treat neurological impairments and solve challenges in neuroscience.

The Undergraduate Certificate will serve students enrolled in STEM B.S. degrees related to biomedical, electrical, computer, or mechanical engineering, computer science, or other related fields. Demand for this program is evidenced by strong enrollment in the core courses in the past 2-3 years. Several of these are graduate courses, but about 50% of the enrollment is undergraduate students each semester:

BME 6430 Systems Neuroscience: Spring 2024 (17 students); Spring 2023 (11 students)
ECE 6654/BME 6440 Neural Engineering & Neuro Robotics: Fall 2023 (37 students); Fall 2022 (45 students)
BME 5005/6005 Computational Neuroscience: Spring 2023 (20 students); Spring 2021 (19 students)
NEUSC 6040 Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience: Fall 2023 (31 students)

customFields.qeWTW:
The prevalence and incidence of neurological disorders are rising, and growing funding from private and public entities is fueling workforce demand. According to Precedence Research, the neurotechnology market is expected to increase 198% over the next decade. At the forefront of this explosion are University of Utah spinoffs Blackrock Neurotech, Ripple Neuro, Ripple Neuromed, Iris Biomedical, Epitel and Intan Technologies. Graduates of this program will be highly competitive for industry jobs.

Neural engineers combine skills from Biomedical Engineering, Electrical and Computer Engineering, Neuroscience, Computer Science, and Mechanical Engineering. The following are a list of job titles from job posting websites and neurotechnology companies that students from our Neural engineering Program would be well-qualified for:

  • Neural Engineering: neural engineer, neuroengineer, neural data engineer, neuroscientist

  • Medical Devices: medical device engineer, medical device developer, regulatory affairs engineer

  • Systems Engineering: embedded system engineer, electrical/electronics engineer, quality engineer, research support engineer, senior/principal scientist, engineering technical lead, principal materials engineer, director of product engineering, mechanical and process engineering manager, manufacturing process engineer, systems engineer, systems support manager

  • Research and Development: research and development engineer, research associate/assistant, research scientist, clinical research scientist, project manager, research fellow, postdoctoral researcher/fellow

  • Computing: software architect, software engineer, data engineer, data scientist, data analyst, machine learning scientist, computational scientist, computational neuroscientist, computational biologist

Analysis of Forecasted Industry Growth in Utah: Utah Workforce projected engineering job growth from 2016 to 2026 in the state of Utah is: Biomedical Engineers (180 positions), Electrical Engineers (540 positions), Software/Systems Software Programmers (1304 positions), and Mechanical Engineers (1240 positions). According to Precedence Research, the neurotechnology market is expected to increase 198% over the next decade, from $12.82 billion in 2022 to $38.17 billion in 2032. This proposal will help attract this growth to Utah.
customFields.wFFLu:
This program is consistent with the University of Utah mission, role, and goal as a Carnegie I research institution. That is, the Neurotechnology Undergraduate Certificate will contribute to undergraduate education, as well as the creation and transmittal of knowledge, through teaching, research, and service. Our undergraduate certificate stacks with STEM associate’s degrees or transfer coursework from other USHE universities, as long as students are admitted to and enrolled in a B.S. degree at the University of Utah. The undergraduate certificate cannot be completed as a standalone certificate or as a non-matriculated student. The program will not be offered outside the designated service area.

To strengthen our partnerships with other institutions of higher education in Utah, we have budgeted travel costs for University of Utah faculty to give annual neurotechnology demonstrations and seminar presentations at partner institutions, including Utah State University, Utah Valley University, Salt Lake Community College, Weber State University, Utah Tech University, and Westminster University, and Brigham Young University. Reciprocally, we will invite students and faculty from these partner institutions to attend the Neural Engineering Research Group Seminar Presentations, the Utah Biomedical Engineering Conference, and the Utah Conference on Undergraduate Research.

We will also encourage undergraduate students from other programs to participate in summer research experiences in neurotechnology at the University of Utah through the Rural & Underserved Utah Training Experience (RUUTE) and Summer Program for Undergraduate Research (SPUR). These events will grow enrollment in the undergraduate Neurotechnology Minor and create a pipeline for students to pursue further, stackable credentials that are only available at the University of Utah due to its prominence as an international leader in neurotechnology research.
customFields.71aB1:
The Neurotechnology Undergraduate Certificate is part of a group of programs, including an MS and PhD Degree in Neural Engineering, undergraduate minor, and graduate certificate in Neurotechnology, which will be funded by a recently awarded USHE Deep Tech Grant that will allow for the hiring of a program coordinator, an instructional assistant to create and teach a new lab course required by the program, and cover one month of summer salary for the grant P.I. The grant will also cover travel for recruitment and marketing, lab supplies and equipment.

The Electrical and Computer Engineering and Biomedical Engineering (and other affiliated) departments will continue to fund faculty and TA support for classes required for these degrees, certificates and the minor, all of which already exist and are taught every year or every other year. Existing faculty also agree to supervise the optional projects for the minor. The implementation of this undergraduate minor won’t require any additional funding to operate than that which is laid out in more detail in the MS and PhD degree proposals. In the event the USHE grant isn't renewed in the future, the ECE and BME have agreed to a conditional continued funding plan that is laid out in the attached MOU document.
customFields.XGV6t: We have assembled an interdisciplinary team of 23 neural engineering faculty, the majority of which come from the Departments of Electrical and Computer Engineering and Biomedical Engineering. All faculty will contribute to curriculum delivery, program development and student mentoring. All faculty have either PhDs or MDs and actively conduct research on emerging neurotechnology. The program PI, Jake George, consulted extensively with faculty and Chairs of the ECE and BME departments to determine program requirements and details of the administration of the programs (see attached MOU).  The programs were also approved by the respective curriculum committees and announced to the remaining faculty in these departments during a faculty meeting.  The Dean of the College Engineering was also consulted during the creation of these programs and is supportive.

learningOutcomes.name: Neural Interfaces: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the design, development, and application of advanced neural interfaces. Upon completion of this certificate, students will be able to critically evaluate various neural interface technologies and methodologies. Students will demonstrate proficiency in analyzing neural signals and comparing single-unit to population activity signals in both the central and peripheral nervous system. Students will gain an understanding of biocompatibility as it relates to neural interfaces and will be able to discuss biocompatibility issues and how they relate to neural interface performance, methods for testing biocompatibility, and possible optimizations to increase biocompatibility. Finally, students will gain hands-on experience in the fabrication and testing of neural electrodes, biosensors, and microelectronic devices tailored for interfacing with the nervous system.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neural Interfaces: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.

learningOutcomes.name: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the analysis of neural signals and the techniques used for neural modeling. Upon completion of this program, students will demonstrate proficiency in mathematical and computational techniques for modeling neural systems, including neural networks, neural circuits, and spiking neurons. Students will gain hands-on experience in computational neuroscience, enabling them to construct and analyze models that replicate neural behaviors and phenomena. Additionally, students will develop skills in data-driven modeling approaches, such as machine learning and statistical analysis, allowing them to extract meaningful insights from experimental neural data. Students will gain hands-on experience with simulation software and programming languages commonly used in neural analysis and modeling.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neural Analysis and Modeling: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Computational Neuroscience (BME 5005) or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME5005

learningOutcomes.name: Neurophysiology: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the structure and function of the nervous system. Upon completion of this certificate, students will demonstrate proficiency in the anatomy and physiology of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nervous system, including the organization of neural systems and circuits and the mechanisms underlying neural signaling. Students will understand experimental techniques for studying neural activity, such as electrophysiology, optogenetics, and imaging methods like fMRI and PET. Through critical review and hands-on experience, students will gain expertise in applying basic physical and physiological principles to resolve questions related to systems or cellular processes in the nervous system.
learningOutcomes.assessment: Neurophysiology: Learning outcomes will be evaluated by the student’s homework, reports, exams, projects, and final grade in Systems Neuroscience (BME 6430), Cellular and Molecular Neuroscience (NEUSC 6040), or an elective course of the student’s choosing from this core area.
learningOutcomes.justification: BME6430, NEUSC6040

learningOutcomes.name: Neuroprosthetics and Neurorobotics: Understanding, knowledge, and practical skills in the design, development, and implementation of robotic and prosthetic systems interfacing with the nervous system. Upon completion of this certificate, students will demonstrate proficiency in various principles of biomechanics, robotics, mechatronics, and control as they relate to neuroprosthetic devices and neurorobotic systems. Students will have an understanding of neuroprosthetic devices that are tailored to individuals with neurological impairments, as well as experience in programming and controlling neurorobotic platforms using neural signals.
